It occurs to us that a chelation enhanced sequential 
single electron transfer mechanism (mechanism c) can 
not be excluded. On the basis of these considerations, a 
plausible stereochemical course of the diastereoselective 
coupling reactions (Schemes 2 and 3) is depicted in 
Scheme 6. The initial chelating conformers could be 
represented by A1 (X＝H)/A2 (X＝Br) versus C1 (X＝
H)/C2 (X＝Br), which are valuable for mechanisms a－
c (mechanism b no shown in Scheme 6). The first single 
electron transfer from SmI2 gives the corresponding 
ketyl-radical anions B1/B2 or D/D2, respectively. The 
subsequent addition of the ketyl-radical anion to 
α,β-unsaturated esters gives E1/E2 or F1/F2, respec-
tively (mechanism a). Alternatively, due to the higher 
reactivity of both methyl (E)-methacrylate and methyl 
(E)-3-bromo-2-methacrylate, the SmI2-mediated cou-
pling reaction might pass through a sequential single 
electron transfer manner to give directly E1/E2 or 
F1/F2 (mechanism c). The conformations A1,2/B1,2 
featured the disposition of the olefin moiety at the 
equatorial position are less congested (and are thus more 
stable) comparing with C1,2/D1,2. This can account for 
the formation of epimers 8/9 as the major diastereomers. 
For conformations A2 and B2, further stabilization ef-
fect gains from orbital interaction between perpenticu-
larly oriented C－Br bond (σ*-orbital) and C＝O 
(π-orbital) bond or •C－O− bond. In addition, the per-
penticularly disposed dipole of C－Br bond and the ni-
trogen lone pair might provide yet additional stabili-
zation effect to the conformations A2/B2; while such 
beneficial effects do not exist in conformations A1/B1, 
C1,2/D1,2. Consequently, compound 12 was obtained 
as the sole observable diastereomer, while the C-9 
epimer of 12 was no observed.

Conclusions 
We have demonstrated that by using bromine atom 
as a traceless directing group, the SmI2-mediated reduc-
tive coupling of ketone 6 and β-bromo-methacrylate 
could proceed with complete anti-diastereoselectivity. 
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of 
applying the halo-directing tactic in the SmI2-mediated 
reductive coupling of ketone with acrylate. 
We also showed that without the presence of any 
α-directing (chelation) group, the one-pot reaction of the 
ketone derived from alcohol 15 with the organozinc re-
agent generated from bromomethacrylate afforded 
spiro-α-methylene-γ-lactone 16 as a single diastereomer. 
These two highly diastereoselective methods would 
find application in the synthesis of the spirolactone/

In addition, on the basis of our previous work,[7,9] we

Comprehensive Summary 
A three-component reaction of 1,3-enynes and cyclobutanone oxime esters in the presence of aryl boronic acids or organozinc rea-
gents via the photoredox/copper or photoredox/nickel catalysis has been established. This redox-neutral 1,4-cyanoalkylarylation re-
action has demonstrated mild condition, high catalytic reactivity and wide functional group compatibility, allowing access to a variety 
of functionalized tetra-substituted allene derivatives with high chemo- and regioselectivity. Moreover, using photocatalytic continu-
ous flow technique to promote this process would result in increased yields (70% in flow vs. 61% in batch), reduced reaction times (7 
min in flow vs. 6 h in batch), and easy scale-up (upgrade to gram scale), showcasing its potential as a synthetic platform.

Background and Originality Content 
Allene scaffolds are not only prevalent in active pharmaceuti-
cals, agrochemicals and materials science, but also recognized as 
an essential class of synthetic intermediates for various organic 
synthesis.[1] In this context, considerable attention has been fo-
cused on developing catalytic allene synthesis, and as a result, 
some elegant methods have been well established including mo-
lecular rearrangement,[2] nucleophilic substitution,[3] 1,4-addi-
tion[4] and other methods.[5] Compared to these classical ap-
proaches, 
the 
radical-mediated 
1,4-difunctionalization 
of 
1,3-enynes was considered as one of the most straightforward 
routes to introduce two functional groups simultaneously for the 
construction of multisubstituted allenes (Scheme 1a). Recently, 
the groups of Liu,[6] Wang,[7] Bao,[8] Lu,[9] and Ma[10] have devel-
oped the methods for the 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes 
via radical pathway. Despite such breakthroughs, there still exist 
several long-standing challenges in this field, e.g., the low reactiv-
ity of the starting materials, the requirement of nucleophiles to 
terminate the reaction and the difficulty to control 1,2- or 1,4- 
radical addition products, which still limit their further develop-
ment. Therefore, it is highly desirable to develop efficient meth-
ods for the radical-mediated 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes 
under mild condition. 
Scheme 1  1,4-Difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes via photoredox/transi-
tion metal dual catalysis  
 
On the other hand, the merger of photoredox and transition 
metal catalysis, termed metallaphotoredox catalysis, has emerged 
as a powerful tool for achieving synthetically valuable transfor-
mations,[11] among which, the most representative is the photo-
redox/copper[12] and photoredox/nickel[13] dual catalytic system. 
In this regard, metallaphotoredox catalysis has been developing 
at a great speed, finding remarkable applications in the 1,4-radical 
addition of 1,3-enynes. Very recently, the Lu and coworkers pre-
sented a photoredox/copper catalysis for the 1,4-carbocyanations 
of 1,3-enynes with alkyl N-hydroxyphthalimide esters and trime-
thylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN).[9b] Later on, the Li’s group developed a 
photoredox/copper catalytic 1,4-sulfonylarylation of 1,3-enynes 
using aryl iodides and sulfinate salts.[14] 
Despite impressive progress, there are still no reports on the 
1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes for the synthesis of the same 
allene derivatives using both photoredox/copper and photore-
dox/nickel dual catalysis. On the basis of the above-mentioned 
studies of the 1,4-addition of 1,3-enynes in the metallaphotore-
dox catalytic system and recent study on the ring-opening of cy-
clobutanone oxime derivatives,[15] we envisioned that the cy-
anoalkyl radicals produced by cyclobutanone oximes might initi-
ate the 1,3-enyne substrates and produce allenyl radical interme-
diates, followed by copper or nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling with 
aryl boronic acids[16] or organozinc reagents, providing a variety of 
tetrasubstituted allenes via different pathways. This protocol can 
efficiently facilitate the 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes and 
access to cyanoalkylarylated allenes with excellent functional 
group tolerance and high chemo- and regioselectivity (Scheme 
1b). Recently, continuous-flow photochemistry is gaining popular-
ity in both academic and industrial settings due to many ad-
vantages. Compared with the traditional batch process, photo-
chemical transformation in continuous flow reactor results in 
often faster, safer, and higher-yielding reactions due to factors 
such as easy amplification of effective energy transfer between 
light source and reaction vessel.[17] We hypothesized that the 
application of continuous flow technique may improve the effi-
ciency of this 1,4-cyanoalkylarylation process. If realized, these 
improvements will bring great hope for the application of this 
method in pharmaceutical industry and other fields. Herein, we 
wish to report a photoredox/copper and photoredox/nickel-cata-
lyzed 1,4-cyanoalkylarylation reaction of 1,3-enynes by the use of 
photocatalytic continuous flow technique, providing a wide range 
of not easily accessible but useful tetrasubstituted allenes under 
mild conditions. 
Results and Discussion 
Our investigation began with the reaction of 1,3-enynes 1a 
with cycloketone oxime ethers 2a and phenyl boronic acid 3a as 
the starting materials with the photoredox/copper dual catalytic 
system in a homemade continuous-flow photoreactor (details see 
Figure S1 in the Supporting Information). After extensive screen-
ing, the optimal conditions were achieved with 2.0 mol% PC-2 
[Ir(ppy)2(bpy)]PF6 (E1/2IV/*III = −0.85 V vs. SCE),[18] 10.0 mol% 
Cu(MeCN)4PF6, 
10.0 
mol% 
4,4'-di-tert-butyl-2,2'-bipyridine 
(dtbbpy, L3), 2.0 equiv of Et3N and 2.0 equiv of MeOH in MeCN : 
DMF co-solvent to irradiation with 395 nm purple LEDs with a 
residence time of 7 min, providing the desired tetrasubstituted 
allene 5aa in 70% yield (see Tables S1—S8 in the Supporting In-
formation). Slightly reduced reaction yields of 5aa were observed 
when other photocatalysts (details see Table S5 in the Supporting 
Information), e.g., fac-Ir(ppy)3 (E1/2IV/*III = −1.73 V vs. SCE)[18] and 
[Ir(ppy)2dtbbpy]PF6 (E1/2IV/*III = −0.96 V vs. SCE),[18] were employed 
instead of PC-2 (Table 1, entries 2, 3). As for the choice of copper 
catalysts, CuI and Cu(MeCN)4BF4 demonstrated lower reactivity to 
that of Cu(MeCN)4PF6 (entries 4, 5). Screening the ligands re-
vealed that L3 was essential in order to realize this unique trans-
formation. Lower yields were obtained when ligands L1—L2, L4—L5 
took the place of L3 as the ligand (entries 6, 7). However, use of 
other solvents, such as N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF), N,N-di-
methylaniline (DMA), methanol (MeOH), failed to yield the 5aa 
(entries 8, 9). The base triethylamine (Et3N) was also necessary for 
this reaction. A series of other bases including 1,4-diazobicyclo-
(2.2.2)octane (DABCO) and N,N-diisopropylethylamine (DIPEA), 
were also examined and found to result in lower yields (entries 10, 
11). Finally, the reaction was conducted under the batch condition, 
with product 5aa being isolated with 61% yield in 6 h (entry 12). 
Notably, the use of continuous-flow photoreactor could not only 
increase the reaction yield (70% in flow vs. 61% in batch), but also 
shorten the reaction time (7.0 min in flow vs. 6.0 h in batch). 
With a set of optimized conditions in hand, we explored the 
scope of this reaction, with a first emphasis on the variations in 
the 1,3-enynes. To our delight, a wide array of functional groups 
with different electronic natures substituents (R1, R2) at the 2- and

When the C2-position (R1) was phenyl substituted, different 
alkyl phthalimide protecting groups located at the C4-position (R2) 
presented no obvious effects on this transformation, giving the 
corresponding cyanoalkylarylated allenes 5aa—5ae with yields 
ranging from 53% to 70%. Other alkyl amine substituted function-

(R2) were also tolerated, leading to the desired products 5af, 5ag 
in 61% and 62% yields, respectively. Additionally, the alcohol 
groups (OBn, OTBS) substituted on R2 were also compatible for 
this reaction, giving the target products 5ah and 5ai in yields of 
45% and 50%, respectively. In addition, an array of phenyl 
(1j—1m) and alkyl (1n, 1o) enyne substrates were all generated 
smoothly, giving the corresponding allene products 5aj—5ao in 
43%—55% yields. Similarly, for the C2-methyl substituent of the 
1,3-enynes, a variety of functional groups, including aryl (1p—1v), 
heteroaryl (1w), and amide (1x, 1y) groups, were all well accom-
modated, to afford the corresponding products 5ap—5ay in 
35%—61% yields. It should be noted that when R1 was H-sub-

5az in 61% yield. 
Next, the scope of aryl boronic acids was evaluated. As ex-
pected, a series of aryl boronic acids bearing substituents includ-
ing Me, Cl, Br, and OBn groups, located on the ortho-, meta- as 
well as para-substituents of the phenyl ring were also suitable for 
this transformation, affording the target products 5ba—5bg in 
50%—71% yields. Encouraged by these results, we then turned 
our attention to examination of the scope of cyclobutanone 
O-benzoyl oximes. Notably, the 3- or 4-monosubstituted cyclobu-
tanone O-benzoyl oximes bearing Me, Et, Bn, Ph, 4-ClPh, CO2tBu 
and OBn groups underwent this radical cyanoalkylarylation reac-
tion efficiently to give the products 5ca—5cg in 40%—53% yields. 
Moreover, 3,3-disubstituted cyclobutanone derivatives were 
well-tolerated, and gave the expected products 5ch, 5ci in 61% 
and 72% yields, respectively. In addition, heterocyclobutan-3-one 
oxime esters (O) oximes were also compatible with this reaction, 
generating the tetrasubstituted allene 5cj in 50% yield (Table 3). 
Currently, the photoredox/nickel-catalyzed reactions used to 
perform multicomponent difunctionalization of unsaturated hy-
drocarbon are of vital importance in modern organic synthesis.[19] 
However, there are still few reports of the photoredox/nickel-cata-
lyzed 1,4-functionalization of 1,3-enynes using organozinc rea-
gents.[7] For this reason, we attempted to carry out the reaction 
using the 1,3-enynes 1a, cyclobutanone O-benzoyl oximes 2a, and 
Ph2Zn 4a as the substrates with the photoredox/nickel dual cata-
lytic systems (See Figure S3 in the Supporting Information). The 
use of organozinc reagents was easy to make the mixer and mi-
croreactor clogging, so we chose to conduct this reaction under 
the batch conditions. 
Subsequently, we focused on screening the aryl zinc reagents 
to furnish adducts 5ab’—5af’ (5 examples). To our delight, a range 
of organozinc reagents bearing ‒Me, ‒Cl, ‒Ph, and ‒OMe substit-
uents at the para-position of the aromatic ring successfully fur-
nished the desired allene products 5ab’—5ae’ in 67%—80% yields. 
The dimethoxy substituted on aromatic ring of the organozinc re-
agent also worked well, and furnished the product 5af’ in 50% 
yield. 
To further explore the utility of our procedure, we focused our 
attention on performing photoredox/copper dual catalytic reac-
tion on a scale of 4.0 mmol (1.14 g) using the continuous flow 
technique to enhance the rate and progress of the reaction 
(Scheme 2). We chose to set up a continuous flow procedure in a 
homemade photo-flow reactor that ensured convenience, repro-
ducibility, and scalability. To our delight, the desired product 5aa 
was obtained in the yield of 69%. These results further highlighted 
the comprehensive potential of our current methods. 
To gain some insight into the 1,4-cyanoalkylarylation reaction, 
we initially carried out several control experiments with the mod-
el substrates 1a, 2a and 3a. Firstly, the addition of 2.0 equivalents 
of 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-1-piperidinyloxy (TEMPO) or diphenyl 
diselenide (PhSeSePh) inhibited the formation of the desired 
product 5aa, providing the radical-trapping products 6 and 7 de-
tected by high-resolution mass spectrometry or nuclear magnetic 
resonance analysis (Scheme 3a).

Scheme 3  Mechanistic experiments  
 
 
Mechanistic studies: (a) radical trapping experiment; (b) radical clock 
experiment; (c) fluorescence quenching experiments with PC-2 and vari-
ous concentrations of 1a and 2a. 
Both of these results suggested that the cyanoalkyl radical 
was involved in the process. The radical clock experiments were 
performed to further confirm this speculation. The radical clock 
1o was added to the system instead of conventional 1,3-enynes, 
yielding the no ring-opening product 5ao in 43% yield (Scheme 
3b), which showed that the coupling of the allenyl radical to the 
Cu(II) complex was much faster. Finally, we conducted the Stern- 
Volmer studies, and the results indicated that the excited-state 
*IrIII could be quenched by the cyclobutanone O-benzoyl oximes 
more efficiently than by 1,3-enynes, which indicated a reductive 
quenching mechanism (Scheme 3c). 
On the basis of the above mechanistic studies and literature 
precedents,[2-17] we propose the photoredox/copper catalytic 
cycles involve a possible cyanoalkyl radical mechanism in Scheme 
4. Initially, the active IrIII species is triggered by the visible light 
induced and produces the excited photocatalyst *IrIII complex. A 
single electron transfer from the excited states of *IrIII to the 
O-acyl oxime 2a results in the generation of the iminyl radical A, 
an alkoxy anion, and an IrIV complex. Then, iminyl radical A un-
dergoes a ring-opening by homolytic C—C bond fragmentation to 
form a highly reactive cyanoalkyl radical B, which can be inter-
cepted by the 1,3-enyne 1 followed by radical shift to give the 
allenyl radical species D. Alternatively, the Cu(II) species could 
form an Ar-Cu(II) species by exchanging its ligand with ArB(OH)2. 
Next, the Ar-Cu(II)Ln species is oxidized by the allenyl radical spe-
cies D to form the Cu(III) intermediate, which undergoes reductive 
elimination to provide the target tetra-substituted allene 5 and 
the Cu(I) species. Afterwards, single electron oxidation of the Cu(I) 
species by IrIV complex generates the Cu(II) species with the con-
comitant regeneration of the photocatalyst IrIII, closing the pho-
tocatalytic cycle. Similarly, the photoredox/nickel catalytic cycle 
was similar to the photoredox/copper catalytic cycle (For details 
see Figure S5 in the Supporting Information).

Conclusions 
We have developed the first example of the 1,4-difunction-
alization of 1,3-enynes for the synthesis of a range of tetra-sub-
stituted allenes via the photoredox/copper or photoredox/nickel 
dual catalysis. An array of synthetically useful cyanoalkyl- and 
aryl-containing tetrasubstituted allenes were obtained in good 
yields, with excellent chemoselectivities as well as remarkable 
functional group compatibility under mild reaction conditions. 
Furthermore, this strategy has also proved to be efficient, with 
the potential for scalability by the use of the continuous-flow 
technique. We believe this method offers not only a straightfor-
ward approach for the convenient and efficient construction of 
allene derivatives but previously inaccessible structures that were 
found as structural motifs in various natural products or drug 
molecules.

General procedure for nickel-catalyzed 1,4-cyanoalkylaryla-
tion of 1,3-enynes 
Under argon atmosphere, an oven-dried resealable Schlenk 
tube equipped with a magnetic stir bar was charged with 
1,3-enyne (1a, 0.2 mmol, 1.0 eq.), cyclobutanone oxime ester (2a, 
0.3 mmol, 1.5 eq.), Ni(OTf)2 (5.0 mol%), Bphen (10.0 mol%), 
Ir[dF(CF3)ppy]2(dtbbpy)PF6 (2.0 mol%), DABCO (0.6 mmol, 3.0 eq.), 
anhydrous THF (1.4 mL), and anhydrous DMF (1.0 mL). Then, 
Ph2Zn (4a, 0.2 mmol, 1.0 eq., c = 0.33 mol/L in THF) was added 
into the mixture. After that, the solution was stirred at a distance 
of ~5 cm from a 20 W blue LEDs (455 nm) at room temperature 
for about 12 h. The reaction solution was extracted with EtOAc (3 
× 25 mL) and chloridamonny, and the organic layer was collected, 
dried with Na2SO4 and evaporated under reduced pressure. The 
resulting crude compound was absorbed on silica gel and purified 
via column chromatography (EtOAc/PE, varying ratios). The iso-
lated compound was analyzed by HRMS and NMR.

Mr. Fangling Lu is currently a first-year Ph. D. student within Prof. Ziwei Gao’s research group at Shaanxi Normal University. 
Mr. Yong Yuan is currently a third-year Ph. D. student within Prof. Aiwen Lei’s research group at Wuhan University. 
Since tetrasubstituted olefins serve as the key structure mo-
tifs in a large number of biologically active compounds, methods 
for synthesis of tetrasubstituted olefins are highly desirable. 
Among various synthetic methodologies, the most known strate-
gies are the functionalization of olefins, alkynes, and allenes. For 
example, Zhang, Gosselin and co-workers prepared a series of 
tetrasubstituted olefins via Suzuki−Miyaura coupling (Scheme 
1a).[1] Morandi and co-workers reported a palladium-catalyzed 
intermolecular aryliodination of internal alkynes (Scheme 1b).[2] 
Ma and co-workers prepared a series of tetrasubstituted olefins 
by using readily available organozinc reagents and 2,3-allenals 
(Scheme 1c).[3] Despite extensive advances, the reported methods 
often require pre-prepared starting materials, inevitably leading 
to some by-products. Recently, under the supervision of Prof. 
Wang and Lei, we and Yang et al., reported an unprecedented 
electrochemical oxidative Csp3-H/S-H cross-coupling reaction 
between thiophenols and acetonitrile (Scheme 1d), yielding a 
series of tetrasubstituted olefins under exogenous-oxidant-free 
conditions.[4]

yield (Scheme 2a). Inspired by these two works, we came up with 
the idea of developing an oxidant-free electrochemical method to 
prepare aryl alkyl thioethers (Scheme 2b). 
Scheme 2  Electrochemical oxidative for C-S bonds formation. 
 
At the initial stage, 4-methylthiophenol and cyclohexanecar-
boxylic acid were employed as the model substrates to examine 
our concept. When the reaction was performed under a 12 mA 
constant current and using KI as the mediator, no expected C-S 
coupling product (3a) was obtained whereas an unprecedented 
Csp3-H/S-H cross-coupling reaction between thiophenols and 
acetonitrile was occurred and tetrasubstituted olefin product (4a) 
was obtained in 82% yield with excellent stereoselectivity (Z/E = 
18 : 1) (Scheme 3). Encouraged by this interesting result, we 
turned our attention to the electrochemical oxidative Csp3-H/S-H 
cross-coupling reaction between thiophenols and acetonitrile to 
construct tetrasubstituted olefins. 
Scheme 3  Electrochemical decarboxylation C-S bonds formation and 
electrochemical oxidative Csp3-H/S-H cross-coupling for synthesis of 
tetrasubstituted olefins. 
 
During the study, the biggest challenge was the structural de-
termination of unexpected product. After a long period of explo-
ration, 
we 
obtained 
the 
single 
crystal 
of 
(Z)-3-amino-2-((4-fluorophenyl)thio)but-2-enenitrile and finally 
determined the structure of the product by single crystal X-ray 
diffraction.[7] During the preparation for publication of this re-
search work, Huang and co-works reported a similar results,[8] 
which provided an extra-evidence for our obesrvation. 
Scheme 4  The strategy for synthesis various different tetrasubstituted 
olefins. 
 
This reaction may provide a new strategy for synthesis of dif-
ferent tetrasubstituted olefins (Scheme 4). Under mild electro-
chemical conditions, acetonitrile is converted to the radical in-
termediate A, while thiophenols are oxidized to the correspond-
ing radical intermediate B. Next, radical/radical cross-coupling 
produces the intermediate C, which undergoes further deproto-
nation leads to the desired product. Until now, we have only real-
ized the synthesis of sulfur-containing β-enaminonitrile deriva-
tives. We believe that by replacing thiophenols with other radical 
precursors, various different tetrasubstituted olefins, such as 
nitrogen-, carbon-, phosphorus-, oxygen-, or silicon-containing 
β-enaminonitrile derivatives, may also be obtained. Further ap-
plication of this strategy for synthesis of tetrasubstituted olefins is 
under way in our laboratory.

Photochemical Carboxylation of Activated C(sp3)─H Bonds with 
CO2 
Yong-Yuan Gui,[a]+ Wen-Jun Zhou,[a,b]+ Jian-Heng Ye,[a] and Da-Gang Yu*[a] 
As well known, the ever increasing concentration of carbon 
dioxide (CO2) in the atmosphere is likely to contribute to global 
warming. Thus, CO2 capture and utilization (CCU) has been 
explored as a potential option in terms of coping with global 
warming and climate change. However, from the view of organic 
synthesis, CO2 may act as an important and ideal one-carbon 
(C1) source. The utility of CO2 to provide high-value-added 
organic chemicals has received considerable attention.[1] 
However, it is challenging to utilize CO2 as a raw material due to 
its thermodynamic stability and kinetic inertness. As a 
consequence, direct carboxylation with CO2 has been mainly 
confined to highly reactive, and in many instances, air-sensitive 
organometallic 
species 
such 
as 
organolithium, 
Grignard 
reagents, or organozinc derivatives. The utilization of these 
organometallic reagents may restrict their general application in 
organic synthesis, especially the late-stage diversification of 
densely functionalized molecules. Another powerful alternative 
to existing methodologies is the development of transition metal-
catalyzed reductive carboxylation of organic (pseudo)halides 
with CO2 by Martin, Tsuji and Fujihara, and others.[2] On the 
other hand, C─H bonds are virtually unlimited in hydrocarbons, 
natural products, drugs, and synthetic and biological polymers. 
Direct C─H carboxylation with CO2 is highly appealing in a 
greener and more atom-economical way. Many developments 
have been achieved in the field of C(sp2) ─H bonds 
functionalization with CO2 by Nolan,[3] Hou,[4] Iwasawa,[5] Olah 
and Prakash,[6] our group[7] and others.[8] However, carboxylation 
of more challenging C(sp3)─H bonds with CO2 achieved much 
less success, which are mainly limited to the compounds 
containing acidic C(sp3)─H bonds such as acidic methylene 
compounds under harsh conditions or high pressure of CO2.[9] 
One formal C(sp3)─H bonds carboxylation was reported by Sato, 
Mita and coworkers, who realized Ru- or Ir-catalyzed C(sp3)─H 
bonds silylation and sequential fluoride-mediated carboxylation 
with CO2.[10] Despite the progress achieved, development of 
direct carboxylation of inert C(sp3) ─H bonds under mild 
conditions is still highly desirable, considering that aliphatic 
carboxylic acids are one of  the most ubiquitous motifs in many 
compounds and display significant biological activity (Figure 
1).[11]  
    Over the past decades, light-driven catalysis, especially 
photoredox catalysis, that harnesses the energy of light to 
accelerate a chemical reaction, has enabled a variety of 
nontraditional bond constructions in organic chemistry.[12]  In this 
context, huge efforts have been devoted to the development of 
light-driven CO2-fixation processes, which mainly focus on the 
photocatalytic reduction of CO2 to give carbon monoxide, formic 
acid, or other reduction products.[13] In sharp contrast, the light-
driven CO2-fixation via C−C bond formation to give carboxylic 
acids or its derivatives still remains a relatively unexplored area.  
 
Figure 1 Bioactive carboxylic acids 
 
In late 2015, Murakami and co-workers reported the first 
example of novel and clean process for direct carboxylation of 
benzylic C(sp3)─H bonds by simply using UV irradiation or 
sunlight as driving force (Scheme 1).[14a] In DMSO solution, o-
alkylphenyl ketones react efficiently with CO2 to generate the 
corresponding o-acylphenylacetic acids at room temperature. 
Mechanistically, o-alkylphenyl ketones are promoted to their 
excited state under photo-irradiation. The excited carbonyl group 
abstracts a hydrogen at the benzylic position to furnish a 1,4-
biradical species, which subsequently generates the o-
quinodimethane. This 1,3-diene moiety undergoes a [4+2] 
cycloaddition reaction with the C=O double bond of CO2 to give 
a six-membered cycloadduct, which delivers the carboxylation 
product through ring opening process.[14] This approach is 
featured by its remarkable mild reaction conditions, an 
atmospheric pressure of CO2, clean process, and no need of 
base, providing a nice alteration to the traditional thermal 
carboxylation reaction.

Scheme 1 UV light-driven carboxylation of benzylic C(sp3)─H 
bonds with CO2 
 
Solar light can also promote such a carboxylation efficiently. 
When phenyl(o-tolyl)methanone was irradiated with solar light in 
an atmospheric pressure of CO2 for 7 h on a sunny day, the 
carboxylic acid was obtained in 72% yield. Moreover, the 
bioactive 2,3-benzodiazepine could be obtained from easily 
available starting materials in 72% total yield by using this 
simple and straightforward carboxylation reaction (Scheme 2).  
 
 
Scheme 2 Application in synthesis of important pharmacophore-
2,3-benzodiazepine 
 
In 2016, Murakami and coworkers further realized the 
unprecedented carboxylation of allylic C(sp3) ─H in simple 
alkenes with CO2 (Scheme 3).[15] After exciting by UV light, the 
carbonyl oxygen of excited ketone intermolecularly abstracts a 
hydrogen at the allylic position to generate the radical pair 
intermediates, which undergo a radical-radical coupling reaction 
to give tertiary homoallyl alcohol (scheme 3, left, ketone cycle). 
Then, this energetic alcohol is deprotonated by copper tert-
butoxide, in-situ generated from copper complex and KOtBu, to 
give copper alkoxide, which undergoes β-carbon elimination to 
produce allylcopper species. Then, its nucleophilic addition to 
CO2 and further ligand exchange produce the desired product 
and regenerate the active copper alkoxide catalyst (scheme 3, 
right, copper cycle). The TON of ketone or copper complex can 
be up to 11 or 53.  
 
 
Scheme 3 UV light-promoted allylic C(sp3) ─H bonds 
carboxylation with CO2  
 
Importantly, the putative intermediates homoallyl alcohol was 
isolated as a major product (70% isolated yield based on 
ketone) in the control experiments of cyclohexene and xanthone 
under standard reaction conditions (Scheme 4). The homoallyl 
alcohol could generate carboxylic acid in 52% yield and 
xanthone in 59% yield in the absence of light. These results are 
consistent with the proposed mechanism and confirm that both 
ketone and copper complex act as catalysts in such allylic C─H 
bonds carboxylation. 
Scheme 4 Control experiments  
 
Contrary to the established strategy of photochemical 
reduction of CO2 to CO or formic acid using sacrificial reductant 
(usually a tertiary amine), very recently, Jamison and co-workers 
disclosed for the first time a photoredox activation strategy of 
CO2 and amines for the α-amino acid synthesis in continous flow 
(Scheme 5).[16] One-electron reduction of CO2 to CO2
•- is highly 
unfavorable with a formal reduction potential of -2.21 V vs SCE 
(saturated 
calomel 
electrode), 
which 
is 
beyond 
the 
photoreducing capabilities of the commonly-used ruthenium and 
iridium catalysts in photoredox catalysis. Inspired by the work of 
Yanagida and co-workers who used p-terphenyl (E0 = -2.63 V 
versus SCE in N,N-dimethylformamide) as photoredox catalyst 
for the reduction of CO2 to formic acid under ultraviolet light,[17] 
Jamison and co-workers applied this organic photocatalyst into 
their system and successfully realized such a unprecedented 
process.

Scheme 5 Photoredox α-carboxylation of amines with CO2 in 
continuous flow 
 
In this protocol, transformation is operated under continues 
flow, which is demonstrated to be more efficient than in batch. 
Moreover, the reaction is featured by its high regioselectivity, 
broad substrate scope and mild reaction conditions. In all cases,  
highly regioselctive carboxylations happen at the benzylic 
positions. The reaction is applicable for a range of N-
benzylpiperidines bearing different electron-neutral and electron-
rich groups on the arenes. Many kinds of functional groups, such 
as ethers, amides, and ketals, are compatiable under the 
reaction conditions. Beside piperidine, other heterocycles, 
including 
piperazine, 
morpholine, 
thiomorpholine 
and 
silapiperidine, also work nicely to afford the amino acids in good 
yields. Notably, acyclic amines can also act as efficient coupling 
partners. The present method also shows its potential 
appliciation in late stage C─H functionalization of complexes, as  
exemplified by the regioselective carboxylation of Ticlopidine, a 
marketed antiplatelet agent.  
As shown in Scheme 6, irradiation of the organic catalyst with 
ultraviolet light produces the excited singlet state of p-terphenyl, 
which is able to oxidize amine to generate the amine radical 
cation and p-terphenyl radical anion. This radical anion is so 
strongly reducing that it could donates an electron to CO2 (E0 = -
2.21 V vs SCE in DMF) and deliver the cosreponding CO2
•-. The 
radical-radical coupling between α-amino radical and CO2
•- 
produces α-amino acid as the desired product.  
 
Scheme 6 Proposed mechanism of light-driven carboxylation of 
amines with CO2 
 
In order to explore the mechanism, some experimental studies 
were carried out. Firstly, when 2.5 equivalents of 2,2,6,6-
tetramethylpiperding-1-oxyl (TEMPO) were added under the 
standard conditions, no desired coupling product was detected, 
indicating a radical species is involved in the reaction. 
Furthermore, Stern-Volmer emission quenching experiments 
were also conducted to demonstrate that the luminescence of 
the excited state of p-terphenyl was quenched by amine instead 
of CO2. Lastly, they also calculated of apparent quantum 
efficiency (AQE) of this transformation to explore the possibility 
of radical chain. The calculated AQE is 0.045, indicating that 
radical chain process is unlikely.  
Obviously, these pioneering works manifest that exploiting 
light energy as the driving force has come to be robust tool for 
transformations of CO2. The challenging C(sp3) ─H bonds 
carboxylation has been successfully realized under very mild 
conditions. Although significant progress has been made by the 
groups of Murakami and Jamison, there are still many more 
challenges remained to be explored in this emerging field. For 
example, the types of reactions and substrates with CO2 need to 
be significantly expanded, especially for unactivated C(sp3)─H 
bond. Furthermore, much more attention should be paid to the 
mechanism of CO2 activation, which will undoubtedly guide the 
design of more effective and novel catalytic systems. Last but 
not least, the asymmetric C(sp3)─H carboxylation should be 
further developed based on the nice pioneering works. We 
envision that this highlight will inspire a new direction in the 
utilization of CO2 with the assistance of light,[18] and more 
challenging work such as direct carboxylation of more normal 
C(sp3)─H with CO2 will be realized one day.

A Ball Milling Enabled Reformatsky Reaction 
Qun Cao,[a] Roderick T. Stark,[a] Ian A. Fallis,[a] and Duncan L. Browne*[a]
Abstract: 
An 
operationally 
simple 
one-jar 
one-step 
mechanochemical Reformatsky reaction using in situ generated 
organozinc intermediates under neat grinding conditions has been 
developed. Notable features are that this reaction protocol requires no 
solvent, no inert gases and no pre-activation of the bulk zinc source. 
The developed process is demonstrated to have good substrate 
scope (39-82% yield), and is effective irrespective of the morphology 
of the zinc source. 
Metal-mediated C-C bond formation is an essential tool in modern 
organic synthesis. Numerous reactions consisting of metal-
mediated nucleophilic addition to electrophiles have been 
developed for the synthesis of complex organic molecules.[1] 
However, the generally high basicity and/or nucleophilicity of 
some organometallic reagents restricts their use in late-stage 
modification, where sensitive functional groups may already exist 
in the chemical structure. Conversely, organozinc species 
represent a class of ‘mild’ organometallic compounds that 
demonstrate 
excellent 
functional 
group 
compatibility.[2] 
Nevertheless, the preparation of organozinc species often 
requires initial access to more reactive organometallics, which are 
then transmetallated on to the desired organozinc reactant via 
metathesis with Zn (II) salts. Alternatively, activated Zn (0) can be 
used for the oxidative addition into carbon-halogen bonds 
(Scheme 1, A). In general the formation and manipulation of 
organometallic compounds is not particularly clean/green when 
considering that solvents often have to be distilled and dried prior 
to use; inert gases are commonly required, and, in the case of 
organozinc reagents, the form of the bulk metal can play an 
important role and chemical additives are typically required to 
generate the activated zinc species.[3] Recently, we identified 
mechanochemistry 
and 
ball-milling 
as 
a 
tool 
for 
the 
straightforward generation of organozinc species without the 
requirement for carefully prepared solvents or inert gases. Under 
these conditions the input of mechanical energy is enough to 
breakdown the resilient metal oxide surface and, in the presence 
of the alkyl/aryl halide, generate the corresponding organozinc 
species (Scheme 1, B).[4] These organozinc species may then be 
intercepted by opening the grinding jar, adding both catalyst and 
coupling partner before then running a telescoped Negishi 
coupling reaction; such a process is applicable to both sp3- sp3 
and sp3-sp2 coupling reactions. In this paper we exploit this 
concept to the one-jar, one-step preparation and use of 
organozinc species in a robust mechanochemical Reformatsky 
protocol (Scheme 1, C). The Reformatsky reaction offers 
excellent potential for the formation of C-C bonds through (1) 
predictable C-C formation, (2) neutral reaction conditions (in 
comparison to obtaining the same products through aldol 
condensation), (3) broad functional group tolerance and (4) the 
ability to impart a high degree of stereocontrol.[5] 
Scheme 1. A) Formation and use of organzinc reagents; B) Previous one-jar 
two-step Negishi coupling; C) This work, one-jar one-step mechanochemical 
Reformatsky reaction. 
The classical Reformatsky reaction, in which β-hydroxy esters 
are formed by reacting aldehydes/ketones with α-halo esters 
using metallic zinc, was reported in 1887.[6] Since this seminal 
work a variety of latent nucleophiles and electrophiles have been 
studied and applied in this reaction, including, its routine use in 
the synthesis of complex natural products.[7] However, in order to 
carry out the Reformatsky reaction, organozinc reagents must be 
prepared at the point of use; the majority of organozinc reagents 
are not commercially available.[8] This process is can be 
problematic due to a layer of passivating zinc oxide which 
hampers the formation of organozinc species and requires 
removal through the treatment with chemical additives. Such 
additives include aqueous acid,[9] iodine,[10] 1,2-dibromoethane,[11] 
or chlorotrimethylsilane.[12] Highly reactive Rieke zinc is an 
alternative, but its preparation is non-trivial and requires the 
reduction of ZnCl2 with alkali metals (Li, Na, K) and 
naphthalene.[13] Further the air-sensitivity of this method renders 
the green credentials of the Rieke method poor, while derived 
form zinc metal are highly dependent on the physical form of zinc 
used, with multiple different forms of zinc commercially available

activation of zinc which renders the process more operationally 
simple and cost effective, but also delivers significant 
improvements of some of the green metrics typically associated 
with this reaction.[14] 
Mechanochemistry has been widely used among the crystal 
engineering 
and 
metal-organic-framework 
community.[15} 
Recently, ball milling and other mechanochemical techniques 
have been explored as a method to complement the synthetic 
toolkit.[16] Running reactions under mechanochemical conditions 
not only offers a more sustainable way to carry out solvent 
minimized/free reactions but can also lead to decreased reaction 
times, increased selectivity or different reaction outcomes when 
compared to results obtained from solution-based reactions.[17] 
Here we describe a green protocol for the Reformatsky reaction 
using the ball mill mechanical activation of elemental zinc in air. 
 
Table 1: Optimization of one-jar one-step Reformatsky reaction using ball mill. 
Studies 
commenced 
by 
treating 
model 
substrates 
benzaldehyde (1, 1 mmol) and ethyl 2-bromoacetate (2, 1.2 
mmol) with 1.6 equivalent of zinc (20-30 mesh zinc granular) at 
30 Hz in a 10 mL grinding jar with a single ball of mass 4 grams 
(Table 1). After 2 hours of grinding, crude 1H NMR analysis 
(mesitylene as internal standard) confirmed that there was 70% 
ethyl 3-hydroxy-3-phenylpropanoate (3) produced during the 
milling process (Table 1, Entry 1). 
Increasing the amount of zinc to 2 equivalents resulted in 81% 
of the desired hydroxy-ester product 3 (Table 1, Entry 2), further 
increasing the amount of zinc led to no significant increase in yield 
(Table 1, Entries 3 and 4). Rather than increasing the equivalents 
of zinc, increasing the amount of ethyl 2-bromoacetate (2) from 
1.2 to 2.0 equivalents also led to no real differences in observed 
yield (Table 1, Entries 5 and 6). With the optimized ratio of 
reagents in hand, a reaction time study assessed four individual 
reaction times; 0.5 h, 1 h, 1.5 h, 2 h (Table 1, Enries 2, 7-9) 
demonstrating that the reaction needs 2 hours to afford complete 
conversion. A control experiment, whereby the zinc was omitted 
from the reaction, returned none of the desired product. 
We then applied the optimized conditions to a further 11 
commercially available zinc forms (Figure S1). Although, these 
different zinc forms have various particle sizes, which may lead to 
differences in the ratio between zinc oxide layer and zinc metal, a 
fixed mass (2 mmol, 0.130 g) of each sample was employed. 
Pleasingly, it was found that in all cases the mechanochemical 
Reformatsky reaction was successful irrespective of the input 
form of zinc (Table 2). Notably, there appears to be a general 
trend that the forms with a higher surface area to volume ratio 
perform better for the Reformatsky reaction under neat ball milling 
conditions, this is perhaps contrary to prediction as these metal 
forms should also contain a higher proportion of zinc oxide. 
 
Table 2: Mechanochemical Reformatsky reaction using different zinc forms. 
 
With the optimized conditions established, application to a 
small range of 11 carbonyl compounds was investigated for 
reactivity with ethyl 2-bromoacetate and zinc flakes (~325 mesh) 
under mechanical grinding (Scheme 2). It was found that the 
mechanochemical Reformatsky reaction demonstrates good 
functional group tolerance. Using highly sterically hindered 2, 4, 6 
trimethyl benzaldehyde afforded the corresponding hydroxy-ester, 
5, in good yield (66%). Halogen containing aromatic aldehydes 
were also effective substrates, leading to good isolated yields of 
the halogen containing products (Scheme 2, 6-8, 77-82%), 
hydrodehalogenation was not observed under these one-pot 
reaction conditions. Acetophenone was also a competent 
electrophilie under these conditions, affording  the tertiary, 
benzylic alcohol product, 10, in 69% isolated yield. Aliphatic 
aldehydes offered mixed results with cyclohexylcarboxaldehyde 
giving the product in 39% yield, 2-phenylethyl aldehyde afforded 
73% yield of the corresponding product and cinnamaldehyde 
resulted in 61% isolated yield (Scheme 2).

Scheme 3. Scope of latent nucleophiles in the mechanochemical Reformatsky

Eight different latent nucleophiles were also examined in this 
process with benzaldehyde as the model electrophile. Pleasingly, 
the corresponding organozinc intermediates could be generated 
under mechanochemical conditions (Scheme 3), both methyl and 
tert-butyl α-halo esters could be used to effectively form their β-
hydroxy esters (14 and 15) in good to excellent yields. Reaction 
with ethyl 2-bromoproprionate provided 67% yield of 16 as a 
mixture of diastereoisomers (syn:anti = 58:42). Notably, reaction 
with more stereocongested ethyl α-bromoisobutyrate maintained 
good yields of 68% (17, Scheme 3), α, α-difluoro-β-hydroxyesters 
18 could also be prepared by this method. Running the ball mill 
enabled Reformatsky reaction using ethyl 4-bromobut-2-enoate 
resulted in 52% α-substituted product 19 with moderate 
diastereoselectivity (syn:anti = 62:38). It is noteworthy that 2-
bromoacetonitrile also participated in the generation of an 
organozinc reagent in situ and formed the corresponding 
Reformatsky product 3-hydroxy-3-phenylpropanenitrile (20). 
Notably, in all cases explored, there was no reductive aldehyde 
coupling (pinacol reaction) observed. 
The applicability of imines as electrophiles was also briefly 
explored under the developed ball milling conditions. It is known 
that other than aldehyde/ketone, non-classical Reformatsky 
electrophiles such as azomethines, nitriles, lactones, anhydrides, 
Υ-thioalactams, amides could also be used for the Reformatsky 
reaction.[18] Although not fully optimized, N-benzylideneaniline 
(21), did undergo a mechanochemical Reformatsky reaction 
(Scheme 4, A), to afford the β-amino ester, 22, in 48% yield and 
a small amount of the corresponding β-lactam, 23 (7%). 
The convenience of the method is well demonstrated against 
a solution-based reaction and that under ball milling (Scheme 4, 
B) using identical reagents. Running a solution based reaction in 
dry THF and under nitrogen gas atmosphere at 50 °C with either 
zinc flakes or granular zinc (no additive used) resulted in low 
observed yields, 7% and 4% respectively (Scheme 4, B). 
Whereas, the results from Table 2, show that under ball milling, 
without any solvent, inert gas or additive, the reaction proceeds 
smoothly in two hours and all forms of zinc explored are effective 
for this transformation. 
Scheme 4. A) Example of mechanochemical Reformatsky type reaction 
with imine electrophile. B) Reformatsky reaction with unactivated zinc source –
milling vs solution. 
 
In conclusion, a reliable operationally simple one-jar one-step 
mechanochemical Reformatsky reaction has been developed. By 
utilizing the organozinc generated in situ upon milling, this 
protocol avoids the requirement for access to dry solvents, inert 
gases and chemical additives and thus furnishes a processes 
where the green metrics are improved. Moreover, the protocol

A Flexible Asymmetric Synthesis of anti-1,2-Sulfanyl Amines
Dieter Enders,*[a] Alexander Moll,[a] Annette Schaadt,[a] Gerhard Raabe,[a] and
Jan Runsink[a]
Dedicated to Professor Reinhard W. Hoffmann on the occasion of his 70th birthday
Keywords: Alkylations / β-Amino sulfides / Asymmetric synthesis / Hydrazones / Nucleophilic addition
An efficient and flexible asymmetric synthesis of various pro-
tected anti-1,2-sulfanyl amines bearing two adjacent ste-
reogenic centres is described. Key steps are the diastereose-
lective α-alkylation of α-sulfanylated acetaldehyde-SAMP-
hydrazones
with
various
electrophiles
and
subsequent
nucleophilic 1,2-addition of organocerium reagents to the hy-
drazone CN double bond. The resulting hydrazines were
converted into the title compounds with excellent diastereo-
Introduction
Chiral 1,2-sulfanyl amines (β-amino sulfides, vic-thio-
ether amines) and 1,2-amino thiols of high diastereomeric
and enantiomeric purity are of great interest in synthetic
organic chemistry. In recent years they have gained particu-
lar attention as N,S-ligands in asymmetric catalysis. N,N-
and N,O-ligands have already been employed in numerous
instances in catalytic asymmetric synthesis and have been
used with great success.[1] vic-Sulfanyl amines offer ad-
ditional possibilities over N,N- and N,O-ligands, since, for
example, the sulfur atom becomes a stereocentre when
coordinated to a metal.[2]
The lack of simple and flexible synthetic routes to suit-
able derivatives of the title compounds has been a major
barrier in investigation of their use in asymmetric catalysis.
Heterobidentate N,S-ligands have proved to be very effec-
tive in enantioselective palladium-catalysed allylic substi-
tution reactions.[3] 1,2-Sulfanyl amines, 1,2-amino thiols,
and their corresponding disulfides have also been shown
to be particularly effective catalysts for the enantioselective
addition of dialkylzinc reagents to prochiral carbonyl com-
pounds.[4] Furthermore, they are also used in the enantiose-
lective conjugate addition of organometallic reagents to
α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compounds.[5]
Several methods for the synthesis of vic-sulfanyl amines
have been described in the literature, but the choice of sub-

stituents is restricted. One possibility is to synthesise them
from natural α-amino acids in an ex-chiral-pool synthesis.[6]
Van Leeuwen et al., for example, synthesised two different
ligands derived from cysteine and pseudo-ephedrine and
used them in iridium()-catalysed asymmetric hydrogenation
reactions.[7] Some diastereoselective syntheses[8] for this
class of compounds have been reported, but to the best of
our knowledge there is only one asymmetric synthesis.[9]
One of the simplest routes is probably through treatment of
thiols with aziridines in a regio- and stereoselective ring-
opening reaction.[10] Kellogg et al., for example, have pre-
pared these aziridines through a Mitsunobu reaction start-
ing from ephedrine.[11] An alternative approach for the syn-
thesis of vic-sulfanyl amines was developed by Ishibashi et
al., who used a mixture of 2-oxazolidinone and thiols in the
presence of alkoxides to afford the desired products.[12]
The 1,2-sulfanyl amine unit has also been found in a
number of important biologically active compounds. It is a
characteristic structural feature found in ecteinascidine
family marine alkaloids that serve as an important class of
anticancer agents.[13]
Our synthetic strategy, which employs the SAMP/
RAMP-hydrazone methodology,[14] should provide an ef-
ficient and flexible route to the desired 1,2-sulfanyl amines
and permit access to both anti-configured enantiomers. The
concept of α-alkylation and 1,2-addition to SAMP/RAMP-
hydrazones and subsequent N,N bond cleavage has already
been demonstrated by our group in various applications.[15]
We now wish to report an important extension of our pre-
vious procedure on the asymmetric synthesis of anti-1,2-
tert-butylsulfanyl amines, as reported in our short com-

Conclusion
In summary, we have developed an efficient method for
the α-alkylation of α-sulfanylated acetaldehyde SAMP-hy-
drazones and subsequent nucleophilic 1,2 addition to the
CN double bond to afford α-sulfanylated hydrazines, which
were easily converted into the title N-protected anti-1,2-sul-
fanyl amines with high diastereomeric and enantiomeric ex-
cesses (de and ee  96%). Deprotection of the 1,2-benzyl-
sulfanyl amines to afford their corresponding 1,2-amino thi-
ols should open a facile route to novel N,S-ligands for
asymmetric catalysis and to useful precursors of oligopepti-
dosulfonamides.[24]

General Procedure for 1,2-Addition, N,N Cleavage and the Protec-
tion of the Amino Groups of tert-Butylsulfanyl Hydrazones (S,S)-4
(GP 4): CeCl3·7H2O (3.0 equiv.) was dehydrated for 2 h at 130 °C
in vacuo (0.1 Torr) and then suspended in dry THF (3.0 mL/mmol)
with sonification. The suspension was stirred overnight at room
temperature. After the mixture had been cooled to 78 °C, organ-
olithium reagent (3.0 equiv.) was added, and the mixture was stirred
for 2 h at this temperature. Hydrazone (S,S)-4 (1.0 equiv.), dis-
solved in dry THF (4.0 mL/mmol), was added to the resulting yel-
low suspension at 100 °C. The solution was allowed to warm up
to room temperature over 15 h. The reaction mixture was quenched
with saturated aqueous NaHCO3 solution and the aqueous portion
was extracted with CH2Cl2. The combined organic layers were
dried with Na2SO4 and concentrated in vacuo. The crude hydra-
zines were used directly in the N,N cleavage. For that purpose, the
crude hydrazines (1.0 equiv.) were dissolved in dry THF (10 mL/
mmol), BH3·THF (12 equiv.) was then added, and the solution was
heated at reflux for 4 h. The reaction mixture was hydrolysed with
methanol and concentrated in vacuo. The residue was dissolved in
methanol (10.0 mL/mmol) and heated at reflux for another 2 h.
The mixture was concentrated in vacuo and the crude amine was
either purified by flash column chromatography on silica gel or
subsequently converted into the benzylcarbamate. For that purpose
the crude amine was dissolved in CH2Cl2 (10.0 mL/mmol), K2CO3
(2.7 equiv.), and CbzCl (2.5 equiv.) were added, and the system was
heated at reflux for 3 days. The aqueous layer was extracted three

General Procedure for the 1,2-Addition to α-Sulfanylated SAMP-
Hydrazones (S,S)-6 (GP 6): CeCl3·7H2O (3.0 equiv.) was dehy-
drated in vacuo (0.1 Torr) for 2 h at 130 °C and then suspended
in dry THF (3.0 mL/mmol) with sonification. The suspension was
stirred overnight at room temperature. After the system had been
cooled to78 °C, lithiumorganyl (3.0 equiv.) was added and the
mixture was stirred at this temperature for 2 h. Hydrazone (S,S)-6
(1.0 equiv.), dissolved in dry THF (4.0 mL/mmol), was then added
at 100 °C to the resulting canary yellow suspension. The solution
was allowed to warm up to room temperature over 15 h. The reac-
tion mixture was quenched with saturated aqueous NaHCO3 solu-
tion and the aqueous portion was extracted with CH2Cl2. The com-
bined organic layers were dried with Na2SO4 and concentrated in
vacuo. The crude hydrazines were purified by flash column chro-
matography (SiO2, pentane/Et2O).

General Procedure for the N,N Bond Cleavage and Protection of the
Amino Groups of the Hydrazines (S,R,S)-7 (GP 7): The hydrazines
(S,R,S)-7 (1.0 equiv.) were dissolved in dry THF (10.0 mL/mmol),
BH3·THF (12 equiv.) was then added, and the solution was heated
at reflux for 4 h. The reaction mixture was cooled to 0 °C and
hydrolysed with 1 HCl. The solvent was removed under reduced
pressure and the residue was dissolved in saturated aqueous
NaHCO3 solution. The crude amine was extracted with CH2Cl2
and either purified by flash column chromatography or directly
used in the next step. For that purpose, the solution of the crude
amine, dissolved in CH2Cl2, was treated with K2CO3 (5.0 equiv.)
and MocCl (5.0 equiv.) and heated at reflux for 2 days. After that,

the reaction mixture was quenched with water and the aqueous
portion was extracted three times with CH2Cl2. The combined or-
ganic layers were dried with Na2SO4 and the solvent was removed
in a rotary evaporator. The residue was purified by flash column
chromatography (SiO2, pentane/Et2O).

(S,R)-8e. Suitable crystals were obtained by crystallisation from n-
heptane. The compound (C22H29NO2S; Mr  371.55) crystallises
in orthorhombic space group P21212 (no.18) with cell dimensions
a  17.715(3), b  21.850(1), and c  5.3278(4) A˚ . With Z  4
the cell volume V  2062.2(4) A˚ 3 results in a calculated density of
dcalcd.  1.197 g·cm3. 4797 reflections were collected at T  150 K
on an ENRAF-NONIUS CAD4 diffractometer by use of graphite-
monochromated Cu-Kα-radiation (λ  1.54179 A˚ ) in the ω)/2Θ
mode. Data collection covered the range 6  h  6, 21  k 
21, and 25  l  27 up to Θmax  72.7°. Lorentz and polarisation
correction were applied to the diffraction data but no absorption
correction (µ  1.503 mm1) was made. The structure was solved
by direct methods as implemented in the Xtal3.7 suite of crystallo-
graphic routines[27] by employment of GENSIN to generate the
structure-invariant relationships and GENTAN for the general tan-
gent phasing procedure. 4015 observed reflections [I  2σ(I)] were
included in the final full-matrix, least-squares refinement on F in-
volving 347 parameters and converging at R(Rw)  0.061(0.065,
w  l/[20σ(F)2]), a final shift/error 0.0002, S  1.075, and a
residual electron density of 1.68/1.00 e·A˚ 3. Xabs 0.014(45)[28]
for the structure shown in Figure 2. All hydrogen positions except
H6 could be located in a difference Fourier map and were refined
isotropically. CCDC 207541 contains the supplementary crystallo-

Christian Alter,[a] Beate Neumann,[a] Hans-Georg Stammler,[a] Lothar Weber,[a] and

Dedicated to the memory of Professor D. J. Burton
Abstract: Many approaches to introduce the CF2P(O)(OR)2 unit
into organic molecules make use of CuI-catalyzed couplings be-
tween organic halides and BrZnCF2P(O)(OR)2. Despite the great
importance of this process for the synthesis of α,α-difluoro-
methylenephosphonates, the constitution and molecular struc-
tures of the organozinc precursor and the catalytically relevant
copper/zinc complex are still unknown. Here we report on the
Introduction
Fluorine or fluorine-containing substituents influence the bio-
logical properties of organic molecules such as their bioavail-
ability or metabolic stability.[1] One prominent functionality in
such
species
is
the
difluoromethylenephosphonate
unit
CF2P(O)(OR)2. As α,α-difluoromethylenephosphonates can be
considered stable metabolic phosphate mimics,[2] they are chal-
lenging candidates for the design of novel pharmaceuticals.
Scheme 1. Coupling reactions with BrZnCF2P(O)(OR)2 in the presence of CuI species.

isolation of these two species, their spectroscopic characteriza-
tion, and the determination of their structure by single-crystal
X-ray diffraction. First orienting experiments on the stability of
the cuprate reagent in solution at room temperature as well as
its reactivity towards allyl bromides were subsequently per-
formed.
Aryldifluoromethylenephosphonates are potent inhibitors of
tyrosine phosphatase, which is an important enzyme for cellular
signal transduction.[3] The CF2P(O)(OR)2 unit is available by
fluorination of keto- or methylphosphonates with diethyl-
aminosulfurtrifluoride (DAST).[4] Aggressive fluorinating agents
may be circumvented by methods based upon metalated
CF2P(O)(OR)2 derivatives. One prominent synthetic approach
to α,α-difluoromethylenephosphonates is centered around
BrZnCF2P(O)(OR)2.
Treatment of bromodifluoromethyldialkylphosphonates with
zinc leads to the formation of BrZnCF2P(O)(OR)2 [Equation (2)].
The required bromodifluoromethyldialkylphosphonates are eas-
ily accessible by the Michaelis–Arbuzov reaction of trialkylphos-
phites with CF2Br2 [Equation (1)].[5] The organozinc compound
reacts readily with various acylation agents.[6] In the presence
Full Paper
of CuI salts the CF2P(O)(OR)2 unit can also be coupled to allyl
halides,[7a] aryl iodides,[7b–7c,7j] alkenyl halides,[7d–7h] and halo-
alkynes[7i] (Scheme 1).
(1)
(2)
In addition to organozinc chemistry, several other copper-
mediated couplings such as those of boronic acids or organo-
iodine(III) halides with Me3SiCF2P(O)(OR)2 have been reported.[8]
(Scheme 2).
Scheme 2. Copper(I) mediated syntheses of difluoromethylenephosphonates.
Despite the number of reports on copper mediated cou-
plings with BrZnCF2P(O)(OR)2, the constitution and molecular
structure of the copper reagent remained virtually obscure.
Yokomatsu and Burton[9,7e] postulated a mixed Cu/Zn species
as the reactive intermediate (Scheme 3).
Scheme 3. Postulated structure of the reactive organocopper intermedi-
ate.[9,7e]
As yet, neither the organocopper intermediate nor the orga-
nozinc precursor have been isolated and structurally authenti-
cated by X-ray diffraction or by means of spectroscopy. In the
course of a program on difluoroorganic compounds, we were
interested in the structure/reactivity properties of the catalytic
system under discussion.
Results and Discussion
Following Burton's protocol we synthesized BrZnCF2P(O)(OiPr)2
by treatment of BrCF2P(O)(OiPr)2 with zinc metal and confirmed
the relevant spectroscopic data as given by the authors [Equa-
tion (3)].[6]
(3)
Crystallization of [Zn(Br){CF2P(O)(OiPr)2}(thf)]2 from a THF
solution at –28 °C afforded colorless needles. The air-sensitive
crystals were stored under a N2 atmosphere at room tempera-
ture for months without any decomposition and were sub-
jected to an X-ray diffraction study.

The compound crystallizes in the triclinic space group P1¯
(Figure 1). The analysis reveals two crystallographically inde-
pendent molecules, both BrZnCF2P(O)(OiPr)2 units are arranged
at a center of inversion in an antiparallel disposition. The zinc
atoms are at the center of a distorted tetrahedron [C1–Zn1–Br1
126.3(1)° and C12–Zn2–Br2 126.8(1)°] which is completed
by a THF ligand and the P=O group of the adjacent molecule
[O1′–Zn1–O4 93.2(1)° and O5–Zn2–O8 93.5(1)°]. The C–Zn dis-
tances are 203.4(2) and 202.7(2) pm, respectively.
Figure 1. Molecular structure of [Zn(Br){CF2P(O)(OiPr)2}(thf)]2 in the solid state
(thermal ellipsoids are set to 50 % probability, hydrogen atoms and the sec-
ond molecule are omitted for clarity).
In the IR spectrum (Figure 3), the band with the highest in-
tensity at 1015 cm–1 results from the P–O–C stretching vibra-
tion. The P=O stretching vibration is assigned to the intense
band at 1179 cm–1. The vibrational stretching of the CF2 unit
gives rise to a band at 1099 cm–1.
In accordance with the suggestion of Burton and Yoko-
matsu,[9,7e] the addition of one equivalent of CuBr to a DMF
solution of BrZnCF2P(O)(OiPr)2 gives rise to the formation of the
heteroorganocuprate [Zn{Cu(Br){CF2P(O)(OiPr)2}}2(dmf)4] [Equa-
tion (4)], which was isolated from a cold THF solution as color-
less needles. The light- and air-sensitive cuprate can be stored
under a N2 atmosphere at –28 °C in the dark for weeks.
(4)
An X-ray structural study shows the picture of a hetero-
organocuprate structure (Figure 2). The compound crystallizes
in the monoclinic space group P21/c with Zn at the center of
inversion. Two cuprate units are coordinated to the central Zn
cation by their P=O functionality [O1–Zn1 206.2(1) pm]. Four
equatorial positions at the Zn atom are occupied by the oxygen
atoms of four DMF ligands. Within the structure, the copper
atom adopts an almost linear arrangement [C1–Cu1–Br1
178.0(1)°] with a C1–Cu1 bond length of 192.0(2) pm. In the IR
spectrum of the product, bands at 1109 and 1053 cm–1 were
assigned to the symmetric and antisymmetric ν(CF) vibrations
(Figure 3). The very intense band at 1643 cm–1 is due to the

C=O stretching of the coordinated dimethylformamide. Intense
bands at 1376 cm–1 (C–N stretching) and at 682 cm–1 (C=O
deformation) are assigned to the DMF ligand.
Figure 2. Molecular structure of [Zn{Cu(Br){CF2P(O)(OiPr)2}}2(dmf)4] in the solid
state (thermal ellipsoids are set to 50 % probability, hydrogen atoms omit-
ted).

solvents, its solutions in CH3CN, DMF, and DMSO suffer from

veals that the decrease of the signal intensity follows a first-

expected, but significantly slower than a stoichiometric amount
of organocuprate 1. A reaction also occurred when catalytic
amounts of the isolated cuprate 1 were added to a solution of
BrZnCF2P(O)(OiPr)2 (2). On the basis of these observations we
conclude that the formation of the organocuprate 1 from
BrZnCF2P(O)(OiPr)2 (2) is crucial for the coupling of the
CF2P(O)(OR)2 unit to organic electrophiles. When a catalytic
amount of CuI is added to a solution of BrZnCF2P(O)(OiPr)2 (2)
cuprate 1 is formed and can undergo further reactions. It is
noteworthy that in our studies Pd0 and PdII show no catalytic
activity in Negishi type coupling reactions of BrZnCF2P(O)(OiPr)2
with allyl halides.
Conclusions
We isolated [Zn(Br){CF2P(O)(OiPr)2}(thf)]2 and [Zn{Cu(Br){CF2P-
(O)(OiPr)2}}2(dmf)4] for the first time and studied their solid-
state molecular structure and spectroscopic properties. Reactiv-
ity experiments on the isolated compounds indicate that the
formation of the reactive [Cu(Br){CF2P(O)(OiPr)2}]– is crucial to
introduce the CF2P(O)(OR)2 unit into organic molecules. Stability
studies reveal that the choice of solvent is important to increase
the stability of the reactive cuprate at room temperature to
avoid decomposition.
Experimental Section
The starting material BrCF2P(O)(OiPr)2[5] was synthesized as de-
scribed in the literature. All other chemicals were obtained from
commercial sources and used without further purification. Standard
high-vacuum techniques were employed throughout all experi-
ments. Nonvolatile compounds were handled in a dry N2 atmos-
phere using Schlenk techniques. IR spectra were recorded with a
Bruker Alpha FTIR spectrometer (Bruker Daltonik GmbH, Bremen,
Germany) equipped with an ATR unit with a diamond crystal for
liquids and solids. NMR spectra were recorded with a Bruker Model

Efficient Solution-Phase Parallel Synthesis of 4-Substituted N-Protected
Piperidines
Xiaoyang Wang,[a] Anna M. Kauppi,[a] Roger Olsson,*[b] and Fredrik Almqvist*[a]
Keywords: Copper / Hydrogenations / Nitrogen heterocycles / Zinc / Parallel synthesis
Practical conditions for the synthesis of 4-substituted N-pro-
tected piperidines through CuCN·2LiBr-catalyzed organo-
zinc additions to 1-acylpyridinium salts and subsequent hy-
drogen-transfer hydrogenation have been established. The
reaction sequence is performed at room temperature and
provides 4-substituted N-protected piperidines in excellent
overall yields without the isolation of intermediate dihy-
dropyridines. In those cases in which the organozinc addition
Introduction
Substituted piperidines constitute one of the most stud-
ied heterocycles, owing to their ubiquitous nature in syn-
thetically challenging alkaloids as well as in pharmaceutical
research.[13] As a result, numerous methods for the syn-
thesis of piperidine derivatives have been reported.[46]
GoetzLuthy reported an attractive synthetic strategy that
takes advantage of the wealth of commercially available
pyridines as starting materials, dihydropyridines being syn-
thesized in low yields by direct alkylation of pyridines.[7]
Recent work by Comins et al., however, has shown that
activation of the pyridines through the formation of N-acyl
pyridinium derivatives prior to the nucleophilic addition
provides dihydropyridines in good yields and with good re-
gioselectivities.[8,9] A wide range of organometallic reagents
have also been used as nucleophiles in these reactions. Un-
catalyzed Grignard[10] and organotin[11] reagents favor the
formation of 2-substituted dihydropyridines, whereas the
use of organotitanium reagents[12,13] and lithium dialkylcu-
prates[14] mainly results in 4-substituted dihydropyridines,
which is also the case for Grignard reagents admixed with
copper iodide.[15] Organozinc reagents are reported to give
mainly mixtures of 4- and 2-substituted dihydropyri-
dines.[16] Although not synthetically useful, owing to the
formation of isomeric mixtures, the advantageous proper-

ties of organozinc reagents  such as their compatibility
with a wide range of functional groups (e.g., chlorides, ni-
triles, esters, amides, and ketones) and the potential to per-
form the reactions at room temperature  makes their use
attractive in parallel synthesis.[1720] Therefore, to improve
the regioselectivity it would be of great interest to investi-
gate the possibilities of the use of organozinc reagents in
combination with CuCN·2LiBr. A few scattered, individual
examples of the use of organozinc reagents in combination
with copper catalysis resulting in good regioselectivities
have been reported.[2124] Further investigation of the scope
and limitations of these reactions is, however, necessary in
the context of developing a reliable method for parallel syn-
thesis. A practical Pd/C-catalyzed hydrogen-transfer re-
duction of the intermediate dihydropyridines, to provide the
substituted piperidines efficiently, was also investigated.
Here we report a practical and efficient procedure, also
amenable for parallel synthesis, for the synthesis of 4-substi-
tuted N-protected piperidines.
Results and Discussion
To study the regioselective alkylation, a set of commer-
cially available organozinc reagents, admixed with catalytic
amounts (5 mol %) of CuCN·2LiBr were added to pre-
formed N-acyl pyridinium salts (Table 1).
Both dialkylzinc reagents and secondary and primary
alkylzinc halides almost exclusively gave the 4-addition
products, with only trace amounts of the 2-substituted iso-
mers being detectable by NMR spectroscopy (Table 1, en-
tries 15). The tertiary alkylzinc nucleophile tert-butylzinc
bromide similarly afforded a high isomeric ratio of 98% of
the desired 4-substituted dihydropyridine 2, and only 2% of

With these results in hand, the focus was turned to sub-

On the other hand, if the pyridine was substituted in both

The presence of additional substituents in the ring, as exem-
plified by 2,3,5-collidine, caused reduced regioselectivity;
when 2-methylphenylzinc bromide was used as nucleophile,
for example, the 2/3 ratio went down to 70:30 (Table 1, en-

be expected, treatment of a 4-substituted pyridine with phe-

clusively the 2,4-disubstituted dihydropyridine 3, with no
4,4-disubstituted derivative 2 detectable (Table 1, entry 24).
Decomposition of the dihydropyridines occurred during
storage in the freezer. Consequently, to accomplish high
overall yields, it was important to reduce the dihydropyri-
dines quickly to the corresponding piperidines. Previously,
these substrates had mostly been reduced by hydrogenation
with H2 gas as the hydrogen source in the presence of a
catalyst[2527] (e.g. 10% Pd/C, 45 psi, 810 h or PtO2, 6 h).
Since parallel synthesis with pressurized hydrogen gas de-
mands advanced equipment, the option to use a hydrogen-
transfer reduction would be particularly attractive. Advan-
tageously, both for avoiding the use of special equipment
and for the time-saving aspect in the reduced reaction times,
ammonium formate in absolute methanol reduced the di-
hydropyridines to piperidines within one hour at room tem-
perature under Pd/C catalysis conditions (Table 2).[28,29] It
should be noted, though, that restricting the reaction tem-

Removal of the N-phenoxycarbonyl group was achieved
by treatment of the N-phenoxycarbonyl-protected piperi-

ene glycol for one hour,[30] resulting in a series of 4-substi-

deprotection method turned out to work conveniently, for
piperidines substituted either with aliphatic or with aro-

tBoc-protected piperidines can easily be deprotected by
various mildly acidic methods and are therefore attractive
as target molecules. However, the organozinc addition is
not compatible with the use of tBocCl or tBoc anhydride
as activating agents, as would be required for the pro-
duction of tBoc-protected piperidines. We therefore treated
the N-phenoxycarbonyl derivatives 2 with KOtBu, resulting
in high yields of the N-tBoc-protected dihydropyridines 6

all reaction steps had been high-yielding and had delivered
fairly pure crude products. Thus, conversion of the pyri-

performed with only quick aqueous washings of intermedi-

Conclusions
A practical method suitable for the parallel synthesis of
4-substituted N-protected piperidines has been developed.
Even though the substituted dihydropyridines were formed
in high diastereomeric ratios, the developed strategy in-
cludes the option to remove undesired 2-substituted di-
hydropyridine to provide isomerically pure products. Fur-
thermore, conditions for exchange of the N-phenoxycar-
bonyl to the N-tBoc protecting groups, which can be con-
sidered
as
orthogonal
protecting
groups,
have
been
established. The high regioselectivities and yields achieved
in the reaction, together with the practical synthetic and
purification procedures, make this procedure attractive for
library synthesis. The incorporation of these building
blocks into more complex derivatives in a parallel manner
will be reported in due course.

Experimental Section
General: All reactions were carried out under inert atmospheres
with dry solvents under anhydrous conditions, unless otherwise
stated. Pyridine was distilled before use. Methanol and ethylene
glycol were dried over molecular sieves (3 A˚ ) in a flask. THF was
distilled from potassium. All the other chemicals were purchased
from Aldrich and were used as received (it should be noted that
some of the aliphatic zinc reagents contained traces of regioiso-
mers, which was confirmed by treatment with benzoyl chloride fol-
lowed by analysis by LCMS and NMR spectroscopy). TLC was
performed on 60 F254 silica gel (Merck) with detection by UV light
and by staining with solutions of potassium permanganate (3 g),
potassium carbonate (20 g), 5% aqueous sodium hydroxide (5 mL)
in water (300 mL), or of 2% Ninhydrin in EtOH 95%. Flash col-
umn chromatography (eluents given in brackets) was performed on
silica gel (Matrex, 60 A˚ , 3570 µm, Grace Amicon). The 1H and
13C NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker DRX 400 instrument
on solutions in CDCl3 [residual CHCl3 (δH  7.26 ppm) or CDCl3
(δC  77.00 ppm) as internal standard] or in [D6]DMSO {residual
[D5]DMSO (δH  2.50 ppm) or [D6]DMSO (δC  40.0 ppm) as
internal standard} at 298 K. First-order chemical shifts and coup-
ling constants were obtained from one-dimensional spectra. Proton
and carbon resonances were assigned from appropriate combi-
nations of COSY and 1H-13C HMQC. IR spectra were recorded
on an ATI Mattson Genesis Series FTIRTM spectrometer. LCMS
analysis was performed with a Waters micromass ZQ spectrometer
[ES], and high-resolution mass spectra [EI or FAB] were recorded
on a Jeol JMS-SX 102 spectrometer. All organic extracts were dried
with solid Na2SO4 unless otherwise stated.
General Procedure for the Preparation of Substituted Phenyl Di-
hydropyridine-1-carboxylates 2 and 3: Pyridine (0.6 mL, 7.5 mmol),
CuCN (45 mg, 0.5 mmol), and LiBr (86 mg, 1 mmol) were dis-
solved in THF (20 mL) at room temperature, which resulted in a
yellow-green solution. Upon the dropwise addition of phenyl
chloroformate (0.63 mL, 5 mmol) the color changed to orange-red
and a lot of solid was formed. The zinc reagent was then added
dropwise at room temperature. After one hour at room tempera-
ture, aqueous NH4Cl (20%, 25 mL) and Et2O (50 mL) were added.
The water layer was separated and reextracted with Et2O (2 
7 mL). The organic layers were combined and washed with aqueous
NH4Cl (20%)/NH4OH (20%) (1:1, 10 mL), water (2  10 mL), HCl
(10% aq., 2  10 mL), water (2  10 mL), and brine (2  10 mL)
and dried. Concentration at reduced pressure gave the crude prod-
ucts 2 and 3. (See Table 1 for isolated yields).
General Procedure for the Synthesis of 4-Substituted Phenyl Piperi-
dine-1-carboxylates by Removal of Undesired 2-Isomers by a [42]
Cycloaddition with Maleic Anhydride: A mixture of the 2- and 4-
substituted dihydropyridine (0.5 mmol) was added to a solution of
maleic anhydride (490 mg, 5 mmol) in THF (1.5 mL). After the
mixture had been heated at reflux for two hours, saturated aqueous
NaHCO3 (5 mL) was added. Et2O (15 mL) was then added, and
the water layer was separated and reextracted with Et2O (2 
5 mL). The organic layers were combined, washed with brine (2 
5 mL), and dried. Concentration at reduced pressure gave the crude
4-substituted dihydropyridine, which was used immediately in the
next step without further purification.
Phase-Transfer Reduction: The crude 4-substituted dihydropyri-
dine, together with dry ammonium formate (20 mol equiv.), dis-
solved in a solution of absolute methanol/THF (11 mL, 10:1), were
added to a slurry of activated 10% Pd/C (30 mg) in absolute meth-

title: Copper-Catalysed, Enantioselective Desymmetrisation of meso Cyclic Allylic Bis(diethyl phosphates) with Organozinc Reagents

FULL PAPER
Copper-Catalysed, Enantioselective Desymmetrisation of meso Cyclic Allylic
Bis(diethyl phosphates) with Organozinc Reagents
Umberto Piarulli,*[a] Philippe Daubos,[b] Christelle Claverie,[b] Chiara Monti,[b] and
Cesare Gennari*[b]
Keywords: Allylic substitution / Asymmetric synthesis / meso Desymmetrisation / Chiral ligands / Copper / Zinc
A highly regio-, diastereo- and enantioselective desymme-
trization of five-, six-, and seven-membered meso, cyclic al-
lylic bis(diethyl phosphates) (3–5) with organozinc reagents
was developed, using catalytic amounts (10 mol%) of
[Cu(OTf)]2·C6H6 and two different classes of chiral ligands:
Schiff bases 1 and phosphoramidites 2. Good to excellent en-
antioselectivities were obtained for every substrate by a sub-
tle balance of ligand structure and experimental conditions.
In particular, ee’s of up to 88 % were obtained for the five-
membered ring substrate 3 with ligands 1cjo and 1cjm using
Et2Zn (94 % ee with Me2Zn, 88 % ee with nBu2Zn). Schiff-
base ligands 1 were not effective with the six- and seven-
Introduction
The substitution of allylic functionalities by hard carbon
nucleophiles, such as organometallics, has recently attracted
much attention and several methods have been developed to
achieve regio-,[1] diastereo- and enantiocontrol. The leaving
group can be displaced either in an α or γ fashion by the
incoming carbon nucleophile, depending on the substrate,
leaving group, organometallic reagent and metal source.
Some catalytic, enantioselective protocols have recently ap-
peared using organozinc[2] or Grignard[3] reagents, and a
chiral copper complex. High ee’s were obtained using hin-
dered organozinc reagents, while reactions of less hindered
reagents proceeded with significantly lower enantioselectivi-
ty.[2a] Cinnamyl chlorides and bromides underwent allylic
alkylation with organozinc reagents with significant enanti-
oselectivity (up to 81 % ee), in the presence of copper phos-
phoramidite complexes.[2e,2f] The allylic substitution of 3-
substituted cinnamyl diethyl phosphates with organozinc
reagents, in the presence of copper pyridinyl peptide Schiff-

membered substrates 4 and 5. The use of phosphoramidite
ligands 2 afforded ee’s of up to 94 % (Et2Zn) for the six-mem-
bered ring product 7, and virtually only one enantiomer (ee
 98 %, with Et2Zn) for the seven-membered ring product 8.
In addition, the desymmetrisation of the conduritol derivative
10 was obtained, with ee’s of up to 86 %. In this case, a fully
functionalised cyclohexane derivative, containing four con-
tiguous stereocentres and a double bond, was obtained as a
single diastereomer and in high enantiomeric excess from an
achiral starting material.
(© Wiley-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, 69451 Weinheim,
Germany, 2005)
base ligands, was also found to proceed with 78–90 % ee
leading to the formation of asymmetric quaternary carbon
centres.[2c,2d] A highly enantioselective allylic substitution of
allylic chlorides by Grignard reagents (ee up to 96 %), cata-
lysed by chiral copper phosphoramidite complexes, was also
recently reported.[3d,3e,3f]
In the case of meso, cyclic allylic diol derivatives, the de-
symmetrisation by allylic substitution is a powerful syn-
thetic methodology for the construction of enantiomerically
enriched functionalised products.[4] This reaction can occur
with α- or γ-substitution, and either with overall retention
or overall inversion. In the case of α-substitution, where an
allylic alcohol derivative is obtained, a second allylic substi-
tution might occur, again in α or γ and either with retention
or inversion. Based on this complex scenario, up to 15 dif-
ferent products may be formed (four pairs of enantiomers
in the case of monosubstitution, and three pairs of enanti-
omers plus one meso compound in the case of disubstitu-
tion). The palladium-catalysed desymmetrisation of meso,
cyclic allylic diol derivatives, pioneered by Trost and co-
workers, is usually performed with soft nucleophiles and oc-
curs with α-substitution and overall retention.[4b,4c] A some-
what related enantioselective ring opening of meso-oxab-
icyclic alkenes with organometallic reagents was reported
by Lautens et al. (palladium-catalysed addition of alkylzinc
reagents and RhI-catalysed addition of arylboronic acids),[5]
and by Pineschi, Feringa and co-workers (CuI-catalysed ad-
dition of alkylzinc reagents).[6] In the first case, the product
of γ-substitution with retention is obtained (the nucleophile
U. Piarulli, P. Daubos, C. Claverie, C. Monti, C. Gennari
FULL PAPER
attacks from the same side of the allylic leaving group),[5]
whereas in the second case the γ-substitution reaction takes
place with inversion.[6]
We have recently disclosed a new highly regio-, diastereo-,
and enantioselective desymmetrisation of meso, cyclic allylic
bis(diethyl phosphates) with organozinc reagents catalysed
by copper(i) complexes of chiral Schiff-base ligands 1[7]
and of chiral, binaphthol derived, phosphoramidites 2
(Scheme 1).[8]
