catalyst can be generated from almost racemic environment
to up to 99.5% ee and subsequently propagates this chirality
to provide propargylic alcohols in up to 86% ee.
reactions, and thus can be described as Frank-like reaction
network operating in a closed system to give rise to absolute
asymmetric synthesis under kinetic control.[1]
Thus, a catalytic sequence where an autocatalyst evolves
with asymmetric amplification and could act as catalyst in
an ensuing asymmetric reaction, would become advan-
tageous; because high enantiopurity is generated from a
minimal fraction through such a proliferation process and
could potentially propagate in a range of chemical transfor-
mations (Scheme 1). Ideally, and perhaps more challenging,
such a catalytic system should operate in a two-step one-pot
procedure. In addition, this autocatalysis–catalysis sequence
opens for alternative asymmetric processes, as it does not
rely on the chiral pool. In our approach to such an autocat-
alytic system we made use of Soai’s compound 1.
Indeed, a practically perfect asymmetric amplification
was observed in the asymmetric autocatalysis of (5-pyr-
imidyl)alkanol 1 by addition of Zn(iPr)2 to (5-pyrimidyl)-
aldehyde 2.[6] Soai’s group also showed that a consecutive
system of asymmetric autocatalysis and asymmetric cataly-
sis provided enantioenriched compounds with significantly
larger amplification of ee in the autocatalytic alkylation of
aldehydes using the formed (5-pyrimidyl)alkanol 1.[7] Sur-
prisingly, this strategy has yet to be extended to a range of
potentially useful asymmetric transformations other than
Soai’s alkylation systems. These properties indicated to us
that 1 should be suitable for propagation of chirality in the
alkynylation of aldehydes as a model reaction.
This reaction is particularly suitable because the zinc alk-
ynylides reagents could be generated in situ and the versatil-
ity of the products that serve as precursors for a variety of
chiral targets.[8] In 1990, Niwa and Soai reported the first
enantioselective addition of alkynylzinc reagents to alde-
hydes using amino alcohols as catalysts to provide proparg-
ylic alcohols in the range of 7–35% ee.[8e] The limited
M. Funes-Maldonado, B. Sieng, M. Amedjkouh
SHORT COMMUNICATION
Scheme 1. Consecutive asymmetric catalyst amplification and subsequent alkynylation of aldehydes.
enantioselectivity of the reaction led to the development of
more efficient chiral ligands, which have successfully been
applied in these reactions. Examples include BINOL and
its derivatives,[9] amino alcohols,[10] imino alcohols,[11] sul-
fonamides,[12] oxazolidines[13] and β-hydroxy amides.[14]
More recently, this methodology also provided access to
chiral propargylamines.[15]
Results and Discussion
Herein, we report an unprecedented enantioselective ad-
dition of alkynylzinc reagents to azaaryl aldehydes in the
presence of (R)-1 as chiral catalyst to generate enantioen-
riched propargylic alcohols in up to 86% ee.[16] In this com-
munication, we also demonstrate the possibility and the ad-
vantage of a one-pot sequence combining autocatalysis with
catalysis. To the best of our knowledge, no use of enantio-
enriched autocatalyst to promote a different enantioselec-
tive reaction such as alkynylation has been reported pre-
viously.
To evaluate the efficiency of autocatalyst (R)-1 for asym-
metric alkynylation, we initially focused our efforts to estab-
lish the optimal working conditions in the reaction of 3-
pyridinecarboxaldehyde
(4a)
with
phenylacetylene
(Table 1). (R)-1 was prepared beforehand by asymmetric
self-replication with  99.5% ee following Soai’s pro-
cedure.[17a]
In our first attempt, the alkynylzinc reagent was prepared
in situ by deprotonation of phenylacetylene with dialkylzinc
in toluene. Thus, stirring both starting materials in the pres-
ence of 20 mol-% of (R)-1 ( 99.5% ee) at room tempera-
ture for 22 hours followed by addition of aldehyde 4a at
0 °C provided 5a in a low yield of 22% and 67% ee (Table 1,
entry 1).[18] The low yield was attributed to the side reaction

Hence, the deprotonation of phenylacetylene by dimeth-
ylzinc in toluene is a relatively slow step. Heating the alkyne
and Me2Zn at 75 °C for 2.5 h helped overcome this side
reaction (Table 1, entry 2). However, decreasing the amount
of Me2Zn and phenylacetylene to an equimolar mixture
gave a disappointing yield of only 11% and a decrease in
ee values (Table 1, entry 3). In this case, 1H NMR analysis
Asymmetric Alkynylation of Azaaryl Aldehydes with Soai Autocatalyst
of the crude revealed only 24% conversion to the corre-
sponding propargylic alcohol 5a. In an attempt to push the
reaction to completion without increasing the risk of meth-
ylation, we decided to increase the amount of phenylacetyl-
ene compared to Me2Zn. Gratifyingly, a ratio of 2.5:7 in
Me2Zn/alkyne not only led to an increase in yield from 64%
to 91% but also increased the enantioselectivity of the reac-
tion from 68% to 76% ee (Table 1, entry 4). A temperature
increase from 0 °C to room temperature or decrease from
0 °C to –40 °C all led to lower yields and ee (entry 5 and
6). Lowering the amount of (R)-1 from 20 to 10 mol-% gave
product 5a with lower yield and ee (Table 1, entry 7).
Several groups reported that the use of DiMPEG 2000
[poly(ethyleneglycol) dimethyl ether, MW 2000] markedly
improved the enantioselectivity in the addition of alkynes
to aldehydes.[11a,19] However, in our hands, addition of
20 mol-% DiMPEG did not show any beneficial effects on
this reaction leading to nearly the same enantiomeric purity
with a slight decrease in yield (Table 1, entry 8). Finally, we
decided to examine other dialkylzinc reagents as precursors
of zinc alkynylides, anticipating an easier deprotonation of
the alkyne, although with a higher risk of competing alkyl-
ation reaction. In addition, this might induce changes in the
structure of the catalytically active zinc aggregates. Indeed,
the use of Et2Zn not only resulted in lower yield (due to
the formation of the alkyl adduct) but also decreased the
enantioselectivity (Table 1, entry 9). Surprisingly and more
interesting, the reaction conducted with the more reactive
iPr2Zn provided the opposite enantiomer of the product
with 42% ee and good yield (Table 1, entry 10). But, again
products from competing alkyl addition side reaction were
observed.
Having optimized the reaction conditions (Table 1, entry
4), we decided to examine the scope of the propagation of
autocatalytic chirality. We used autocatalyst (R)-1 to pro-
mote the reaction of alkynylzinc with substituted nicotinal-
dehyde. Results depicted in Table 2 demonstrate that alk-
ynylation proceeds with high enantioselecivity up to 86%
ee and good yields, and no alkylation by-products were de-
tected. While the reaction is compatible with a range of
substituents on the substrate, these results also reveal a ge-
neral trend for the alkynylation, e.g., substituents at the 5-
position seemed to be more suitable (Table 2, entry 1 and
4). However, substituents at the 4-position had a detrimen-
tal effect on the enantioselectivity as the propargylic alcohol
was obtained as a racemate (Table 2, entry 6). The observed
failure could be attributed to σ-EWG at C2 and C4 re-
sulting in lower Lewis basicity at nitrogen and thus less co-
ordination to the active catalyst (Table 2, entries 2, 5 and
6). It is important to mention that alkynylation also works
with the regioisomers, 2- and 4-pyridinecarbaldehydes, but
the propargylic alcohol rearranged to the corresponding en-
one.[20] The same rearrangement was observed when using
ethyl propiolate as nucleophile. Another commercially avail-
able and highly versatile nucleophile TMS-alkyne was suc-
cessfully employed to yield the product with high enantio-
selectivity (Table 2, entry 11). As we mentioned above, zinc
alkynylide formation required heating of the alkyne and di-

of TMS-alkyne and makes its use very difficult. We decided
to pursue our studies with phenylacetylene as nucleophile

Interestingly, autocatalyst (R)-1 was also successful with
other heterocycles providing a moderate 40% ee in the reac-
tion with 5-thiazolecarbaldehyde (Table 2, entry 7), whereas
3-quinolinecarbaldehyde afforded the corresponding prod-
uct with increased enantioselectivity of 65% ee (Table 2, en-
M. Funes-Maldonado, B. Sieng, M. Amedjkouh
SHORT COMMUNICATION
try 8). Notably, quinolinecarbaldehyde also provided the
corresponding propargylic alcohol 5i with the same abso-
lute configuration as the autocatalyst (R)-1. To explore the
extent of the substituent effect on the stereoinduction at the
6-position on the pyridine, we first investigated the reaction
of 6-(3,3-dimethylbut-1-yn-1-yl)nicotinaldehyde, a reminis-
cence of the Soai aldehyde. The latter was converted into
alkynol 5j in 76% yield, with 65% ee (Table 2, entry 9).
More notable is that formation of alkynol 5j also favored
the R enantiomer in the presence of (R)-1. In sharp con-
trast, 5-(3,3-dimethylbut-1-yn-1-yl)nicotinaldehyde exhib-
ited opposite enantioselectivity and low reactivity, provid-
ing the S enantiomer of 5k in 63% ee (Table 2, entry 10).
To verify whether an asymmetric induction may have
been promoted by alkynylation product 5, i.e. asymmetric
autocatalysis, a set of reactions was performed. First, the
ee of product 5a was analyzed over time as aldehyde 4a was
treated with alkynylzinc in the presence of catalyst (R)-1.
These experiments revealed that product 5a was formed at
its highest 79% ee at the early stages of the reaction; fol-
lowed by erosion to 72% ee at the end of the reaction,
which indicated that no asymmetric amplification occurred
in the alkynylation reaction.
We then performed several alkynylation reactions in the
absence of the Soai catalyst but using 20 mol-% of the en-
antioenriched products 5a, 5d, and 5e. All experiments gave
the corresponding alkynols in racemic mixture after sub-
tracting the 20 mol-% of the initial chiral product, which
shows the absence of asymmetric autocatalysis of alkynols.
This provides evidence that asymmetric alkynylation is cata-
lyzed by Soai alcohol (R)-1.
Furthermore, it was appealing to examine the correlation
between the ee of the catalyst derived from (R)-1 and ee of
product. Thus, a series of alkynylations of 3-pyridinecarbal-
dehyde (4a) with phenylacetylene catalysed by 20 mol-% of
(R)-1 with variable ee values were performed. Interestingly,
the variation of ee values of precursor (R)-1 generated
asymmetric alkynylation and a positive nonlinear effect is
observed (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Plot of ee of propargylic alcohol 5a as a function of the
ee value of catalyst (R)-1. The ee values were determined by HPLC
with a Daicel Chiralcel OD column.

4084
This positive effect may be attributed to aggregation pat-
terns of (R)-1/Zn to form homo- and heterochiral dimer
species with different reactivity and enantioselectivity.[4]
However, as the alkynylation products are structurally sim-
ilar to Soai product, such a (+)–NLE might also stem from
a synergistic interaction between (R)-1/Zn and 5/Zn. There-
fore, further investigations are carried out to elucidate this
question.
Due to the high efficiency of the amplification of ee in
asymmetric autocatalysis of (R)-1, we next focused our at-
tention on the autocatalysis–catalysis sequence without iso-
lation of (R)-3 as shown in Scheme 2. We envisioned a pro-
liferation sequence in which (R)-1 is able to amplify itself
enantiomerically, and consecutively become a chiral catalyst
for the alkynylation of aldehydes. To do so, 20 mol-% of
(R)-1 with  98% ee were generated in situ through auto-
catalytic amplification by reaction of 2-(tert-butylethynyl)-
pyrimidine-5-carbaldehyde (2) with iPr2Zn in presence of
an initial amount of 2 mol-% of (R)-1 originally with 16%
ee, in three consecutive cycles. Progress of asymmetric am-
plification was monitored by sampling and HPLC analyses
and showed a prompt increase in ee already in the first cycle
(see supporting information). Thus, the isopropylzinc alk-
oxide (R)-3 becomes an efficient catalyst in the enantiose-
lective alkynylation of nicotinaldehyde 4a to yield 91% of
the corresponding propargylic alcohol 5a with 65% ee.
Scheme 2. Asymmetric alkynylation of nicotinaldehyde.
In summary, Soai’s autocatalyst 1 – which is readily avail-
able in 99% ee by asymmetric amplification from virtually
achiral precursor – becomes a catalyst in an ensuing enan-
tioselective alkynylation of azaaryl aldehydes with moderate
to good level of asymmetric induction (up to 86% ee). This
observed specific reactivity confirms the uniqueness of the
Soai autocatalyst. Interestingly, the reaction exhibits poten-
tial for a two-step one-pot autocatalysis–catalysis sequence
as the active isopropylzinc alkoxide 3 could be amplified
Asymmetric Alkynylation of Azaaryl Aldehydes with Soai Autocatalyst
enantiomerically to 98% ee, and used without isolation.
Further investigations are currently focused to address the
working mechanism in order to access a more efficient one-
pot process leading to improved ee. This provides entry to
chiral catalysts beyond the traditional chiral pool and indi-
cates a potentially novel approach to access enantiomer-
ically pure molecules.
Experimental Section
General Procedure for the Asymmetric Alkynylation Reaction: In an
oven-dried flask under an inert atmosphere of nitrogen a solution
of Me2Zn 1.2 m in toluene (0.77 mL, 0.93 mmol) was added slowly
to a solution of alkyne (2.6 mmol) in 2.6 mL of dry toluene. The
resulting solution was stirred at 75 °C for 2 h. Then the reaction
mixture was cooled down to room temperature and a solution of
ligand 1 (0.075 mmol) in 0.3 mL of toluene was added and stirred
at room temp. for 1 h. The reaction mixture was then cooled to
0 °C and the aldehyde (0.373 mmol) was added and stirring contin-
ued for 18–22 h. The reaction was quenched by adding aqueous
saturated NH4Cl (2.5 mL) and stirred vigorously for 10 min. The
toluene phase was separated, and the aqueous phase was extracted
with EtOAc. The combined organic fractions were dried with
Na2SO4, filtered, and concentrated under reduced pressure. The
crude product was then purified by flash column chromatography
on silica gel.

Aluminum chloride promoted cross-coupling of trisubstituted 
enol phosphates with organozinc reagents en route to 
stereoselective synthesis of tamoxifen and its analogues 
Vladislav Kotek,[a] Peter Polák,[a] Hana Dvořáková,[b] and Tomáš Tobrman*[a] 
 
Abstract: A new methodology for the stereoselective cross-coupling 
reaction of aryl zinc chlorides with trisubstituted enol phosphates is 
described. The developed methodology requires aluminum chloride 
as a promoter, and the reaction conditions tolerate various functional 
groups. The observed reactivity pattern of trisubstituted enol 
phosphates was used for the stereoselective preparation of 
tamoxifen and its analogues. 
Introduction 
Substrates bearing acyclic tetrasubstituted double bond form an 
important structural motif that has found many applications, for 
instance as biologically active compounds. The importance of 
tetrasubstituted alkenes can be illustrated by increasing effort 
placed on the stereoselective synthesis of tetrasubstituted 
alkenes.1 The diversity of building blocks used for the synthesis 
of substituted alkenes has been reviewed.2 Among these 
templates, mono-, di-, and trisubstituted enol phosphates play 
an important role, mainly due to their availability and variability. 
Thus, a wide variety of cross-coupling reactions of di- and 
trisubstituted enol phosphates have been reported.3 Quite 
surprisingly, acyclic trisubstituted enol phosphates have found 
only a few applications in transition metal-catalyzed cross-
coupling reactions. Their typical applications include copper(I) 
catalyzed methylation,4 the Kumada-Corriu reaction,5 and 
Suzuki and Negishi cross-coupling.6 In addition to the above 
reports, transformations of trisubstituted enol phosphates, 
including 
elimination 
reactions,7 
radical 
processes8 
and 
heterocycle synthesis have been reported.9 In a paper by 
Nakatsuji,6 the stereoselective synthesis of tetrasubstituted 
alkenes was performed via the reaction of phosphates 4 or 6 
with organozinc reagents under harsh reaction conditions 
(Scheme 1). Similarly, Brown5 described the cross-coupling 
reactions of enol phosphates with Grignard reagents in THF at 
70 °C. 
 
 
 
 
 
Scheme 1. Overall scheme of the AlCl3 promoted Negishi reaction of enol

As part of our synthetic efforts, we have disclosed that the 
triply electrophilic template 1 can be transformed to the 
trisubstituted enol phosphates 2 in a highly stereoselective 
fashion ( 98% E or Z) using a two-fold Suzuki reaction.10 Next, 
the introduction of the alkyl group was accomplished by coupling 
with the trialkylaluminum reagent, and aryl substituents were 
installed by the 
Kumada-Coriu coupling reaction 
using 
PdCl2(SPhos)2 
and 
2-[2-(dimethylamino)ethoxy]ethanol 
(DMAEE). Compared to the work of Nakatsuji, our protocol 
possesses several key advantages, including an improved 
stereochemical outcome of the process as well as a virtually 
general scope that would enable the synthesis of almost any 
tetrasubstituted alkene starting from simple and easily available 
dibromo enol phosphates. However, the high reactivity of 
Grignard reagents conflicts with the preparation of functionalized 
tetrasubstituted alkenes. 
Results and Discussion 
Therefore, we looked for a more convenient methodology for the 
introduction of aryl substituents into the molecule of phosphate 2 
by a cross-coupling reaction with organometallic reagents. 
Similar to our first report,10 dialkyl enol phosphates were used as 
the starting compounds because of their simple synthetic 
availability and better atom economy compared to diaryl enol

The optimized reaction conditions were used for the 
introduction of diverse aryl substituents. In contrast to the 
optimized results (Table 1, entry 10), a 4-tolyl substituent was 
introduced by the coupling reaction of the neopentyl glycol 
phosphate 2b in 91% yield (Scheme 2, entry 1). Both E and Z 
stereoisomers 3b,c were prepared by using phosphates 2c,d as 
the starting compound. Thus, the present methodology enabled 
the regio- and stereoselective introduction four different aryl 
substituents while retaining the stereoselective configuration of 
the double bond (Scheme 2, entries 2 and 3). The methodology 
also tolerates sensitive ester and nitrile functional groups, as 
demonstrated by the preparation of alkenes 3e,f (Scheme 2, 
entries 5 and 6). The AlCl3-mediated coupling reaction also

The significant yield dependence of the cross-coupling outcome 
on the structure of the phosphate ester during the preparation of 
alkenes 3a drove us to study the reaction course in detail. 
Analogously to the McKenna reaction,12 we reasoned that 
aluminum chloride is responsible for the cleavage of the EtO 
bond, affording the product 4b and lowering the yield of the 
coupling reaction. Thus, a model phosphate 2a was mixed with 
4-CH3C6H4ZnClLiCl, and the resultant mixture was heated to 
60 °C. No conversion of the starting phosphate 2a to the product 
4b was observed within two days. When aluminum chloride was 
added to the reaction mixture, complete conversion to the 
product 4b was observed. The structure of the observed product 
4b was confirmed as the sodium salt 4c using HR MS. However, 
the cyclic phosphate 2b was inert to decomposition even if 
heated to 60 °C in the presence of 4-CH3C6H4ZnClLiCl and 
AlCl3. Based on observed experimental evidence, we reasoned 
that the side product 4b is formed via aluminum chloride-
mediated nucleophilic substitution at the methylene center 
(Scheme 3). On the other hand, tris(p-tolyl)aluminum, and 
dichloro(p-tolyl)aluminum do not react with phosphate 2a in the 
presence of PdCl2(SPhos)2 at 45 °C, excluding ZnAl 
transmetalation as an alternative route of the coupling reaction. 
Therefore, analogously to the above case, we believe that 
coordination of AlCl3 to the phosphate moiety facilitates oxidative 
addition of Pd(0) to OCsp2 bond. However, precise role of 
aluminum chloride for the cross-coupling of trisubstituted enol 
phosphates is a subject of further studies.

In addition to an effort of other groups,13 we performed the 
synthesis of tamoxifen (3r) and its analogues 3p,q (Scheme 4). 
Following a previous report,10 we prepared dibromo enol 
phosphate 1a starting from propanal and bromoform. Then, the 
Suzuki reaction of 1a with phenylboronic and 4-TBSO 
phenylboronic acid afforded substituted alkenes 2q,r as the sole 
Z-stereoisomers. The second bromine atom substitution by the 
Suzuki reaction of 2q,r with para substituted boronic acid was 
used for the introduction of a 2-chloroethoxyphenyl substituent 
to the cis-position. Subsequently, a Lewis acid-catalyzed Negishi 
reaction or the cross-coupling reaction with tribenzylaluminum, 
phenyl zinc chloride and ferrocenyl zinc chloride led to the 
tetrasubstituted alkenes 3l-o. The overall synthesis of tamoxifen 
and its analogues 3p-r was finished by a simple chlorine 
displacement using dimethylamine or pyrrolidine. Thus, the 
preparation of alkenes 3p-r was accomplished in four simple 
steps starting from the dibromo enol phosphate 1a in overall 
yields ranging from 47-73%. Moreover, the prepared compounds 
were >98% (E) or (Z), as deduced from the 1H and 13C NMR 
spectra of the isolated compounds.

Conclusions 
In conclusion, we have shown that developed methodology for 
the aluminum chloride-promoted cross-coupling reaction of 
trisubstituted enol phosphates catalyzed by PdCl2(SPhos)2 in 
THF at 45 °C is a valuable method for the cross-coupling

reaction of acyclic trisubstituted dialkyl enol phosphates. The 
methodology tolerates diverse functional groups, including ester 
and nitrile groups. Moreover, the combination of a previously 
developed methodology for the three-fold cross-coupling 
synthesis of tetrasubstituted alkenes with a Lewis acid-promoted 
coupling reaction provides simple and efficient access to the 
highly stereoselective synthesis of tamoxifen and its derivatives. 
Further experiments to explore benefits of AlCl3 promoted cross-
coupling reactions of phosphates are ongoing in our laboratory. 
Experimental Section 
All reactions were performed under an argon atmosphere. NMR spectra 
were measured on a Varian Gemini 300 (1H, 300.07 MHz; 13C, 75.46 
MHz), a Agilent Technologies 400-MR (1H, 399.80 MHz and 13C, 100.51 
MHz) spectrometer at 298 K. Mass spectra were measured on ZAB-SEQ 
(VG Analytical). The solvents were dried and degassed by standard 
procedures; silica gel (Merck, Silica Gel 60, 40-63 m) was used for 
column chromatography. BuLi (2.5 M solution in hexane), and other 
compounds were purchased. Compounds 2a,c,d,e,f, 1a were prepared 
according to the literature procedure.10 Concentration of BuLi was 
determined by titration using menthol and 1,10-phenanthroline before 
use. Arylzinc reagents were prepared by the reaction of arylzinc 
iodides/bromides with butyllithium in dry THF at -78 °C followed by the 
reaction with ZnCl2. 
General procedure for AlCl3 promoted cross-coupling reaction of 
phosphates 2 with organozinc reagents 
A solution of organozinc reagent (1.2 equiv, 0.7 mmol) in dry THF (1 mL) 
was added to a solution of phosphate (1.0 equiv, 0.5 mmol) and 
PdCl2(SPhos)2 (4 mol %) in dry THF (1 mL/mmol). Then a solution of 
aluminum chloride in dry THF (1 mL, 0.7 M solution in dry THF) was 
added. The resultant mixture was stirred for 24 hours at 45 °C. The 
reaction mixture was diluted with ether and 1M tartaric acid or 1M 
potassium sodium tartrate was added. Clear organic layer was washed 
with brine, dried over MgSO4, and concentrated under reduce pressure. 
Column chromatography afforded the title compound.  
(Z)-1-phenyl-1-(4-methoxyphenyl)-2-(4-methylphenyl)hexene (3a): 
Prepared according to the general procedure starting from phosphate 2b 
(0.215 g, 0.50 mmol), 4-methylphenylzinc chloride [prepared from 4-
bromotoluene (0.120 g, 0.70 mmol), nBuLi (0.28 mL, 0.7 mmol), and zinc 
chloride (0.7 mL of 1 M solution in THF)], PdCl2(SPhos)2 (20 mg, 4 mol %, 
0.02 mmol) and AlCl3 (1 mL, 0.7M solution in THF). The reaction mixture 
was stirred for 24 h at 45 °C. Column chromatography (DCM/hexane 1:4,

Palladium-Catalyzed Formylation of Alkenylzinc Reagents with S-
(4-Nitrophenyl) Thioformate 
Ryosuke Haraguchi,* Sho-go Tanazawa, Naoya Tokunaga, and Shin-ichi Fukuzawa* 
Abstract: We report the synthesis of enal compounds by palladium-
catalyzed formylation of alkenylzinc reagents with S-(4-nitrophenyl) 
thioformate. Various functional groups were tolerated in the present 
reaction. 
1H NMR experiments revealed that the products had a non-
protected formyl group, which can be utilized for further C−C bond 
formation reactions. We successfully achieved the one-pot synthesis 
of a 1,5-diene-3-ol compound via sequential formylation and 
allylation. 
Introduction 
α,β-Unsaturated aldehydes are useful intermediates in organic 
synthesis as they can be employed as Michael acceptors or 
reactive carbonyl groups.1 Among the number of synthetic 
routes to these compounds,2-4 introduction of a formyl group into 
organic molecules is considered as the most straightforward 
approach.5-9 Formylation of organolithium or organomagnesium 
reagents with formamide derivatives is the simplest protocol for 
the preparation of enal derivatives, although their high 
nucleophilicity makes it difficult to synthesize the functionalized 
enal compounds.5 Alternatively, the transition-metal-catalyzed 
hydroformylation of alkynes has been achieved by several 
research groups.6 Moreover, palladium- and nickel-catalyzed 
reductive formylation of vinyl halides or pseudohalides has been 
also reported.7 However, harsh reaction conditions and the use 
of uncommon ligands and additives are the practical limitations 
of these synthetic methods. Moreover, the functional tolerability 
of these reactions in most cases has not been studied well. Thus, 
the development of synthetic methods for the preparation of 
functionalized enals is still sought after. Recently, Mariano, Xie, 
and Wang reported the organocatalytic formylation of aryl- and 
alkenylboronic acids, which has excellent functional tolerability.9  
We 
have 
recently 
developed 
the 
palladium-catalyzed 
formylation of arylzinc reagents with S-phenyl thioformate 
(Fukuyama-type formylation).10,11 As a logical extension of this 
report, we focused on the palladium-catalyzed formylation of 
alkenylzinc reagents. However, we expected this formylation to 
be much more difficult than that of the arylzinc reagents because 
of a side reaction of the enal products with a thiolate anion 
generated in situ. As expected, the reaction of alkenylzinc 
reagent 1a with thioformate 2a under the optimized reaction 
conditions employed in the formylation of arylzinc reagents 
yielded only 8% of the product (Scheme 1), with the formation of 
the Michael adduct. Thus, the choice of formylating reagents 
and optimization of the catalytic reaction conditions are crucial 
for the success of this reaction. Herein, we report the palladium-
catalyzed formylation of alkenylzinc reagents with S-(4-
nitrophenyl) thioformate, which dramatically promoted the 
present reaction. Under mild reaction conditions, the formylation 
reaction was completed within 10 min to afford the enal 
derivatives in high yields. 1H NMR monitoring of the reaction 
mixture revealed that a formyl group of the enal product existed 
in a non-protected form. We also achieved the one-pot synthesis 
of the 1,5-diene-3-ol compound via the formation of two C−C 
bonds by sequential formylation and allylation. 
 
Scheme 1. Formylation of alkenylzinc reagent 1a with thioformate 2a. 
Results and Discussion 
Initially, we screened the formyl sources, ligands, solvents, 
and additives used in the palladium-catalyzed formylation of 
alkenylzinc reagent 1a. We found that the treatment of 1a with 
S-(4-nitrophenyl) thioformate (2b) in the presence of Pd(OAc)2 
(5.0 mol%), P(3,5-F2C6H3)3 (9.0 mol%), and ZnBr2 (1.0 eq) in 
THF at −20 °C for 10 min gave enal 3a in 87% yield. The 
important reaction parameters for the present reaction are 
shown in Table 1. Tri(2-furyl)phosphine, which is the most 
effective ligand for the palladium-catalyzed formylation of 
arylzinc reagents,11 decreased the chemical yield (entry 2). 
Although PPh3 gave the desired product in high yield (entry 3), 
other monodentate phosphine ligands bearing electron-donating 
or electron-withdrawing substituents provided the desired 
product in somewhat lower yields (entries 4-8). Bidentate 
phosphine ligands such as dppf and binap were not effective for 
the present reaction (entries 9 and 10). The use of zinc bromide 
as an additive is the most effective although other zinc salts also 
increased the reaction efficiency to some extent (entries 1 and 
11-14).12 Notably, the efficiency of this reaction relied on the 
choice of thioformates. We examined various thioformates 2a-f 
in the formylation reaction, and found that the thioformates 
bearing electron-withdrawing substituents gave 3a in good yield 
(entries 1 and 16), while those with electron-rich aromatic rings 
or an alkyl substituent decreased the chemical yields (entries 
17-19). 
We next investigated the reaction profile using different 
thioformates 2a-d in the present formylation. As shown in Figure 
1, the reaction rate was dramatically enhanced when 2b was 
used as the formylating reagent. 
The scope of the alkenylzinc reagents was examined (Table 2). 
Alkenylzinc reagents bearing diverse functional groups on the 
arene ring underwent the palladium-catalyzed formylation to 
afford the corresponding products in high yield. Halogen groups 
(entries 2 and 3) and an acetal group (entry 8) remained intact 
under these reaction conditions. The present reaction also

of an oxothioacetal 4 (eq 1). In order to obtain structural 
information on products 3, we carried out a 1H NMR experiment 
of the reaction mixture using 1a and 2b under the optimized 
conditions except for the solvent and reaction time. The 1H NMR 
spectra of (i) alkenylzinc reagent 1a, (ii) thioformate 2b, (iii) 
product 3a, and (iv) the reaction mixture of 1a and 2b in THF-d8 
within 5 min are shown in Figure 2. The doublet peak around 10 
ppm for the spectrum (iv) was attributed to the unprotected 
formyl group of 3a. In addition, we did not observe any peaks 
around 5-7 ppm, which could be attributed to the signal for 
oxothioacetal derivatives,13 other than that for 1a in the spectrum 
(iv). These results indicated that the desired product 3a had an 
unprotected formyl group, which can be further utilized for the 
C−C bond formation in a one-pot system. 
 
 
Figure 2. 
1H NMR spectra of (i) 1a, (ii) 2b, (iii) 3a, and (iv) the reaction mixture 
of 1a and 2b in THF-d8. 
Finally, we present an application of the present reaction, as 
shown in Scheme 2. After the formylation of 1a under the 
optimized reaction conditions, the addition of allylzinc reagent 5 
to the reaction mixture with subsequent stirring at −20 °C for 10 
min afforded 1,5-diene-3-ol 6 in 76% yield over two steps.[14] 
This transformation enabled two C−C bond formations in the 
one-pot reaction, which demonstrated the versatility of the 
unprotected enal synthesis. 
 
Scheme 2. One-pot transformation: formylation and allylation. 
Conclusions 
In summary, we have demonstrated the palladium-catalyzed 
formylation of alkenylzinc reagents using S-(4-nitrophenyl) 
thioformate. Various functional groups were tolerated in the 
formylation. 1H NMR analysis of the reaction mixture revealed 
that the formyl group of the enal product existed in the 
unprotected form. Thus, the addition of allylzinc reagent 5 to the 
reaction mixture enabled the subsequent allylation to give the 
1,5-diene-3-ol 
compound. 
Further 
investigations 
including 
formylation with alkylzinc reagents are underway in our 
laboratory. 
Experimental Section 
General 
procedure 
for 
palladium-catalyzed 
formylation 
of 
alkenylzinc reagents 1 with 2:  The reaction was performed in a 20-mL 
Schlenk flask equipped with a teflon-coated magnetic stirrer. ZnBr2 (45 
mg, 0.20 mmol) was heated to 140 °C under high vacuum for 1 h. After 
cooling to room temperature, Pd(OAc)2 (2.3 mg, 0.010 mmol) and 
tris(3,5-difluorophenyl)phosphine (6.7 mg, 0.018 mmol) were added to 
the vessel. Varying amounts of THF were added in order to reach a total 
volume of 1.5 mL, and the mixture was stirred at –20 °C for 5 min. After 
the addition of S-(4-nitrophenyl) thioformate (2b, 37 mg, 0.20 mmol) at –
20 °C, alkenylzinc reagent 1 (0.24 mmol, in THF) was then added at –
20 °C. The resulting mixture was stirred at –20 °C for 10 min. The 
reaction was quenched with saturated aqueous NH4Cl solution (3.0 mL). 
The resulting mixture was extracted with ethyl acetate. The combined 
organic layers were washed with brine, dried over sodium sulfate, and 
concentrated in vacuo. Purification by flash silica gel column 
chromatography using hexane/ethyl acetate as an eluent gave the 
corresponding enal 3.

In situ generation of alkynylzinc and its subsequent cross-
coupling reaction in a flow reactor  
Mohanraj Kandasamy, [a] Yu- Hsuan Huang, [a] Balaji Ganesan,[a] Gopal Chandru Senadi[c] and Wei-Yu 
Lin*[a, b] 
Abstract: A highly efficient and convenient Negishi cross-coupling 
reaction has been developed for the synthesis of unsymmetrical 
alkynes and enynes in a continuous-flow process. The reaction 
proceeds through an in situ generated alkynylzinc reagent by the 
reaction of lithium acetylide with zinc halide at room temperature 
followed by a cross-coupling with aryl or vinyl iodides. The notable 
features of this work over the conventional benchtop method are mild 
reaction conditions, good to excellent yields, broad functional group 
compatibility, short residence time (73 sec) and especially desilylation 
of TMS group with the residence time of only 10.5 sec. 
Introduction 
Alkynes are valuable building blocks because of their versatile 
use 
in 
natural 
products, 
pharmaceuticals, 
and 
material 
sciences.[1] In this context, the alkynylation of aryl halides by 
Sonogashira reaction[2] has gained significant attention for the 
synthesis of functionalized alkynes.[3] However, the production of 
these alkynes on an industrial scale using the conventional 
method still remains a potential challenge.[4]  
 
Continuous-flow mediated transition-metal catalysis has gained 
much attention in recent years as an alternative for benchtop 
chemistry because of the key benefits like enhanced mass and 
heat transfer, reduced reaction volumes, improved sample and 
reagents mixing.[5] Thus, the development of new synthetic 
methods under flow technology that could deliver the desired 
compounds in an environmentally benign manner on a larger 
scale with ease of operation is an essential area of research in 
the scientific community.  
 
The pioneering work developed by Yoshida and co-workers on 
organolithium flash-chemistry has created a bench mark for the 
researchers to do synthetic transformations from in situ generated 
organolithium in the flow-process.[6] For instances, Buchwald and 
Yoshida independently developed the continuous-flow synthesis 
of biaryls enabled by multistep lithiation / borylation / Suzuki–
Miyaura cross-coupling sequence.[7] Ryu et al developed the 
synthesis of metalloproteinase inhibitor having a high space time 
yield (STY) of 20.4 g/Lh,[8] by Sonogashira cross-coupling 
reaction. Similarly, James et al reported the drug-like 3- 
aminoindolizine derivatives with STY of 1.6 g/Lh[9] from milligram 
to gram scale.[8-10] Despite these significant advancements, some 
of the methods require copper as co-catalyst that may lead to the 
undesired homocoupled product (Glaser coupling), stoichiometric 
bases, high temperatures and long reaction times. To overcome 
the drawbacks, modified catalytic conditions has been reported in 
the literature,[4]but, those reagents are expensive or need to be 
prepared in the laboratories which may hamper the practicality in 
the large scale.  
 
On the other hand, the formation of C(sp2)-C(sp) and C(sp3)-
C(sp3) bonds via the Negishi reaction using palladium- or nickel-
catalyzed coupling of organozinc compounds with various 
halides[11] have been extensively studied because of its mild 
conditions and low toxicity of zinc salts.[12] However, the high 
reactivity and sensitivity of organozinc reagents to air/moisture 
makes it difficult to prepare under cryogenic conditions.[13] To date, 
only a few methodologies have been reported for the in situ 
generation of organozinc and its subsequent use in cross-
coupling or electrophilic reactions in flow chemistry.[14] Knochel 
and co-workers demonstrated the in situ zincations of 
functionalized arenes and heteroarenes using (Cy2N)2Zn·2LiCl in 
a continuous flow system followed by a batch process.[14a] 
Buchwald and co-workers[15] reported the synthesis of aryloxirane 
derivatives via an in situ generated organozinc reagents followed 
by Negishi cross-coupling. Recently, Alcázar and co-workers 
reported the photoinduced[16] Pd or Ni catalyzed Negishi cross-
couplings in a flow reactor using the zinc metal. Nevertheless, 
applying these methods for the preparation of organozinc by a 
lithium base still demands a low temperature conditions nor 
further transformation in a batch reactor and excessive amount of 
starting materials. By considering the above facts and our 
continuing interest in lithium acetylide chemistry[17] Herein, we 
designed an alternative approach for the synthesis of internal 
alkynes and enynes via Negishi cross-coupling between an in situ 
generated alkynylzinc reagents and aryl or vinyl iodides in a 
simple and robust flow system using commercial catalyst and 
ligand that can enable the gram scale synthesis. 
Results and Discussion 
A flow setup has been made using three T-shaped micromixers 
(M1, M2 and M3), three tubing reactors [(R1 (800 µm), R2 (1000 
µm) and R3 (1000 µm), and a heating unit as presented in 
Scheme 1. We began our preliminary investigation by choosing 
phenylacetylene 1a and iodobenzene 2a as the model substrate 
for Negishi cross-coupling reaction. The active lithium 
phenylacetylide was generated according to our previous 
reported literature [17] using 1a with n-butyllithium at mixer M1 at

With the optimized reaction conditions in hand for the synthesis 
of internal alkynes, the scope of the reaction was examined with 
different terminal alkynes and aryl iodides as presented in 
Scheme 2. The electron-donating substituents such as p-Me (2b), 
p-Cl (2g) and p-Br (2h) iodobenzenes reacted with 1a to afford 
the desired products (3ab-3ah) in good to excellent yields. 
Similarly, p-Methoxyphenylacetylene (1b) also underwent smooth 
conversion with 2a to give 3ba in 70% yield. The reaction of 
electron-donating aryl iodides (2b-e) with aliphatic alkyne such as 
1-hexyne (1c) gave the required internal alkyne scaffolds 3cb-3ce 
in excellent yields except in the case of m-iodoanisole (2d). The 
practicality of the reaction was demonstrated on an 8.4 mmol 
scale to beget compound 3ca within 28 minutes over 90% 
conversion and an isolated yield of 85% with a space time yield 
of 27.1 g/Lh (See Table S1). Whereas, the space time yield  range 
is only 2.1 [19]  to 6.2 [20] g/Lh in a commercial batch reactor for the 
synthesis alkynyl derivatives, suggesting that the flow system 
enables a 12.3 fold increase in throughput for a given reactor 
volume.   
 
Electron-deficient groups such as -CN, and -CF3 as well as 
halo- functional groups (2f-2k) were tolerated well to give the 
corresponding products 3cf-3ck. Interestingly, when the di-iodo 
compound 2m was employed, the desired mono- alkynylated 
3cm was obtained as a major product with a 62% yield, and di-
alkynylated 3cm’ was observed with a 25% yield, which illustrated 
the precise control of reagent over the batch conditions.[21] 
Notably, acetyl functional groups, hetero aryl iodides and bulky 
substituents (2l, 2n-2p) were proceeded smoothly and the cross-
coupling products 3cl, 3cn-3cp were obtained in moderate to 
excellent yields. In addition, 1-pentyne (1d), 1-octyne (1e), TMS 
acetylene (1f), cyclic enyne (1g) and N-propargyl carbazole (1h) 
were efficiently coupled with various aryl iodides under these 
reaction conditions to afford the desired alkynes in moderate to 
excellent yields (49-99%). 
 
With the successful outcome of alkyne derivatives, we applied 
this methodology for the synthesis of various enynes, which are

To show a broader application of this process, the deprotection 
of TMS protected alkynes was investigated by reacting alkyne 3fa 
with K2CO3 as base using one T-shaped micromixer (M1), one 
tubing reactor [R1(800 µm)] at room temperature. The reaction 
underwent complete desilylation with a residence time of 10.5 s 
(See SI, Table S2, entry 1-3). With this success, two flow systems 
(Scheme 4 and see SI) were used to demonstrate the stepwise 
Negishi cross-coupling of TMS-protected alkyne and the 
deprotection of the corresponding TMS-alkyne. In this regards, 
compound 3fh was synthesized in a 3 mmol scale using the first 
flow system and the resulting solution was worked up, re-
dissolved in THF/MeOH to react with an aqueous solution of 
K2CO3 in the second flow system. This two-step reaction worked 
well to get the desired terminal alkyne 3fh’ in 92% yield (496 mg, 
2.75 mmol).  
 
Conclusions 
In summary, we have successfully developed a C(sp)-C(sp2) 
Negishi cross-coupling reaction in a continuous flow system using 
three T-shaped micromixers and three microtubular reactors. The 
reaction proceeds via an in situ generated alkynylzinc reagent 
from lithium acetylide and zinc bromide followed by a Pd-
catalyzed cross-coupling with aryl iodides to form internal alkynes 
in good to excellent yields. The key advantages of this flow 
protocol are low catalyst/ligand, excellent conversion, short 
reaction time, highly controllable, broad substrate scope and 
desilylation of alkynes. Moreover, the synthesis of 1,3-enynes 
were achieved with retention of configuration using vinyl halides 
as the coupling partners. 
Experimental Section 
General information  
      Dry THF was freshly distilled under a nitrogen atmosphere over sodium 
and used for the reaction. All the compounds were commercially available 
and used without further purification unless otherwise noted. Compounds 
1b, 1g, 1h, 1i, 1j, 2o, 2p, 4a, 4b and 4c were prepared according to 
previous literature report.[23] n-BuLi was purchased from Rockwood 
Lithium company and ZnBr2 was purchased from Alfa Aesar. ZnBr2 
solution (0.60 M in THF) was prepared by drying ZnBr2 (8.10 g, 36 mmol) 
in a Schlenk-flask under flame dried for 5 minutes. After cooling to 25 oC, 
dry THF (60 mL) was added and stirred until the salts were dissolved. 
Micro mixture 500 µm was purchased from Sanko Seiki company, 
stainless tube and peek were purchased from Idex health & science. 
Harvard syringe pump model-11 elite were used for the reaction.  
General procedure for synthesis of aromatic internal alkynes and 1,3-
enynes: A microreactor system consist of three T-shaped micromixers 
(M1, M2 and M3), three tubing reactors (R1, R2 and R3) and two 
precooling units P1 (inner diameter = 800 µm, length L = 50 cm), P2 (inner 
diameter = 1000 µm, length L= 50 cm), and one preheating unit P3 (inner 
diameter = 1000 µm, length L = 342 cm)) were used. A solution of terminal 
alkyne (0.40 M in THF) (flow rate: 1.125 mL/min) and a solution of n-BuLi 
(1.60 M in Hexane) (flow rate: 0.3 mL/min) were introduced into M1 (Φ = 
1.0 mm) by syringe pumps. The resulting solution was passed through R1 
(Φ = 0.8 mm, L = 50 cm, 251 µL) and was mixed with a solution of a ZnBr2 
(0.60 M in THF) (flow rate: 0.75 mL/min) at M2 (Φ = 1.0 mm). The resulting 
solution was passed through R2 (Φ = 1.0 mm, L = 50 cm, 392 µL) and 
introduced M3 (Φ = 1.0 mm). A solution of aryl iodide or vinyl iodide, 
palladium acetate (1 mol %) and triphenyl phosphine (2 mol %) and 
introduced in M3. The resulting final solution passed through R3 (Φ = 1.0 
mm, L = 350 cm, 2749 µL) at 80 oC. After a steady state was reached (after 
1 min), the final product solution was collected for 60 seconds in vial 
containing saturated solution of NH4Cl.The reaction mixture was analysed 
by GC. The crude mixture was diluted with EA and water, organic phase 
was separated and the aqueous phase extracted twice with EA (2 × 20 
mL). The combined organic layer was dried over MgSO4, and purified by 
column chromatography and product was analysed by 1H, 13C NMR, IR 
and mass spectrometer.

title: Synthesis of 2‐Substituted Cyclobutanones by a Suzuki Reaction and Dephosphorylation Sequence
markdown_content:
Synthesis of 2-Substituted Cyclobutanones by a Suzuki
Reaction and Dephosphorylation Sequence
Jakub Koudelka[a] and Tomáš Tobrman*[a]
We report a novel process for the preparation of 2-substituted
cyclobutanones. Such a method relies on the cross-coupling
reaction of bromocyclobutenyl diethyl phosphate with either
boronic acids or organozinc reagents. Dephosphorylation of the
prepared 2-substituted cyclobutenyl phosphates affords 2-
substituted cyclobutanones. We observed that the course of the
dephosphorylation reaction depends on the properties of the
substituents found on the cyclobutene nucleus. The presence
of groups capable of stabilizing
the negative charge
is
necessary for ring opening of cyclobutanones. The scope of the
reported process for the preparation of 2-substituted cyclo-
butanones has also been extended to the preparation of
cyclobutenyl sulfides.
Introduction
A cyclobutane is a kind of naturally occurring four-membered
cyclic molecule that exhibits interesting chemical properties.[1]
The synthesis and various applications of substituted cyclo-
butanes have been the subject of several reviews.[2] The
tetrasubstituted cyclobutane skeleton represents a key part of
both katsumadain C[3] and the palhynosides A-H.[4] Moreover,
substituted cyclobutane[5] and the cyclobutene[6] ring have been
identified as constituents of the sesquiterpenes. Among the
various substituted cyclobutanones,[7] significant research atten-
tion has been paid to the synthesis[8] and functionalization of 2-
substituted cyclobutanones.[4] The synthetic applications of 2-
substituted
cyclobutanones
also
cover
natural
product
synthesis.[9] In relation to the above-mentioned applications of
2-substituted cyclobutanones, it has been reported that 2-
alkylated cyclobutanones exhibit both cyto- and genotoxic
properties under in vitro conditions.[10] As a result, significant
attention has been paid to the detection of 2-alkylated cyclo-
butanones in food.[11] In addition, substituted cyclobutanones
have been designed and tested as analogues of various β-
lactam antibiotics.[12]
Similar to three-membered carbocycles, the four-membered
ring that characterizes cyclobutanones renders them valuable
building blocks for ring-opening reactions[9a,13] due to the high
ring-strain energy of the cyclobutanone skeleton. Indeed 2,2-
dichlorocyclobutanones can be converted into methyl 4,4-
dichlorobutanoates by means of sodium methoxide.[14] Similar
reactivity was observed by Trost, who proposed that the
presence of an electron-stabilizing group could facilitate the
cyclobutanone ring-opening process.[15] However, this assump-
tion has not yet been satisfactorily confirmed. Further, Trost
also observed that 2,2-diphenylcyclobutanone and 2-phenyl-
cyclobutanone can be opened to the corresponding methyl
butanoates via the reaction with sodium methoxide in refluxing
methanol.
The ability of 2-substituted cyclobutanones to undergo ring
expansion raises the question of how 2-substituted cyclo-
butanones can be prepared. In fact, two main approaches to
the preparation of 2-substituted cyclobutanones have evolved.
The first such approach is based on the formation of a
cyclobutanone ring by means of ring expansion, ring contrac-
tion,
and
[2+2]
cycloadditions.
The
ring-expansion-based
processes of cyclic molecules involve Lewis acid-,[16] oxidative-
,[17] and cobalt-[18] or gold-catalyzed[19] rearrangements of the
substituted cyclopropanes. Moreover, the microwave-assisted
Wolff rearrangement of substituted 2-diazocyclopenta-1,3-dio-
nes represents an example of a ring-contraction-based ap-
proach for the preparation of cyclobutanones.[20] The concept of
using [2+2] cycloadditions for the synthesis of substituted
cyclobutanones was first reported in 1964[21] and still counts
among the near-endless number of examples of approaches to
substituted cyclobutanones synthesis;[17c,22] however, this ap-
proach continues to be frequently used for the synthesis of
polysubstituted cyclobutanones.[23]
The second approach for the preparation of 2-substituted
cyclobutanone bearing alkyl substituents involves the chemical
modification
of
commercially
available
cyclobutanone
(Scheme 1).
Aldol-type
reactions[24]
and
Mannich-type
reactions[25]
are
both typical
examples of
such reactivity
(Scheme 1a, Scheme 1b). The direct alkylation of the cyclo-
butanone-derived
enolate
provides
low
product
yields
(Scheme 1c),[26] likely due to the low stability of the correspond-
ing enolate. Substantially improved yields can be obtained by
means of α-allylation via singly occupied molecular orbital
(SOMO) alkylation,[27] imine[28] or oxime alkylation,[17c,29] and
palladium-catalyzed cyclobutanone alkylation.[30]

1a and 1b and 2a–2f (Figure 1), which were prepared from the
bromocyclobutenyl diethyl phosphate 1a by means of the
Suzuki reaction under previously reported conditions.[36] The
same reaction conditions as used for the Suzuki reaction were
then used for the one-pot two-step procedure for the synthesis
of
2-substituted
cyclobutanones
(Scheme 2).
The
isolated
phosphate 2a was treated with different nucleophiles in order
to optimize its conversion into the ketone 3a. The use of

a 49% isolated yield (Table 1, entry 1), while the use of
potassium hydroxide and acidic hydrolysis failed (Table 1,
entries 2 and 3). Potassium carbonate and sodium ethoxide
gave only moderate yields of the ketone 3a (Table 1, entries 4
and 5). Similar reactivity was observed in relation to pure
sodium 2,2,2-trifluoroethoxide in tetrahydrofurane (THF), while
the use of a 1 M solution of sodium 2,2,2-trifluoroethoxide
(TFENa) in 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (TFE) gave an almost quantita-

Following the successful optimization of the reaction
conditions, we tested whether it was possible to prepare
substituted cyclobutanones without having to separate the
product of the Suzuki reaction 2a. Thus, the phosphate 1a was
reacted with 4-methoxyphenylboronic acid in the presence of
palladium acetate and RuPhos as a ligand, thereby affording
the desired product 2a, which was crudely isolated. The
isolated crude phosphate was stirred with a 1 M solution of
TFENa. The final cyclobutanone 3a was obtained in a 76%
isolated yield (Scheme 2). The other tested boronic acids
bearing electron-neutral and electron-rich aryl substituents
gave similarly high isolated yields of the cyclobutanones 3b–
3g. The 3-thienylboronic acids also gave the ketone 3h in a
high isolated yield over two steps. It is worth noting that no
cyclobutane ring opening was observed in either case. In the
case of 1-cycloheptenylboronic acid, we observed the isomer-
ization of the double bond to the α,β-unsaturated ketone 3i,
which was obtained in a 77% isolated yield. The use of boronic
acids with electron-poor aryl substituents resulted in the
opening of the cyclobutene ring. We soon found that a solution
of tetrabutylammonium fluoride in THF could be used for the
conversion of these phosphates into the cyclobutanones 3j–
3m in moderate isolated yields. In addition, tetrabutylammo-
nium fluoride also gave the ketone 3i in a 72% isolated yield
during the deprotection of the phosphate 2e.
Bromenol phosphate 1a can also be used in the Negishi
reaction to replace the bromine atom with alkyl and aryl
groups, as illustrated in Scheme 3. Our recently developed
conditions
for
the
Negishi
reaction
of
cyclic
bromoenol
phosphates[34b] proved efficient for the conversion of the
phosphate 1a into the ketone 3d. This approach is sensitive to
the preparation of the organozinc reagent, as shown for the
compound 3d, which was obtained in lower isolated yields
when starting from 4-tolylmagnesium chloride. The cyclobuta-
none 3n was formed in a lower isolated yield when the Negishi
reaction was performed at 60°C. Aside from the preparation of
cyclobutanones with aromatic and heteroaromatic substituents,
the Negishi reaction of the bromenol phosphate 1a is also
suitable for the introduction of the alkyl substituents 3p and
3q in average isolated yields.
During the preparation of the cyclobutanone 3j, we
observed the opening of the formed cyclobutanone to the
corresponding butanoate by means of a base. Thus, we studied
the effect of cyclobutane ring substitution on the course of the
dephosphorylation process (Scheme 4). A two-step procedure
starting from the bromocyclobutenyl phosphate 1a gave the
corresponding 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl butanoates 4a and 4b in
high isolated yields, albeit only for those boronic acids with
electron-withdrawing groups. We also succeeded in converting
the phosphate 2b into the methyl ester 4c using a 1 M solution
of sodium methoxide in methanol at room temperature. The
protocol is also suitable for the synthesis of trisubstituted
butanoates, as represented by the ester 4d. Scheme 2 shows
that boronic acids with electron-donating substituents are
resistant to cyclobutanone ring opening even at elevated
reaction temperatures. Yet, in the case of both 1-pyrenylboronic
acid and 2-benzothienylboronic acid, the smooth opening of
the cyclobutanone moiety occurred during the dephosphoryla-
tion process to give the esters 4e and 4f. This procedure should
enable the synthesis of other carboxylic acid derivatives,
although the dephosphorylation process represents the key
step in the transformation. We initially started with the
synthesis of the morpholine amide 4g from phosphate 2b, but
all attempts to use the morpholine, or a combination of

We also demonstrated the broader scope of our method-
ology through the synthesis of the sulfide 5 (Scheme 5). The
phosphate 1a was cross-coupled with boronic acids and the
crudely isolated phosphates was treated with three equivalents
of sodium thiolate in the presence of the corresponding thiol.
Although the reaction is limited to cyclobutenyl phosphates
with substituents capable of stabilizing the negative charge,
which allows for phosphate substitution by means of the
preferential addition–elimination mechanism, we synthesized
the series of sulfides 5a–5d. The use of thiophenol proved less
efficient, affording the sulfide 5e in a 20% isolated yield.
Conclusion
We have developed a novel process for the preparation of
substituted cyclobutanones that relies on the cross-coupling
reaction of bromocyclobutenyl phosphate with either boronic
acids
or
organozinc
reagents.
The
resulting
cyclobutenyl
phosphate is then dephosphorylated by means of 2,2,2-
trifluoroethanol at room temperature. This process allows for
the preparation of cyclobutanones with electron-rich and
electron-neutral substituents. For those substituents with the
ability to stabilize the negative charge, the preparation of
cyclobutanones is performed via the reaction with TBAF in dry
tetrahydrofuran. We observed that the groups capable of
stabilizing the negative charge facilitated the opening of the
cyclobutanones to γ-substituted butanoates and butanamides.
This approach for the preparation of 2-substituted cyclo-
butanones has a broader scope because it also allows for the
synthesis of cyclobutenyl sulfides by means of the reaction of
sodium thiolates with cyclobutenyl phosphate in tetrahydrofur-
an at room temperature.

General procedure for „one-pot“ two-step synthesis of
cyclobutanones by the Negishi reaction of
bromocyclobutenyl diethyl phosphate (GP2)
A solution of organozinc reagent (1.3 equiv) was added to a
solution of 2-bromocyclobuten-1-yl diethyl phosphate (1.0 equiv)
(1a), palladium acetate (4 mol%) and XPhos (8 mol%). The reaction
mixture was stirred for 18 h at 23°C. The reaction mixture was
diluted with ether (30 mL/1 mmol), washed with water (10 mL/
1 mmol), brine (10 mL/1 mmol) and the organic phase was dried
over MgSO4. The solvents were evaporated under reduce pressure
and the crude phosphate was dried under reduce pressure. A
solution of the crude phosphate in dry THF (3 mL/1 mmol) was
added to a solution of CF3CH2ONa (3 equiv) in dry CF3CH2OH (3 mL/
1 mmol) and THF (2 mL/1 mmol) at 23°C, and the resultant mixture
was stirred for 1 h at 23°C. The crude reaction mixture was diluted
with ether (30 mL/1 mmol), washed with water (10 mL/1 mmol) and
brine (10 mL/1 mmol) and the organic layer was dried over MgSO4.
The solvents were evaporated under reduce pressure and column
chromatography (Silica gel) gave the final product.
General procedure for „one-pot“ two-step synthesis of
butanoates (GP3)
Toluene (4 mL/mmol) was added to a mixture of 2-bromocyclobut-
en-1-yl diethyl phosphate (1.0 equiv) (1a), boronic acid or boronic
acid ester (1.3 equiv), palladium acetate (1 mol%) and RuPhos
(2 mol%). The reaction mixture was stirred for 1 min at 23°C, and
then 2 M K3PO4 (3 equiv) was added at once. The reaction mixture
was stirred for 18 h at 60°C. The reaction mixture was diluted with
ether, washed with 1 M KOH (10 mL/1 mmol), water (10 mL/
1 mmol), brine (10 mL/1 mmol) and then the organic phase was
dried over MgSO4. The solvents were evaporated under reduce
pressure and the crude phosphate was dried under reduce
pressure. A solution of the crude phosphate (1.0 equiv) in dry THF
(3 mL/1 mmol) was added to a solution of CF3CH2ONa (3 equiv) in
dry CF3CH2OH (3 mL/1 mmol) and THF (2 mL/1 mmol) at 23°C, and
the resultant mixture was stirred for 1 h at 23°C. The crude reaction
mixture was diluted with ether (30 mL/mmol), washed with water
(10 mL/1 mmol) and brine (10 mL/1 mmol) and the organic layer
was dried over MgSO4. The solvents were evaporated under reduce
pressure and column chromatography (Silica gel) gave the final
product.
General procedure for „one-pot“ two-step synthesis of
butanamides (GP4)
Toluene (4 mL/mmol) was added to a mixture of 2-bromocyclobut-
en-1-yl diethyl phosphate (1.0 equiv) (1a), boronic acid or boronic
ester (1.3 equiv), palladium acetate (1 mol%) and RuPhos (2 mol%).
The reaction mixture was stirred for 1 min at 23°C, and then 2 M
K3PO4 (3 equiv) was added at once. The reaction mixture was stirred
for 18 h at 60°C. The reaction mixture was diluted with ether,
washed with 1 M KOH (10 mL/1 mmol), water (10 mL/1 mmol),
brine (10 mL/1 mmol) and then the organic phase was dried over
MgSO4. The solvents were evaporated under reduce pressure and
the crude phosphate was dried under reduce pressure. A solution
of crudely isolated phosphate (1.0 equiv) in dry THF (3 mL/1 mmol)
was added to a solution of CF3CH2ONa (3 equiv) in dry CF3CH2OH
(3 mL/1 mmol), THF (4 mL/1 mmol) and amine (3.0 equiv) at 23°C,
and the resultant mixture was stirred for 2 h at 60°C. The crude
reaction mixture was diluted with ether (30 mL/1 mmol), washed
with 1 M HCl (5 mL/1 mmol), water (20 mL/1 mmol) and brine
(20 mL/1 mmol) and the organic layer was dried over MgSO4. The
solvents were evaporated under reduce pressure and column
chromatography (Silica gel) gave the final product.
General procedure (GP5) for the synthesis of cyclobutenyl
sulfides
Toluene (4 mL/mmol) was added to a mixture of 2-bromocyclobut-
en-1-yl diethyl phosphate (1.0 equiv) (1a), boronic acid or boronic
ester (1.3 equiv), palladium acetate (1 mol%) and RuPhos (2 mol%).
The reaction mixture was stirred for 1 min at 23°C, and then 2 M
K3PO4 (3 equiv) was added at once. The reaction mixture was stirred
for 18 h at 60°C. The reaction mixture was diluted with ether,
washed with 1 M KOH (10 mL/1 mmol), water (10 mL/1 mmol),
brine (10 mL/1 mmol) and then the organic phase was dried over
MgSO4. The solvents were evaporated under reduce pressure and
the crude phosphate was dried under reduce pressure. Thiol
(6 equiv) was added to a suspension of NaH (3 equiv) in dry THF
(4 mL/mmol) cooled to 0°C. The resultant mixture was stirred for
30 min at 23°C followed by addition of a solution of crude
phosphate (1.0 equiv) in dry THF (2 mL/1 mmol) and the reaction
mixture was stirred for 1 h at 23°C. The crude mixture was diluted
with ether (30 mL/1 mmol), washed with water (10 mL/1 mmol) and
brine (10 mL/1 mmol) and the organic layer was dried over MgSO4.
The solvents were removed under reduce pressure and column
chromatography (Silica gel) gave the final product.

MINIREVIEW 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Alkylation of electron-deficient olefins through conjugate addition 
of organozinc reagents: An update  
Biswajita Baruah,[a] Mohit L. Deb,*[b] 
Abstract: This review focuses on the applications of organozinc 
reagents in conjugate addition reactions. Organozinc compounds 
are a class of organometallic reagent used in various reactions like 
addition, substitution and coupling reactions. The conjugate addition 
or 1, 4-addition is one of the most useful bond forming strategies 
used in organic synthesis since broad range of nucleophiles can be 
employed in the reaction. Addition of organozinc to electron-deficient 
olefins attracts synthetic chemists as it preferably undergoes 
conjugate addition over 1,2-addition unlike other organometallic 
reagents, such as Grignard reagent or organolithium. Many natural 
products were also synthesized by applying the conjugate addition 
reaction of organozinc. Moreover, organozinc reagents have 
superior functional group compatibility and can be easily prepared 
relative 
to 
other 
organometallic 
compounds. 
Consequently, 
conjugate additions of organozinc reagents were highly studied and 
having a review on it is very important at present. Though a few 
reviews are available, they are either not directly on the organozinc 
reagents or on the conjugate addition. We hope that this review 
article will be of great use to organic researchers. 
1. Introduction 
Organozinc reagents are known to be the first organometallic 
compounds ever synthesized in organic chemistry having a C–
Zn chemical bond.[1] It was first synthesized by Edward 
Frankland in the 1850s. As carbon and zinc atoms have 
electronegativity differences, the C-Zn bond is always polarized 
towards carbon. Hence, organozinc reagents are used as 
nucleophiles in organic reactions, such as addition reactions, 
substitution reactions, coupling reactions, etc.[2] However, 
initially when they were employed as nucleophiles in organic 
synthesis, poor yields of the corresponding products were 
formed.[1b] As a result, synthetic chemists preferred more 
reactive Grignard reagents over organozinc reagents as 
nucleophiles. 
Consequently, 
organozinc 
reagents 
were 
overlooked for more than 10 decades until the 1970s when 
Negishi et al.[2c,3] noticed that use of a palladium or nickel 
catalyst increases the reactivity of organozinc reagent. Today 
organozinc reagents are one of the most useful classes of 
organometallic compounds because of their advantages, such 
as ease of preparation and superior functional group 
compatibility relative to Grignard reagents and organolithium 
(Figure 1). Moreover, their brilliant reactivity in the presence of a 
catalyst makes them a very powerful tool for natural product 
synthesis. Organozinc reagents can be divided into three types, 
such as organic zinc halogen compound (R-Zn-X), dialkyl or 
diarylzinc (R-Zn-R), lithium or magnesium zincate. However, it is 
observed that different methods of preparation of organozinc 
reagents could lead to dissimilar structures showing their special 
compatibilities. Organozinc reagents undergo conjugate addition 
or 1,4-addition like organocopper reagents[4] when react with 
α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compounds. 
 
 
Figure 1. Advantages of using organozinc reagents 
 
Conjugate addition reaction is the addition of a nucleophile 
to an electron-deficient olefins. A carbanion is generated first in 
the reaction, which can either be protonated to give the β-
substituted product or an electrophilic species can be added to 
produce the α,β-disubstituted product. The conjugate addition is 
one of the most useful bond forming strategies and has been 
broadly used in organic synthesis.[5] The reason of versatility of 
the conjugate addition is mainly because of the different types of 
nucleophiles (organometallic reagents, Michael donors, other 
carbanions) that can be employed in the reaction.[6]  
 
Dialkylzinc reagents were first developed for conjugate 
additions through catalytic process. Thereafter, different types of 
organozinc reagents were used in conjugate addition. There are 
many natural products which were synthesized by the conjugate 
addition of dialkylzinc. A few such natural products are depicted 
in Figure 2. For instance, R-(-) muscone,[7] clavularin B,[8] 
pumiliotoxin C,[9] and PEG1 methyl ester[10] were synthesized by 
applying the conjugate addition of organozinc reagent. For that 
reason, many research articles were published on the conjugate 
addition of organozinc. A few reviews and book chapter were 
also published, but they are much old.[11] More recently, a few 
review articles have been published, but they are either not 
specific to organozinc reagents or do not focus on conjugate 
addition reactions.[12] Therefore, we planned to write a review 
primarily on the conjugate addition of organozinc reagents. The 
main objectives of this article are (i) to highlight the important 
research on conjugate additions of organozinc reagents, (ii) to 
highlight the limitations and possibilities for improvement, (iii) to 
attract the synthetic chemists so that they can use the strategy 
in the synthesis of natural products and drug molecules. We 
have discussed here the reactions and their results since 2005 
to till date. We have divided the article into two major sections

Figure 2. Natural products synthesized via conjugate addition of dialkylzinc 
 
 
2. Non-asymmetric conjugate addition 
 
In non-asymmetric conjugate addition the product has no 
chirality, though new stereogenic centre(s) may generate. One 
such conjugate addition of organozinc reagents to conjugated 
enals was reported using Pd catalyst without competing 1,2-
additions. The reaction produced good to excellent yields in the 
presence of 5 mol% of Pd(OAc)2.PPh3 precatalyst in THF 
solution at -78 to -20 oC (Scheme 1).[13] Without using the PPh3 
ligand, the reaction still gave comparable yield of 1,4-adducts 
(Scheme 1). However, difficulties in the purification of products 
owing to the precipitation of persistent palladium by-products 
encourage the authors to use the ligand. The intermediate zinc 
enolates can be trapped by quenching the reaction with TBSOTf 
which afforded predominantly the (E)-enol silanes with moderate 
to excellent yield (Scheme 2). However, the 1,4-additions to 
conjugated acyl oxazolidinones, nitriles or esters were 
unsuccessful.  A plausible mechanistic pathway is delineated in 
Scheme 3. 
 
 
 
Scheme 1. Conjugate addition of dialkylzinc to conjugated enals 
 
Scheme 2. Trapping of intermediate zinc enolates 
 
 
Scheme 3. The plausible mechanism for Pd-catalyzed conjugate addition of 
dialkylzinc 
 
Conjugate addition of allylzinc and benzylzinc reagents to 
-nitroalkenes was reported by Wang and co-workers. The 
reactions were performed without solvent and catalyst at room 
temperature which produced the desired products in moderate 
to good yield (Scheme 4).[14] It was noticed that the presence of 
electron withdrawing groups (EWGs) on the phenyl ring of 
nitrostyrenes decreased the product yield. In contrast, electron 
rich heterocyclic nitroalkenes furnished higher yield. With 
benzylzinc bromide the reaction gave lower yield and required 
comparatively longer time. When the reaction of benzylzinc 
bromide and -nitroalkenes were performed in THF solvent, no 
1,4-addition product was formed which indicated the necessity of 
solvent-free reaction. This reaction has a few advantages, such 
as milder conditions, shorter reaction time and environmentally 
benign. 
 
Scheme 4. Conjugate addition of allylzinc and benzylzinc reagents to -
nitroalkenes 
 
Recently, Aera et al. disclosed the addition of lithium 
tetraorganozincates to nitroolefins (Scheme 5).[15] They initially 
investigated the reaction of diethylzinc or lithium zincates 
(Et3ZnLi and Et4ZnLi2) with -nitrostyrene using deep eutectic

under air. Although a good amount of conjugated addition 
product was obtained, a substitution product was also formed 
(8:2 to 9:1) as by-product in which the nitro group was displaced 
by the nucleophilic alkyl group of organozinc reagents. When the

3.1. Copper-catalyzed asymmetric conjugate addition 
 
In 2002, an improved method for copper-catalyzed conjugate 
addition of organozinc to electron-deficient olefins was 
developed by Alexakis et al. in which >99% of enantiomeric 
excess was observed.[22] In 2005, another asymmetric conjugate 
addition of dialkylzinc to cyclic enones was disclosed by 
Hoveyda and co-workers. Tetrasubstituted alkene moiety was 
considered for the reaction and the product obtained was having 
two quaternary stereogenic centers (Scheme 13).[23] The  
 
 
Scheme 13. Asymmetric conjugate addition of dialkylzinc to cyclic enones 
reaction was catalyzed by air-stable CuCN along with chiral 
ligand that contains an anthranilic acid-based N-terminus. The 
reaction produced up to 98% conversion with 95% enantiomeric 
excess. Both six- and five-membered cyclic enones were utilized 
in the reaction. All the reactions were conducted in undistilled 
toluene solvent under nitrogen atmosphere at -15 to 0 oC. 
Interestingly, purified solvent offered lower enantioselectivities. 
Different commercially available dialkylzinc reagents were used 
in the reaction. This was the first enantioselective conjugate 
addition of any alkylmetal reagent to tetrasubstituted olefins. 
One important review on copper-catalyzed enantioselective 
conjugate addition was published in 2008 by Alexakis et al.[24]  
 
In the same year, the same group developed another 
asymmetric conjugate addition of dialkylzinc reagents to acyclic 
nitroalkenes resulting to the formation of all-carbon quaternary 
carbon stereogenic centers (Scheme 14).[25] Enantiopure organic 
compounds containing quaternary carbon are important because 
of their relevance to the synthesis of biologically active 
compounds. Reactions were performed in the presence of 
Cu(OTf)2 catalyst in toluene at -78 to 0 oC which produced 
products with high enantiomeric excess (up to 98%). A variety of 
dialkylzinc reagents and nitroolefins were used in the reactions. 
Chiral peptide based ligand was used to induce chirality in the 
product. The enantiopure nitroalkanes may be converted 
effectively to synthetically versatile enantiopure compounds, 
such as the derived nitriles, amines, carboxylic acids, and 
aldoximes.

3.2. Copper-free asymmetric conjugate addition 
 
In the asymmetric conjugate addition reactions of organozinc to 
electron-deficient olefins, copper salts are usually added. The 
copper cations influence the electronic behaviors of the carbonyl 
group and therefore, can determine which alkyl/aryl moieties are 
transferred and also perform as bridging units in the transition 
state. The first copper-free asymmetric conjugate addition of 
diethylzinc or diisopropylzinc to ,-unsaturated aldehydes was 
reported by Bräse and Höfener (Scheme 21).[36] The reactions 
were carried out in toluene or hexane at -20 oC though the 
temperature was kept 0 oC for chromene substrate. Though 
enantioselectivities were excellent, yields were poor because of 
the formation of little amount of 1,2-addition products (not shown 
here). Another copper-free asymmetric conjugate addition of 
dialkylzinc to enones was developed by Cimarelli et al.[37] 
Several enantiopure 1-(aminoalkyl)naphthols and 2-(aminoalkyl) 
phenol were checked as ligands in which Ni(acac)2 was used as 
catalyst instead of copper salts. Reactions were performed in 
CH3CN solvent at -30 oC. However, in all the cases poor to 
moderate enantioselectivity were observed (up to 71% ee).

A probable mechanism was proposed in which a mixed 
zinc alkoxide A was first formed from the reaction of Et2Zn, chiral 
β-amino alcohol and the cyclopropanol. The alkoxide A acted as 
a catalytically competent species in the reaction (Scheme 23). 
This species then underwent ring opening to form the 
corresponding homoenolate B. This then coordinated to the 
enone and underwent asymmetric conjugate addition to give a 
zinc enolate D. This enolate then abstracted a proton from the 
cyclopropanol 
molecule 
to 
give 
the 
1,6-diketone 
and 
regenerated the mixed alkoxide A. 1,6-Diketone further 
underwent intramolecular aldol condensation upon heating to 
produce the desired cyclopentene. If the asymmetric conjugate 
addition is sluggish the homoenolate B can abstract a proton 
from cyclopropanol to generate the ketone E, which can further 
take part in enolate conjugate addition under zinc catalysis.

For instance, chiral nickel complex catalyzed conjugate addition

This was probably the first report of Ni-catalyzed conjugate

Conclusions 
 
The organozinc reagents are highly useful in conjugate addition 
reactions because of their numerous advantages over other 
organometallic reagents. For instance, organozinc reagents 
have broad functional group tolerance, compatibility with 
transition metals, and simple preparation procedures. Moreover, 
they prefer 1,4-addition over 1,2-addition unlike many other 
organometallic reagents thus providing regioselective products. 
Many exciting results of non-asymmetric and asymmetric 
conjugate additions of organozinc reagents are discussed here, 
but some of the major contributions are for example, asymmetric 
conjugate addition of in situ generated zinc homoenolate to 
synthesize tri-substituted cyclopentene (Scheme 22), conjugate 
addition of in situ generated organozinc compound to synthesize 
pyridine-2-cyclopentane or –cyclohexane (Scheme 9), tandem 
conjugate 
addition-cyclization 
to 
produce 
substituted 
cyclopentane 
(Scheme 
7). 
In 
spite 
of 
wonderful 
accomplishments in this area, challenges still remain. For 
example, in a few reactions (Scheme 7, 14, 18-19) large amount 
(3 eq.) of organozinc reagents were used and therefore, the 
reactions became costlier and bulky amount of by-products were 
also formed. Thus new methods should be developed where low 
amounts of organozinc may be sufficient for the reaction. In 
addition, 
developing 
environmentally 
benign 
and 
milder 
conjugate addition reactions of organozinc reagents is highly 
desirable. Synthetic chemists need a lot of effort and interest to 
improve the methodology.

title: An Alternative Synthesis of Cycloalkyl‐Substituted CPA Catalysts and Application in Asymmetric Protonation Reactions**
markdown_content:
An Alternative Synthesis of Cycloalkyl-Substituted CPA
Catalysts and Application in Asymmetric Protonation
Reactions**
Liam A. McLean[a] and Allan J. B. Watson*[a]
An alternative synthesis of cycloalkyl-substituted CPA catalysts
is reported. A Negishi coupling offers improved yields and
purity of the necessary 1,3,5-tri(cycloalkyl)benzenes. Limitations
in the use of commercial organozinc reagents have been
identified and a robust procedure for the preparation of these
reagents is detailed. Similarly, a robust procedure for the key
Kumada coupling is also provided. The route is demonstrated
by preparation of three different tri(cycloalkyl)aryl-substituted
CPAs and the utility of these catalysts in asymmetric protona-
tion reactions is shown.
BINOL-derived chiral phosphoric acids (CPAs) are privileged
catalysts
for
a
broad
range
of
asymmetric
reactions
(Scheme 1a).[1] Of this class, the 3,3’-di(2,4,6-triisopropylphenyl)-
substituted phosphoric acid 1 (TRIP) has become a workhorse,
delivering excellent yields and enantioinduction across a range
of
asymmetric
transformations
including
1,2-additions,[2]
rearrangements,[3]
and
reductive
aminations,[4]
amongst
others.[5] More recently, the TRIP analogue TCYP (2) has
emerged[6] and shown increased selectivity in a series of recent
asymmetric transformations including aminations,[7] dynamic
kinetic resolutions,[8] and borylation.[9]
The synthesis of 1 is well-documented;[10] however, there
are few procedures for the preparation of 2.[11] In recent work in
our group, we found some difficulty in synthesis of 2 and
sought to overcome these problems. Here we report the
development of an alternative synthetic approach to 2 and
other
novel
tri(cycloalkyl)aryl
CPAs
(Scheme 1b).
We
also
compare the effectiveness of these catalysts in asymmetric
protonation reactions.[12]
Existing approaches to 2 are based upon synthetic access to
1,3,5-tri(cyclohexyl)benzene 4 via Friedel-Crafts alkylation of
benzene (Scheme 2).[13]
While this process does allow access to 4, we found the
reaction to produce mixtures of 3 and 4 in moderate overall
yield.[14] Purification by distillation is possible but tedious, and
often requires several distillations to increase purity to a
satisfactory level. This process also does not allow general
access to other 1,3,5-tri(cycloalkyl)benzenes, such as the cyclo-
heptyl variant.
We therefore proposed an alternative and straightforward
approach to circumvent this issue based on exhaustive Negishi
coupling of 1,3,5-tribromobenzene (Scheme 3a).
Initial experiments using commercial organozinc reagents
(c-hexylzinc bromide and c-pentylzinc bromide; not shown)
were unsuccessful – no product was observed. However, use of
the organozinc reagents prepared in house by transmetalation
from the Grignard reagent (also prepared in house) delivered
the tri(cycloalkyl)benzene products 4, 6, and 7 in good yield at
first attempt. The origin of the difficulty experienced with the
commercial reagents is currently unexplained.
