nates. Later in 2014, Sreedhar et al. disclosed a convenient
procedure for syntheses of β-keto sulfones via nucleophilic
addition of the in situ generated enolates to sulfonyl iodides.[17]
Shortly afterwards, a mild CuBr2/DBU catalyzed cross-coupling
reactions between aryl ketones and sodium sulfinates at room
temperature
was
reported.[18]
Most
recently,
Tang
group
described a convenient oxidative sulfonylation of aryl ketones
employing sodium sulfinates as the sulfone source and DMSO
as the oxidant.[19] Although these procedures are mild and
efficient, they all have limits in practical laboratory synthesis
because of the employment of expensive hypervalent iodine
reagents or limited starting materials (some protocols are only
effective to aryl ketones), thus a general and efficient method
to the synthesis β-ketosulfones is therefor highly desired.
During the past decade, we have interests on the synthesis
of sulfur containing compounds employing sulfonyl chlorides
as the sulfur candidates.[20] Previously, we reported a reductive
sulfonylation of alkyl chlorides with sulfonyl chlorides whereby
various type of sulfones were prepared in good to high
yields.[20d] Recently, We reported a convenient NaI-catalyze
oxidative amination of aromatic sodium sulfinates employing
both air and ethylene dibromide (EDB) as the oxidants.[20c] Our
previous findings led us to investigate the more challenging
reaction
of
sulfonylation
of
ketones
with
chlorozinc
sulfinates,[21] which could be easily obtained from correspond-
ing sulfonyl chlorides in nearly quantitative yields in our
laboratory,[20d] for the synthesis of β-ketosulfones.[22]
Our initial trial with p-TolSO2ZnCl (1a, 1.5 mmol) and
acetophenone (2a, 1.0 mmol) in the presence of two equiv-
alents of EDB, NaHCO3 (2.0 mmol) in DMF at 60°C for 8 h did
not initiate the desired reaction (Table 1, entry 1). To our
delight, when 2 equivalents of Na2CO3 was introduced as the
base, the coupling reaction occurred at 60°C in DMF and the
desired product 3aa was obtained in 33% yield (entry 2).
Replacement of Na2CO3 with K2CO3 as a base further improved
the yield of 3aa to 42% (entry 3). Interestingly, when water
alone was introduced as the solvent, the yield of 3aa was
further improved to 62% yield (entry 4). However the use of
organic bases such as Et3N, DIPEA (N,N-Diisopropyl ethylamine)
and DBU (1,8-Diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene) did not improve
the yield of 3aa further (entries 5–7). The amount of EDB plays
a key role in the oxidative coupling of acetophenone and
chlorozinc sulfinates as was denoted in entry 8, when only one
equivalent of EDB was employed, the yield of 3aa was
dramatically decreased to 36% yield. The best yield of 3aa was
obtained when 2 wt.% of TPGS-750-M was introduced (Table 1,
entry 9). A control experiment proceeded under nitrogen
atmosphere showed that oxygen in air might play a role in this
transformation also (entry 10).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand (table 1,
entry 9), the scope of ketones for this reaction was then
examined with p-TolSO2ZnCl (1a) (Table 2). First, acetophenone
bearing a strong electron-withdrawing group (i.e. NO2) pro-
ceeded this reaction quite well and yielded 3ab in 88% yield.
Nevertheless, reactions of acetophenones with a halogen
substituent at para position always give a slightly lower yields
of products (3ac-3ae). Acetophenones bearing an electron
donating group (i.e, Me, OMe) generally produce good yields of
β-ketosulfone products (3af & 3ag). Other aryl alkyl ketones
screened such as 1-acetonaphthone, 1-indanone and 2-aceto-
thienone are all capable to perform this transformation and
deliver the corresponding products in 72% to 79% yields (3ah-
3ak). Notably, dialkyl ketones, as exemplified by acetone,
cycloheptanone and 1-cyclopropylethanone, are applicable
materials in our reaction system, affording the desired products
in good to high yields (3al-3an). Unexpectedly, the highly
steric hindered aliphatic ketones, i.e. bicyclo[2.2.2]octane,

Afterwards, we examined the scope of this protocol using
various chlorozinc sulfinates. As shown in table 3, phenyl-
sulfinyloxyzinc chloride reacted with 1-phenylpentan-1-one to
give 3ba in 54% yield. 4-Chlorophenylsulfinyloxyzinc chloride
reacted with 1-indanone to give 3bb in 77% yields. Benzene-
sulfinyloxyzinc chlorides having CF3 or plural halogen substitu-
ents (especially F) on the benzene ring worked similarly and
produced the desired products in low isolated yields (less than
60%), possibly because these substituents (CF3 and F) were
partially hydrolyzed under this basic reaction condition, thus
reduced the yields of isolated products. For examples, the
reaction
of
4-(trifluoromethyl)phenylsulfinyloxyzinc
chloride
with acetophenone in air afforded the corresponding β-
ketosulfone (3bc) in 59% yield. Heteroaromatic sulfinate, as
exemplified by quinolin-7-ylsulfinyloxyzinc chloride, could also
be
employed
to
react
with
2’-methylacetophenone
and
produced 3bg in a yield of 76%. Notably, aliphatic chlorozinc
sulfinates are applicable substrates here. As exemplified by
3bh to 3bj, under our optimized conditions, normally good to
high yields of corresponding β-ketosulfones could be obtained.
We next carried out control experiments to elucidate the
reaction mechanism (Scheme 2). In the presence of two
equivalents of TEMPO under our optimized conditions, the
reaction between 1a and 2a gave only 34% yield of 3aa.
HRMS analysis on the reaction mixture showed that adducts 4
and 5 were formed, demonstrating the occurrence of both
acetophenone radical and sulfonyl radical, which indicated the
operation of a single-electron-transfer pathway. Furthermore,
these reactions are only effective under base condition,
suggesting
that
the
equilibrium
amount
of
the
enolate
generated from a ketone in the presence of K2CO3 is most likely
the active species that reacts with the sulfonyl iodide, in situ
formed from chlorozinc sulfinate with iodine, to afford β-
ketosulfone.
Based on these experimental results and our previous
results,[20c] we propose the catalytic cycles as shown in
Scheme 3. The key steps include (i) EDB and oxygen oxidized
iodide ions into elemental iodine which then converted
chlorozinc sulfinate (III) into sulfonyl iodide (IV). (ii) Decom-
position of IV provided the iodine radical and sulfonyl radical.
In addition, IV could react with enolate (II) to give the β-keto
sulfone product (V). (iii) Under heat, molecular iodine was
activated into iodine radical which convert ketone into ketone
radical (VII). (iv) Ketone radical was trapped with sulfonyl iodide
(IV) to give the desired β-keto sulfone product (V) and
regenerate the iodine radical. Notably, β-keto sulfone (V)
encompasses a more acidic α-H than that of ketone (I) and
thus, under basic condition, enolate (VIII) may be formed.
However, enolate VIII is less nucleophilic than enolate II owing
to the weaker basicity and higher steric constraints around the
α-carbon, thus the second sulfonylating reaction on enolate
(VIII) was suppressed.
In conclusion, we have described a mild, practical, and
environmentally friendly NaI catalyzed oxidative coupling of
chlorozinc sulfinates with ketones method to prepare β-
ketosulfones. A wide range of functional groups can be
tolerated in the reaction conditions and the corresponding β-
ketosulfones were obtained in moderate to good yields. The
key feature of this process is the greater solubility of NaI and
sulfinates in micellar arrays where the oxidation is taking place.

title: The Synthesis of Tetrasubstituted Cycloalkenes Bearing π‐Conjugated Substituents and Their Optical Properties

z Organic & Supramolecular Chemistry
The Synthesis of Tetrasubstituted Cycloalkenes Bearing
π-Conjugated Substituents and Their Optical Properties
Marek Čubiňák,[a] John Bigeon,[b] Pavel Galář,[b] Lukáš Ondič,[b] and Tomáš Tobrman*[a]
We report the development of a new methodology for the
preparation of cyclic tetrasubstituted alkenes with π-conju-
gated substituents. The synthesis of the target compounds was
accomplished through the regioselective cross-coupling reac-
tion of diphenyl bromocyclohexenyl phosphate with organo-
zinc reagents. The procedure succeeded in the preparation of
alkenes with two pyrene moieties. The absorption and photo-
luminescence
spectra
of
the
prepared
compounds
were
measured.
Introduction
A cyclic or acyclic tetrasubstituted double bond represents a
valuable motif in a wide variety of substances. Cephalosporin
P1,[1] fusidic acid,[2] and tamoxifen[3] are all examples of
compounds that have either been isolated from natural
resources or are used for their biological properties. Another
example of a tetrasubstituted alkene is tetraphenyl ethylene
(TPE), which is considered a cornerstone in the field of materials
chemistry.[4]
Thus,
hexaphenyl,[5]
meta-terphenyl,[6]
[2.2]
paracyclophane,[7]
9,10-diazaanthracene,[8]
cyclopentadiene,[9]
and naphthalene[10] have all been decorated with TPE units to
determine the physical properties of the prepared compounds.
Such efforts have resulted in, for example, the design of novel
blue tandem organic light-emitting diodes[11] or a fluorescent
probe for the detection of hypochlorite.[12] A TPE unit is also a
suitable candidate for the synthesis of polycyclic aromatic
hydrocarbons (PAHs) by means of 6π-electrocyclization.[13]
Yet, pyrene is a representative example of a simple PAH
that also plays an important role in materials chemistry. The
applications of substituted pyrenes include the preparation of
fluorometric and colorimetric sensors,[14] the formation of
metal-organic frameworks,[15] the construction of probes for
studying protein conformation and conformational changes,[16]
and the development of supramolecular chemical sensors.[17]
The significant properties of both TPE and substituted pyrenes
have led to the design and attempted preparation of a wide
range of tetrasubstituted alkenes featuring a tetrasubstituted
double bond and a pyrene moiety. Although a wide variety of
procedures are available for the preparation of substituted
pyrenes[18] and tetrasubstituted alkenes,[19] the preparation of
alkenes with four, three, two, or one pyrene unit(s) can only be
achieved using a few procedures. For instance, alkenes bearing
four 4,5,9,10-tetrahydropyren-2-yl units can only be synthesized
using the McMurry reaction,[20] whereas alkenes bearing two
pyrenyl units directly attached to the double bond can be
synthesized by means of the McMurry reaction,[21] the Wittig
reaction,[22] Horner-Wadsworth-Emmons (HWE) modification,[23]
metathesis,[24] carbonyl group condensation,[25] and the rho-
dium-catalyzed deoxygenation-Suzuki reaction sequence.[26] A
similar trend can also be observed in relation to alkenes with
two pyrene units that are connected to the double bond via a
spacer. Such substances can be efficiently synthesized through
the formation of a substituted double-bond moiety via the
McMurry reaction[27] or cross-metathesis[28] followed by the
Suzuki reaction. The widest range of procedures for the
preparation of pyrenyl alkenes is available for alkenes with one
pyrene moiety. In addition to the above-mentioned procedures,
dehydration,[21] the Heck[29] and HWE[30] reactions, carbonyl
group condensations,[31] and carbonyl-olefin metathesis[32] rep-
resent the methods of choice in this regard.
The good availability of acyclic alkenes with two pyrenyl
substituents contrasts with the limited availability of cyclic
alkenes with two pyrenyl substituents. The latter alkenes can
be
synthesized
via the
McMurry
reaction,
although this
procedure has been used to prepare only a single alkene
(Scheme 1).[33] A different approach to the preparation of a
cyclic alkene with pyrenyl substituents makes use of the Suzuki
and
Negishi
reactions
of
bromocyclobutenyl
diethyl
phosphate.[34] It is expected that tetrasubstituted cyclic alkenes
with pyrenyl moieties may find various applications in the field
of materials chemistry. Therefore, based on our experience with
cross-coupling reactions,[35] we decided to develop a new
methodology for the preparation of cyclic tetrasubstituted
alkenes derived from cyclohexene using the pyrenyl substitu-
ent 3 as a model compound for future applications. The
proposed approach for the preparation of the cyclohexene 3

Results and Discussion
The route proposed for the preparation of cyclic tetrasubsti-
tuted alkenes with 1-pyrenyl substituents makes use of the
cyclic vinyl phosphate 1 as a model compound for studying the
course of the double Negishi reaction to form the alkene 3
(Scheme 1). The choice of cyclic phosphate 1 offers several
advantages,
including
the
availability
of
the
starting
2-
bromocyclohexanone[40] and the sufficiently different reactivity
of the C� Br and activated C� O bonds for regioselective cross-
coupling reactions.[35c] In addition to the optical properties of
the alkene 3, this work will help to reveal the patterns of the
cross-coupling reactions of bromovinyl phosphates with 1-
pyrenyl-base organozinc reagents. This is important because
these substituents differ in terms of their electronic and steric
properties from substituted benzenes, which are more com-
monly
used
to
determine
the
extent
of
cross-coupling
reactions.
A simple retrosynthetic analysis showed that three common
phosphates, namely 2a, 2b, and 2c, could be designed for the
preparation of diverse alkenes with the 1-pyrenyl substituents
3 (Scheme 2). An important intermediate in this case is the
phosphate 2b, the use of which should allow the preparation
of the cyclohexene 3b with two pyrene groups directly
attached to the double bond.
The preparation of the starting phosphates was performed
by
means
of
the
Negishi
reaction
of
the
cyclohexenyl
phosphate 1 with organozinc reagents in the presence of both
palladium acetate and the dicyclohexyl[2’,4’,6’-tris(propan-2-
yl)[1,1’-biphenyl]-2-yl]phosphane (XPhos) ligand (Scheme 3).
The phosphates 2aa, 2ab, 2cd, and 2b were prepared in good
yields. The other phosphates were all obtained in similar
isolated yields.[35c]
Using the prepared phosphates, we studied the scope of
the Negishi reaction of the phosphates 2ca–2cf and 2b
(Scheme 4). In contrast to previous results,[35c] the tested
phosphates 2ca–2cf smoothly reacted with 1-pyrenylzinc(II)
chloride at elevated temperature. The isolated yields of the
alkenes 3ca–3cf ranged from 68–89%. The reaction of the
phosphate 2cf with (6-(4-(N,N-diphenylamino)phenyl)pyrene-1-
yl)zinc(II) chloride gave the reaction product 3cg in an average
isolated yield. Surprisingly, the phosphate 2b did not react
with
1-pyrenylzinc(II)
chloride
or
4-methoxyphenylzinc(II)
chloride under the tested conditions. Varying the reaction
conditions to include an elevated reaction temperature (60°C
and 80°C in dry THF) and the use of other ligands (DPEPhos,
Ruphos, XPhos, etc.) did not prove successful. The substitution
of 1-pyrenylzinc(II) chloride for 1-pyrenylmagnesium bromide
resulted in the decomposition of the starting phosphate 2b.
We assume that the limited reactivity of the phosphate 2b
during the Negishi reaction was caused by electronic and steric

The photoluminescence (PL) characterizations of the se-
lected alkenes are presented at Figure 1b. Unlike to the
absorption, the PL spectra were significantly affected by the
presence of substituents. The pyrene (4a) and the alkene 4b
have their spectra composed of an intensive band in the blue
spectral region.
A hypsochromic shift (29 nm) was observed for the basic
alkene 4b compared to the pyrene (4a) (Table 1). A more
pronounced hypsochromic shift (65 nm) was observed for
alkene 3cd, but this may be influenced by a significant self-
absorption. Alkenes bearing substituted phenyl rings had a low
bathochromic shift (27 nm) as illustrated by selected alkenes
3ca, 3ce and 3aa. On the other hand, a significant bath-
ochromic shift was observed for alkenes 3cg, 3aj, 3cga and
3cgb with thienyl substituents. A similar situation was also
observed for the Stokes shift, which reflects the reorganization

values of the Stokes shift were in the range of 6000–8800 cm� 1,
but the alkenes with thienyl substituents 3aj and 3ad reached

We also tested the thermal stability of the selected alkenes
by means of a thermogravimetric analysis (TG). The results are
shown in Figure 4. The thermal decompositions of the alkenes
3aa and 3ca started at 130°C and 96°C, respectively, and both
samples were completely decomposed at around 400°C (421°C
for 3aa and 376°C for 3ca). Exceptional thermal stability was
observed in the case of the alkene 3af, for which significant
decomposition was observed at 358°C, although the complete
decomposition of the studied sample was not observed under
the experimental conditions.
Conclusion
We have demonstrated that diphenyl bromocyclohexenyl
phosphate is a suitable building block for the preparation of a
cyclic tetrasubstituted double bond with π-conjugated sub-
stituents. More specifically, the substitution of the bromine and
phosphate groups was conducted via the reaction of the
starting diphenyl bromocyclohexenyl phosphate with organo-
zinc reagents at room temperature in dry tetrahydrofuran. The
studied reactions were catalyzed using a palladium catalyst
with the XPhos ligand for the substitution of the bromine atom
and
1,3-bis(diphenylphosphino)propane
or
bis[(2-diphenyl-
phosphino)phenyl] ether for the substitution of the phosphate
group. The prepared alkenes were studied with regard to their
optical properties by means of absorption and photolumines-
cence spectroscopy. In addition, we observed the high thermal
stability of the alkene 3af through a thermogravimetric
analysis. The results obtained suggest that the tetrasubstituted
alkenes bearing thienyl and pyrenyl moieties have optical
properties with promising applications in materials chemistry.
However, further experiments and quantum chemical calcu-
lations with respect to: (i) the substitution and E/Z-configu-
ration of the double bond, (ii) the influence of heteroatoms of
the five-membered ring, and (iii) a position of the pyrene ring
are required to tune and explain physical properties of the
synthesized alkenes.

Catalytic Enantioselective Organozinc 
Addition Toward Optically Active 
Tertiary Alcohol Synthesis
MANABU HATANO, KAZUAKI ISHIHARA
Graduate School of Engineering, Nagoya University, Furo-cho, Chikusa, Nagoya, 464-8603, Japan
Received 14 February 2008; Accepted 6 March 2008
ABSTRACT: A highly enantioselective organozinc (R2Zn) addition to a series of aldehydes and 
ketones was developed based on conjugate Lewis acid–Lewis base catalysis. Optically active secondary 
and tertiary alcohols were obtained in high yields with high enantioselectivities without Ti(IV) 
compounds. Bifunctional chiral 3,3′-diphosphoryl-BINOL ligands were designed and prepared 
through a phospho-Fries rearrangement as a key step. On the other hand, bifunctional chiral phos-
phoramide ligands were designed and prepared from -valine. Mechanistic studies were performed 
by X-ray analyses of Zn(II) cluster and chiral ligands, a 31P NMR experiment on Zn(II) complexes, 
and stoichiometric reactions with some chiral or achiral Zn(II) complexes to propose a transition 
state assembly that includes monomeric active intermediates. © 2008 The Japan Chemical Journal 
Forum and Wiley Periodicals, Inc. Chem Rec 8: 143–155; 2008: Published online in Wiley Inter-
Science (www.interscience.wiley.com) DOI 10.1002/tcr.20146
Key words: alcohol; asymmetric catalysis; Lewis acid–Lewis base catalyst; organometallics; zinc(II)

Introduction
Optically active secondary and tertiary alcohols are versatile 
building blocks for the synthesis of natural products and 
pharmaceuticals. One important strategy for synthesizing these 
alcohols is a carbon–carbon bond-forming reaction between 
carbonyl compounds and organometallic reagents.1,2 In par-
ticular, catalytic enantioselective organozinc addition to 
aldehydes is one of the most important reactions involving 
carbon–carbon bond formation, and optically active secondary 
alcohols are obtained.3 However, it is still difﬁ cult to achieve 
a high yield and enantioselectivity for tertiary alcohols from 
ketones and organozinc reagents due to conspicuous steric and 
electronic constraints between ketones and organometallic 
reagents.4 Furthermore, organometallic reagents often cause 
the enolization of ketones due to their high basicity or com-
petitive reduction via β-H transfer to give undesired secondary 
alcohols. To date, numerous efﬁ cient chiral ligands have been 
developed for secondary alcohol synthesis from aldehydes, but 
their application to tertiary alcohol synthesis from ketones via 
alkylation or arylation is still extremely limited.5–10 In princi-
ple, we can classify organometallic alkylation or arylation into 
three types: (i) double activation by only Lewis acidic organo-
metallic reagents, (ii) double activation by a Lewis acid–Lewis 
base, and (iii) double activation by a conjugate Lewis acid–
Lewis base (Scheme 1). Usually, organomagnesium and 
organoaluminum reagents belong to type (i). Most of the 
reported enantioselective organozinc additions to aldehydes are 
type (ii), where the Lewis acid and Lewis base are attached to 
each other.11 In sharp contrast to types (i) and (ii), type (iii)

catalysis involves an electron charge transfer at the ligand inte-
rior. Thus, type (iii) catalysis should offer a great advantage for 
enhancing catalytic activity because the direct linkage between 
the acid and the base in type (ii) may weaken or negate both 
activities. Recently, to overcome these essential problems in 
carbonyl compounds and organozinc reagents, we developed 
two type (iii) catalyses for the synthesis of optically active ter-
tiary alcohols. One of these has a 3,3′-diphosphoryl-BINOL 
[BINOL = 1,1′-bi(2-naphthol)] skeleton and the other has a 
phosphoramide structure, which is derived from -valine. 
Here, we report the development of a highly efﬁ cient enanti-
oselective organozinc addition to not only aldehydes but also 
ketones using a conjugate Lewis acid–Lewis base catalytic 
system.12,13
Design of Chiral 3,3′-Diphosphoryl-
BINOLate–Zn(II) Complexes14
In early investigations, it has been shown that the 
BINOLate–Ti(IV) catalyst is highly effective in diethylzinc 
addition to aldehydes, although more than a stoichiometric 
amount of Ti(Oi-Pr)4 is necessary to achieve high yields 
and high enantioselectivities.15 Moreover, 3,3′-disubstituted 
BINOLs have been designed for active Zn(II) catalysts in 
diethylzinc addition to aldehydes without Ti(Oi-Pr)4.16 
However, sterically demanding 3,3′-disubstituted BINOLs are 
often difﬁ cult to synthesize in satisfactory yields because of the 
multistep transformations from the starting BINOL. To 
overcome this difﬁ culty, we devised 3,3′-diphosphoryl-

organozinc addition to aldehydes without Ti(Oi-Pr)4. The key 
in designing our catalysts is conjugation between a 2-naphthol 
moiety and a 3-phosphoryl group (P¨O) to doubly activate 
the electrophile and nucleophile.17,18 In particular, we exam-
ined enantioselective organozinc addition to aldehydes using 
chiral BINOLate–Zn(II) catalysts bearing phosphine oxides 
[P(¨O)R2], phosphonates [P(¨O)(OR)2], or phosphorami-
des [P(¨O)(NR2)2] at the 3,3′-positions (Fig. 1).
Preparation of (R)-3,3′-Diphosphoryl-BINOLs
(R)-3,3′-bis(diphenylphosphinoyl)-BINOL (1) was prepared 
almost quantitatively from commercially available (R)-BINOL 
in two steps via phospho-Fries rearrangement (Scheme 2).14a 
The starting (R)-BINOL in THF was treated with NaH. 
Subsequent dropwise addition of diphenylphosphinic chlo-
ride gave the corresponding phosphinates 5 quantitatively 
without further puriﬁ cation. The rearrangement of 5 
proceeded with LDA in THF at −78° C for 1 h to give 1 
quantitatively as colorless crystals after recrystallization 
from toluene/hexane. Phosphonate [P(¨O)(OR)2] ligands 
2 and 3, which had substituents that were more electron 
donating than the phenyl groups in 1, were also prepared 
in a similar manner via phospho-Fries rearrangement of 
6 and 7.
Unfortunately, our promising 4 could not be prepared 
by the simple procedures described earlier because the key 
phospho-Fries rearrangement could not proceed on both 
sides of the 3- and 3′-positions. However, protection of 
2-naphthol in 10 with a PMB (p-methoxybenzyl) group 
after the ﬁ rst phospho-Fries rearrangement enabled the second 
rearrangement to 14, and 4 was obtained after deprotection of 
the PMB group (Scheme 3).14b,c This synthetic method was 
also effective for preparing 2, which was obtained in low 
yield by a usual phospho-Fries rearrangement, as shown in 
Scheme 2. The total yields of 2 were improved to 59% in 
Scheme 3.

In particular, aromatic aldehydes with electron-donating or 
electron-withdrawing groups showed high enantioselectivities 
(up to 95% ee) (entries 1–4). The reactions also proceeded 
smoothly for heteroaromatic aldehydes and α,β-unsaturated 
aldehydes (entries 5–8). For aliphatic aldehydes, in which 
competitive reduction often occurs along with ethylation, 
the corresponding secondary aliphatic alcohols were obtained 
with high enantioselectivities (up to 94% ee) (entries 
9–11). An increase in the catalytic activity of 1 was observed 
at 50° C with a slight loss of enantioselectivity, and the catalyst 
loading could be decreased to 5 mol % (parentheses in 
Table 1).
BINOLate–Zn(II) Catalysts Bearing Phosphonates 
or Phosphoramides
To achieve a higher Lewis basicity of phosphoryl moiety 
to increase the nucleophilicity of organozinc reagents, 
chiral ligands (2 and 3), which had electron-donating P-
substitutions, were examined (Table 2).14b,c The reaction with 
3 mol % of 1 proceeded with high enantioselectivity (93% ee), 
but was slow. However, even 3 mol % of 2 or 3 was more 
effective than 1 for the enantioselective addition of diethylzinc 
(1.5 equiv) to benzaldehyde (15a) in THF–toluene at room 
temperature (entries 1–3). This preference for 3 to 2 was prob-
ably because of the strong electron donation and compact 
structure required by a ﬁ xed ring conformation. For a promis-
ing ligand with a higher Lewis basicity, we next examined a 
BINOLate–Zn(II) catalyst bearing conjugate phosphoramide 
moieties [P¨(O)(NMe2)2]. The reaction proceeded smoothly 
with 3 mol % of 4 and 1.5 equiv of Et2Zn at room temperature 
for 24 h to give the product in 98% yield with 97% ee (entry 
4). Therefore, the catalytic activity of 4 was extremely higher 
than those of 1, 2, and 3, and the order of reactivity was 
4 > 3 > 2 > 1, according to their electron-donating abilities to 
phosphoryl moieties.19 Using 1–4 at a warm temperature 
(50° C) increased the reactivity with almost the same enanti-
oselectivity (within 0–2% ee) (entries 5–8). In particular, by 
using 4, the Et-adduct was obtained in quantitative yield with 
95% ee within only 4 h (entry 8).

Enantioselective Ph2Zn Addition to Aldehydes
Catalytic enantioselective diphenylzinc addition to 15 was 
examined in the presence of conjugate Lewis acid–Lewis base 
BINOLate–Zn(II) catalyst and 10 mol % of Et2Zn.14a,14c,20 
Unexpectedly, low yield and low enantioselectivity were 
observed in the phenylation of 4′-chlorobenzaldehyde when 4, 
3, and 2 were used (Table 5, entries 1–3). However, 1 showed 
good reactivities, and the corresponding Ph-adduct was 
obtained in 96% yield and 88% ee (entry 4). For other 
aromatic aldehydes bearing electron-donating or electron-
withdrawing groups, 1 was so effective that the reactions 
proceeded smoothly to give the corresponding 1,1-diarylcarbi-
nols with 73–88% ee. The reason for the unexpected reversal 
of catalytic activity between phenylations (1 > 2 > 3 > 4) and 
alkylations (4 > 3 > 2 > 1) is not clear, and further examina-
tions are necessary. For one reason, a steric factor involving 
π–π interactions among the catalysts and Ph2Zn cannot be 
denied. Eventually, our Lewis acid–Lewis base BINOLate–
Zn(II) catalysts [i.e., 1–Zn(II) and 4–Zn(II)] gave comple-
mentary results in enantioselective phenylation and alkylation, 
respectively.

Dinuclear Zn(II) Complexes Through

equiv each) in dichloromethane–hexane at room temperature 
for 24 h under open-air conditions.14a The ORTEP drawings

Effect of Phenol and Biphenol Structures
Next, the effect of phenol and biphenol on the catalytic activity 
was examined.14c Catalytic diethylzinc addition to 15a was 
explored with achiral ligands 26 and 27 (Scheme 6). The cata-
lytic activity of 26 (20 mol %) with a phenol backbone was 
low, and 33% of 16a was given for 24 h (Eq. 4). The low 
reactivity of 26 could probably be rationalized by a six-
membered Zn(II) chelation as a stabilized structure. In high 
contrast, 10 mol % of 27 with a biphenol backbone could 
catalyze the reaction effectively, and 16a was obtained in 89% 
for 6 h (Eq. 5). Therefore, the biphenol moiety might be an 
essential structure to enhance the reactivity. These results indi-
cated that a new seven-membered chelation of diethylzinc with 
R(OZnEt)2 [R(OH)2 = biphenol] could trigger the dissocia-
tion of the original six-membered Zn(II) chelation to relieve 
steric hindrance before the transition states (Eq. 5).

Proposed Transition State Assembly With 
Conjugate Acid–Base BINOLate–Zn(II) Catalysts
The mechanistic aspect of the transition state assembly, which 
should be regarded as a working model, is considered (Fig. 
6).14c Based on the previous examinations, the active Zn(II) 
complex in this catalysis is likely to be monomeric tetra- or 
pentanuclear species (Scheme 6). The proposed transition 
state assembly (28) may provide the conformation as shown 
in Figure 4B with π(2-naphthol) orbital interactions to 
σ*(P—O) through hyperconjugation. Compound 28 has two 
conjugate Lewis acidic NaphO–Zn(II)–Et centers to activate 
aldehyde and Lewis basic phosphoryl groups to activate dieth-
ylzinc. From the results of the catalysis by phenol and biphenol 
(Scheme 7), tetranuclear complexes might change to penta-
nuclear complex 25, and then a dissociation of P¨O…Zn in 
25 would lead to 28. Due to the steric hindrance between 
aldehyde and two substituents to phosphoryl moiety, re-face 
attack should be favored exclusively. Eventually, (R)-products 
can be obtained along with the regeneration of the tetra- and 
pentanuclear species.

Evaluation of Conjugate Acid–Base Catalyst, 
Chiral Phosphoramide–Zn(II)
The chiral phosphoramide ligands (30–33) were readily pre-
pared from commercially available N-Boc-protected -valine 
(29) (Scheme 8). In each step, good to excellent yields were 
observed when diphenylphosphinic chloride [Ph2P(O)Cl] was 
used. To develop conjugate Lewis acid–Lewis base catalysts 
suitable for tertiary alcohol synthesis from ketones, we initially 
investigated -valine-derived chiral phosphoramide ligand (30, 
10 mol %) in the catalytic enantioselective phenylation of 
4′-chloroacetophenone (34a) with diphenylzinc (1 equiv) and 
diethylzinc (2 equiv) in heptane at room temperature (Table 
6).21 Fortunately, simply designed 30 gave 35a with high enan-
tioselectivity (80% ee), although the yield was low (30%). 
Chiral ligand 31 or 32 bearing a pyrrolidinyl or piperidinyl 
group instead of a NMe2 group in 30 showed improved cata-
lytic activity, but the enantioselectivity was the same or less. 
However, 33 bearing a sterically demanding P-(1-naphthyl) 
moiety showed considerable improvement in both yield 
and enantioselectivity (up to 95% ee). After optimization, 35a 
was obtained in 98% yield with 92% ee by using 1 mol % 
of 33.
We next examined the generality of this catalysis for other 
ketones (Table 7).21 For aryl ketones with either an electron-
withdrawing or electron-donating group, cyclic ketones, het-
eroaryl ketones, and α,β-unsaturated ketone with 10 mol % of 
(S)-33, high enantioselectivities (91–98% ee), and high yields 
(up to 98%) were observed in the products. Moreover, the 
aliphatic ketones also provided the corresponding tertiary 
alcohols with 80–82% ee in high yields. In particular, a 1 g 
scale (5 mmol) preparation of (R)-35a was established in 91%

Conclusion
In summary, we have developed a highly efﬁ cient enantioselec-
tive organozinc addition to not only aldehydes but also ketones 
using conjugate Lewis acid–Lewis base catalysts. These chiral 
Zn(II) catalysts (i.e., chiral 3,3′-diphosphoryl-BINOLate–
Zn(II) complex and chiral phosphoramide–Zn(II) complexes, 
which are simply prepared in situ) are derived from an inex-
pensive BINOL or -valine. From a variety of aromatic and 
aliphatic ketones and aldehydes, optically active tertiary 
alcohols and secondary alcohols, respectively, were obtained in 
high yields with high enantioselectivities under mild reaction 
conditions without Ti(Oi-Pr)4. Further investigations to estab-
lish more efﬁ cient reaction conditions with minimum amounts 
of both organozinc reagents and catalysts are underway.

ABSTRACT: In the ﬁeld of asymmetric synthesis, the development of new chiral ligands has been
regarded as an attractive challenge for decades. Novel chiral ligands can often have a great impact
on synthetic protocols. In this context, we are currently interested in the application of 1,10-
phenanthroline (phen) as an entirely new class of chiral ligand. To handle this issue, we designed a
chiral phen ligand that provides the N,N,O-tridentate coordination of the phen moiety and an
additional phenolic hydroxyl group. As phen possesses greater coordination ability with various
ions, our chiral phen ligand would be valuable as one of the "privileged" chiral ligands applied to a
broad range of metal catalysts and new reactions. This account summarizes the results of the
application of the chiral phen ligand to various kinds of metal catalysis.
Keywords: asymmetric synthesis, chiral ligands, homogeneous catalysis, transition metals, tri-
dentate ligands
1. Introduction
The development of new classes of chiral ligands has been
regarded as one of the most fundamental and important
research topics in asymmetric synthesis. Our research group is
currently interested in the use of 1,10-phenanthroline (phen)
as a backbone for chiral ligands.[1] The phen backbone is one
of the most classical and widely applied chelate reagents and
has two cis-oriented nitrogen atoms (Figure 1).[2] Its strong
afﬁnity with a wide range of metal ions, including not only
transition metals but also typical elements, is due to the rigid
and planar structure containing the two cis-oriented nitrogen
atoms, thus enabling the formation of entropically favored
strong complexes compared to structurally analogous 2,2-
bipyridine ligands.[2]
Therefore, phen has also been employed as an effective
ligand in various reactions catalyzed by transition-metal com-
plexes.[3] However, it is a somewhat surprising fact that chiral
ligands utilizing the phen backbone have been rarely studied,
even though there is the potential for broad applications and
versatile performances with transition-metal catalysts.[1,4] The
ﬁrst chiral phen, with a simple (R)-sec-butyl group at the C-3
position, was designed by Gladiali et al. in 1987. The catalytic
activity was evaluated in Rh-catalyzed enantioselective transfer
hydrogenation of ketones, albeit with low enantioselectivity
(Scheme 1).[5a]
Although this survey surely conﬁrmed the applicability of
chiral phen in asymmetric synthesis, the following project on
the development of chiral phen ligands has been less
explored.[5–9] The major studies with these chiral phen ligands
have been limited to (i) Rh-catalyzed reduction,[5] (ii) Cu-
catalyzed cyclopropanation,[6a,b] (iii) Cu-catalyzed allylic oxi-
dation,[6c] (iv) Cu-catalyzed Henry reaction and amination
reaction,[6d,e] (v) Pd-catalyzed Tsuji–Trost reaction,[7] (vi) Sc
or In-catalyzed ring opening of meso-epoxides,[8] and (vii) Fe-
catalyzed epoxidation.[9] We assumed that this is due to the
inherent difﬁculty of structural modiﬁcation of phen, which
lacks sp3 carbons at which a chiral center can be introduced.
Therefore, the basic strategy to design chiral ligands common-
ly relies on the use of central or axial chirality to establish the
effective chiral environment. However, previous examples of
chiral phen ligands were mainly based on the attachment of
pendent chiral auxiliaries at the C-2 or C-3 positions of the
phen backbone (Figure 2).[5–8] In addition, most of these chi-
ral side chains were derived from natural chiral sources and
the difﬁculty in structural manipulations leads to a lack of
molecular accuracy. One exception of natural chiral auxiliary-
free
phen
ligands
was
reported
by
Nishikawa
and
Yamamoto.[9]
Another difﬁculty in the design of chiral phen ligands
with pendent chiral auxiliaries is controlling the conforma-
tional ﬁxation. The C–C bond between phen and the chiral
auxiliary rotates freely and the attainment of the appropriate
and effective chiral environment is basically troublesome
(Figure 3a). We envisioned that design of tridentate chiral
phen ligands bearing the other coordinative chiral auxiliary
would enable the formation of more stable complexes
(Figure 3b).
In this context, we recently designed the novel chiral phen
ligand (S)-1 with axial chirality provided by the binaphthyl
backbone (Figure 4).[11] The signiﬁcant difference from previ-
ous chiral phen ligands is the introduction of a phenolic
hydroxy group, which provides not only classical N,N-

2. Synthesis of Axially Chiral N,N,O-Tridentate
Phen Ligands

available (S)-BINOL is shown in Scheme 2. Preparation of the
reported compound (S)-4 was carried out by the modiﬁed proce-

of monotriﬂate (S)-2 with Tf2O and N,N-diisopropylethyl-
amine. Nickel-catalyzed Kumada cross-coupling of (S)-2 with
Grignard reagents provided compounds (S)-3 having a variety of
aromatic substituents. The hydrogenation of (S)-2 with Pd/C
gave (S)-3 without any substituent at the R position (R 5 H).[14]
The protection of the hydroxyl moiety with the MOM protect-
ing group furnished (S)-4.

3. Application in Zn Catalysis
In the evaluation of new chiral (S)-1, we kept in mind that a very
limited range of metals have been applied to enantioselective
reactions catalyzed by chiral phen ligands as mentioned above,[5–
9] in sharp contrast to the non-asymmetric reactions where a vari-
ety of metal catalysts are used.[15] We expected ligand (S)-1 would
form the corresponding complexes with a wide range of metals
and show unexplored utility in asymmetric catalysis. Among the
various metal candidates, we initially investigated the catalytic
activity in Zn catalysis.[16] Zinc complexes of phen are also
reported in inorganic chemistry; however, the organic reactions
catalyzed by such complexes have been limited.[17]
3.1. Enantioselective 1,2-Addition of Organozinc
Reagents to Aldehydes
We started our investigation into the catalytic activity of (S)-1
with the model reaction of 1,2-addition of organozinc reagents

Although a variety of chiral ligands for the enantioselective
addition of organozinc reagents have been discovered so far,
the employment of phen derivatives has been rarely investigat-
ed, even achiral ones.[18] On the other hand, N,N,O-tridentate
chiral ligands prepared from natural chiral sources were
applied to asymmetric organozinc addition.[19]
Scheme 3 summarizes the results of screening (S)-1 in the
model reaction of diethylzinc and p-phenylbenzaldehyde 7a in
Et2O at 08C (Table 1). The study of substituent effects in (S)-1
revealed that the presence of an aromatic ring as substituent R of
the naphthyl ring is very important to obtain the product (R)-8a
in good yield with high enantioselectivity. For example, the use
of ligand (S)-1a with a phenyl group resulted in the formation of
(R)-8a in 85% yield and 84% ee. On the other hand, the reaction
in the presence of ligand (S)-1b without any aromatic group led
to the dramatic decrease of both yield and ee (37% yield, 3% ee).
Therefore, further study on the substituent effect of the phenyl
group of (S)-1a determined that (S)-1f with the 3,5-bis(triﬂuoro-
methyl)phenyl group was the most effective ligand.
Selected substrate scope is shown in Table 2. Regardless of
the position of the substituent on the aromatic ring, the reac-
tions of o-, m-, and p-tolualdehydes uniformly furnished the
corresponding alcohols (R)-8b–d with high enantioselectivity.
Concerning the electronic effects in the substrate, both p-
anisaldehyde and p-(triﬂuoromethyl)benzaldehyde were toler-
ated. The reaction of 1-naphthaldehyde gave the product
(R)-8g with the highest ee of 95%.
In control experiments, we observed that the analogous
bidentate ligands (S)-9a and 9b gave poorer results and the
monoanionic N,N,O-tridentate property of (S)-1 was essential
to obtain high enantioselectivity (Scheme 3).
A plausible mechanism for the asymmetric induction is
illustrated in Figure 6. Since ligand (S)-1 displays C1 symme-
try, the orientation of carbonyl coordination should be distin-
guished as in I-1 and in I-2. We assume that the more favored
intermediate should be I-1 due to the steric repulsion between
the aromatic ring of (S)-1 and the aldehyde in the case of I-2.
The nucleophilic addition occurs from the Re face of the car-
bonyl carbon to give (R)-8a as a major enantiomer. This plau-
sible mechanism clearly matches the fact that (S)-1b without
any aromatic rings did not function (Table 1).

3.2. Enantioselective Amination of b-Keto Carbonyl
Compounds with Azodicarboxylate
Encouraged by the enantioselective addition of organozinc
reagents, we investigated the utility of the Zn(II) complex of (S)-1
as a chiral Lewis acid catalyst. The screening of several model reac-
tions revealed that Zn(II)-catalyzed electrophilic amination of b-
ketocarbonyl compounds with azodicarboxylates[20,21] gave a
promising result. We selected ethyl 2-oxocyclopentanecarboxylate
10a as a model substrate and conducted the amination reaction
of 10a with diisopropyl azodicarboxylate 11a in the presence of
complexes of (S)-1 and Zn(OTf)2 in DCE for 24 h at room tem-
perature. The study on the effect of ligand structure is shown in
Table 3. Also in this case, the substituent R on the naphthyl ring
of (S)-1 had a signiﬁcant impact on the ee value. Chiral phen (S)-
1d with a 3,5-xylyl group was the best ligand, giving the desired
product 12a with 87% ee.
Also in this reaction, we performed control experiments
using control ligands (S)-9a and 9b (Table 3). The reaction
with (S)-9a led to a complete loss of enantioselectivity, proba-
bly due to the weaker coordination ability of (S)-9a than (S)-1.
The reaction with (S)-9b gave the corresponding product 12a
with a similar enantiomeric excess as (S)-1a (76% ee vs 78%
ee), whereas (S)-9b was an ineffective chiral ligand in the enan-
tioselective addition of organozinc reagents. The present result
suggests that the presence of a free proton within (S)-1 does
not have signiﬁcant inﬂuence on the asymmetric induction
and (S)-1 might work as a neutral ligand toward Zn(OTf)2,
even though it is difﬁcult to determine the coordination as
N,N-bidentate or N,N,O-tridentate.
The selected scope of amination using the optimized azo-
dicarboxylate 11b is shown in Table 4. The reactions of several
ﬁve-membered cyclic b-ketoesters 10b–e provided 12b–e with
ee values of 90–93%. The ring size of 10 affected the enantio-
selectivity. For example, six-membered and seven-membered
products 12f and 12g were obtained with lower selectivity.
4. Application in Cu Catalysis
To expand the utility of (S)-1, we wished to make clear the scope
of its use in other transition-metal catalysis. In this vein, we tried
to understand the structure of metal complexes with (S)-1 by
spectrographic analysis. Only one example of a metal complex
with N,N,O-tridentate ligand based on the combination of phen
backbone and phenol derivatives was found in the literature.
Stack et al. synthesized and characterized achiral phen-phenolate
Cu(II) complexes 13 as a chemical model of galactose oxidase
(Scheme 4).[22] Even though such Cu(II) complexes should have
promising properties for alcohol oxidation, further studies on the
catalytic activity toward organic synthesis have been limited.
Owing to the abundance of optically active a-hydroxy car-
bonyl compounds in nature, the asymmetric introduction of a
hydroxyl group at the a-carbon of carbonyl compounds has
gained considerable attention in asymmetric synthesis.[23]
Treatment of a metal enolate with N-sulfonyloxaziridine
(Davis’s oxaziridine) offers a versatile route to nucleophilic a-
hydroxylation of carbonyl compounds.[24] Several research

The proposed explanation of the asymmetric induction is
illustrated in Figure 7. We assume that the role of the Boc group

bulky Boc group and the aromatic ring of (S)-1 in I-2. The naph-
thyl ring of (S)-1 blocks the Si face of the Cu(II) enolate and the
oxaziridine 16a would approach from the Re face to furnish (R)-

5. Application in Ni Catalysis
Our mechanistic study of the Cu(II)-catalyzed enantioselective
Davis oxidation of 14 suggests that the asymmetric induction
of this hydroxylation reaction should be controlled by the
effective shielding of prochiral Cu(II) enolate surrounded by
chiral ligand (S)-1 (Figure 7). Based on this consideration, we
envisioned that the present catalytic system could be further
extended to the use of other electrophiles. We investigated the
enantioselective Michael addition of 14 to methyl vinyl ketone
(MVK) (Scheme 7).[27]
Disappointingly, the reaction of 14a with the Cu(II) com-
plex of (S)-1a gave the product 18a in a low yield and the race-
mic form. The subsequent screening of metal precursors
revealed that only the reaction with the complex of nickel(II)
acetate tetrahydrate and (S)-1a gave (R)-18a in quantitative
yield and with moderate enantioselectivity.[28] To further
increase the ee value, we introduced an additional effective chi-
ral environment within (S)-1a. We anticipated that the intro-
duction of the additional phenyl substituent within the phen
backbone of (S)-1a would enhance steric factors. Gratifyingly,
the reaction with this modiﬁed ligand (S)-1g gave the corre-
sponding Michael adduct (R)-18a in 92% yield and with 87%
ee. The selected scope of the Michael addition of 14 to MVK is
shown in Table 7.

6. Application in Rh Catalysis
We have succeeded in demonstrating the catalytic activity of
(S)-1 in chiral Lewis acid catalysis of Zn(II), Cu(II), and
Ni(II) for enantioselective C–C and C–heteroatom bond
formations. The following interest in the application of (S)-
1 focused on the use of unprecedented transformations
using transition-metal catalysis involving the redox cycle. In
this chapter, we discuss the Rh-catalyzed enantioselective
desymmetrization of hydrosilanes towards the construction
of chiral silicon stereogenic centers,[29] which have been of
great interest considering their unique chemical and physical
properties. In this context, the aim of our synthetic plan is
the utilization of the enantioselective desymmetrization of
prochiral silanes 19 via intramolecular hydrosilylation in the
presence of a chiral transition-metal catalyst, thus giving
chiral silicon-containing oleﬁns 20 (Scheme 8).[30] A few
examples of the catalytic asymmetric preparation of chiral
silicon compounds utilizing hydrosilylation protocols were
reported by Tamao and Tomooka.[31]
To identify effective catalytic systems, we performed the
model reaction of hydrosilane 19a with various transition-
metal complexes of (S)-1 in toluene at 608C (Table 8).
[Rh(cod)Cl]2 was found to be an effective transition-metal
complex of (S)-1a to give the corresponding ﬁve-membered
cyclic organosilane 20a in moderate yield and with good ee
(53% yield, 70% ee), whereas the use of Pt(dba)2, Ni(cod)2, or
Pd(dba)2 resulted in no reaction. The screening of Rh(I) salts
demonstrated that [Rh(cod)OMe]2 was the most effective pre-
cursor to provide 20a in quantitative yield and with 75% ee.

7. Summary and Outlook
1,10-Phenanthroline is deﬁnitely a powerful chelating reagent
and it has been applied to a broad range of academic research
areas. In contrast, the utilization of this highly coordinative
ligand as a structural motif for chiral ligands has remained a
frontier in the ﬁeld of asymmetric synthesis. We introduced
the axially chiral N,N,O-tridentate phenanthroline ligand (S)-
1. The design of (S)-1 is based on the concept of renovation of
optically active phen derivatives as chiral ligands efﬁcient for
versatile asymmetric metal catalysis. Our endeavor to develop
enantioselective transformations has been devoted to several
enantioselective reactions such as (i) addition of organozinc
reagents to aldehydes,[11] (ii) Zn(II)-catalyzed electrophilic
amination of b-ketoesters with azodicarboxylate,[21] (iii)
Cu(II)-catalyzed a-hydroxylation of oxindole derivatives,[26]
(iv) Ni(II)-catalyzed Michael addition of oxindole derivatives
to MVK,[27] and (v) Rh(I)-catalyzed intramolecular hydrosily-
lation for the construction of chiral silicon stereogenic cen-
ters.[30] Further applications using other metal catalysts are
ongoing to broaden the utility of (S)-1. Furthermore, we are
attempting to realize the unique elaboration of the structural
features of (S)-1, for example, (i) cooperative catalysis with
N,N-bidentate metal complexes and intramolecular hydrogen
bonding provided by phenolic hydroxyl groups and (ii) the
preparation of hetero-bimetallic complexes of (S)-1 having
transition-metal ions coordinated with the N,N-bidentate
phen backbone and oxophilic metals trapped by phenolic
hydroxyl groups. We believe that the chiral phen ligands (S)-1
could display a broad utility for more varied metal catalysts
and transformations in future investigations.

ABSTRACT: The catalytic enantioselective carbonyl addition reaction has long attracted the
interest of chemists because of its synthetic importance. Although many highly enantioselective
reactions have been developed, with few exceptions the reactions are carried out at relatively high
catalyst loadings, making them less practical for scale-up applications. In addition, organometallic
reagents employed as carbon nucleophiles have been limited to those with relatively low reactivity,
such as diorganozincs and arylboronic acids. In an effort to enhance the practicality, a highly active
and enantioselective chiral titanium catalyst system was recently developed in our laboratory,
enabling the enantioselective carbonyl addition reaction to aldehydes using various organometallic
reagents (RM; M 5 MgX, Li, BY2, ZnX, AlMe2) at lower catalyst loadings (5 mol %).
Keywords: alcohols, asymmetric catalysis, asymmetric synthesis, nucleophilic addition, titanium
1. Introduction
1.1. Ligand Acceleration
The addition of organometallic reagents to carbon–heteroa-
tom double bonds in aldehydes, ketones, imines, and so on is a
fundamental reaction in organic synthesis, providing alcohols
and amines with simultaneous carbon–carbon bond forma-
tion. Since the early days, there has been a continuing interest
in synthesizing one of the enantiomers selectively through
these reactions. The ﬁrst attempt was reported in 1940 by Betti
and Lucchi, who examined the Grignard reaction in the pres-
ence of (1)-bornyldimethylamine.[1] Although the results
could not be reproduced later, Cohen and Wright reported an
appreciable selectivity in the Grignard reaction with (2R,3R)-
2,3-dimethoxybutane in 1953.[2] After the late 1960s, many
chemists joined in this research area and made their contribu-
tions. Enantioselectivities higher than 95% ee were reported in
the early 1980s.[3,4] However, all reactions required more than
a stoichiometric amount of chiral additives or modiﬁers. The
catalytic enantioselective carbonyl addition appeared to be far
away from realization at that time.
In the mid-1980s, a breakthrough was made with the dis-
covery of a chiral amino alcohol catalyzed enantioselective
addition of diethylzinc to aldehydes by Oguni et al.[5] and by
the subsequent development of the highly efﬁcient DAIB cata-
lyst 1 by Noyori and co-workers. (Scheme 1).[6] Only 2 mol %
of the amino alcohol is sufﬁcient to achieve high enantioselec-
tivity. In comparison with previously employed Grignard and
organolithium reagents, dialkylzincs are much less reactive.
However, once modiﬁed by the appropriate chiral amino alco-
hols, they are activated to undergo enantioselective addition to
aldehydes, thus realizing the catalytic enantioselective reaction.
Three general requirements were pointed out by Noyori to
realize catalytic enantioselective addition of organometallic
reagents (Scheme 2).[6e] First, chiral ligand L* should have high
selectivity to enable enantioselective addition of a chirally modi-
ﬁed reagent R-M-L*. Second, the ligand should enhance signiﬁ-
cantly the reactivity of the modiﬁed reagent (ligand acceleration)
in such a way that the racemic reaction by unmodiﬁed reagent R-
M is negligible. Finally, at a catalyst turnover step, ligand L*
should be transferred rapidly to R-M to regenerate R-M-L*. It
has been demonstrated by mechanistic study that the DAIB-
catalyzed reaction fulﬁlls these three requirements well.[6c]

1.2. Chiral Titanium Catalysts
In 1989, enantioselective alkylation of a different type was
reported by Yoshioka, Ohno, and co-workers (Scheme 3).[10]
The reaction was carried out with a mixed reagent of diethylzinc
and Ti(OiPr)4 in the presence of chiral bis-triﬂylamide 2. The
mixed reagent generates ethyltitanium species EtTi(OiPr)3
under equilibrium, which undergoes enantioselective addition
by a chiral titanium catalyst derived from 2 and Ti(OiPr)4.[11]
High enantioselectivity was reported even at 0.05 mol % of 2,
demonstrating the high activity of the titanium catalyst.
The discovery of mixed reagents derived from dialkylzincs
and Ti(OiPr)4 led to the subsequent development of titanium
catalysts derived from chiral diols such as TADDOLs[12] and
BINOLs.[13] Taking advantage of the relative ease of modiﬁca-
tion of the steric and electronic nature, extensive work has
been performed for the later ligands (Scheme 4).[14]
The use of organotitanium reagents themselves in the cat-
alytic enantioselective addition was reported in 1994 by See-
bach and co-worker.[15] The titanium reagents were prepared
by treatment of a Grignard reagent or lithium reagent with
ClTi(OiPr)3 and used after the strict removal of inorganic salts
by precipitation and centrifugation (Scheme 5). Otherwise,
enantioselectivities were degraded considerably.

1.4. Highly Active Catalyst System for Practical
Application
The catalytic enantioselective carbonyl addition reaction has long
attracted the interest of chemists because of its synthetic impor-
tance. The studies in this area have resulted in the development of
many highly enantioselective reactions. However, with few excep-
tions, the reactions are carried out at relatively high catalyst load-
ings (5 mol %), making them less practical for scale-up
applications. In addition, organometallic reagents employed as
the carbon nucleophiles have been limited to those with relatively
low reactivity, such as diorganozincs and arylboronic acids. To
enhance the practicality, it is necessary to develop reactions that
can be carried out at lower catalyst loadings and utilize more con-
ventional organometallic reagents of high reactivity, including
Grignard and organolithium reagents. For such practical reac-
tions, a chiral catalyst system with a superb turnover frequency is
essential, that not only exhibits a high degree of ligand accelera-
tion but also rapidly regenerates an active catalyst species at the
turnover step, to overwhelm potential non-catalyzed background
carbonyl addition at the low catalyst loading.
This account describes our recent development of a highly
active chiral titanium catalyst system for the enantioselective
carbonyl addition reaction to aldehydes by using a variety of
organometallic reagents RM (M 5 MgX, Li, BY2, ZnX,
AlMe2) at the lower catalyst loadings.
2. Catalytic Enantioselective Alkylation and
Arylation of Aldehydes Using Grignard Reagents
2.1. Discovery of DPP-BINOL and DPP-H8-BINOL
We found that the introduction of a substituent at the 3-
position of BINOL and H8-BINOL enhances signiﬁcantly the
activity of the resulting chiral titanium catalysts in the enantio-
selective ethylation of aldehydes with the mixed reagent of
Et2Zn and Ti(OiPr)4 (Scheme 7).[19] Although the parent
BINOL was reported to provide the ethylation product in
92% ee at 20 mol % loading,[13b] the reaction employing
2 mol % of the ligand did not reach full conversion even after
5 h and the product was obtained in 85% ee. The decrease in
the enantioselectivity implies that background direct addition
of EtTi(OiPr)3 proceeded concurrently with the ligand-
accelerated enantioselective reaction. Under similar condi-
tions, the reaction with DPP-BINOL 7 (DPP 5 3,5-diphenyl-
phenyl) was accomplished within 1 h to give the product in
93% ee, suggesting the high activity of the titanium catalyst
derived from 7. Examination of a series of BINOL derivatives
revealed that (i) the catalytic activity, assessed by the conversion
after 1 h, is increased by the increase of the size of the substitu-
ent at the 3-position of the ligands (H < PhCC < Br 
Me < Ph, 3,5-Me2-C6H3 < 3,5-Ph2-C6H3); (ii) the enantiose-
lectivity is increased almost in this order; (iii) the introduction
of the 2,6-Me2-C6H3 group of excessive steric hindrance
results in a signiﬁcant decrease in the catalytic activity; (iv) cat-
alytic activity is almost lost by the introduction of the two phe-
nyl groups at the 3- and 30-positions symmetrically; and (v)
enhancement in catalytic activity is also observed for H8-
BINOL derivative 8 (DPP-H8-BINOL), which exhibits the
highest selectivity of 98% ee at 2 mol % in these ligands.

The scope and limitations of the enantioselective alkyla-
tion using Grignard reagents are summarized in Scheme 10.
The reactions of primary alkyl Grignard reagents proceed with
high enantioselectivity to give the corresponding alkylation
products. The yields of the ethylation products are moderate,
owing to the lower stability of the mixed reagent derived from

MeMgCl undergoes smooth addition, but exhibits poor enan-

tert-alkyl Grignard reagents decompose rapidly and cannot be
used. The reaction is applicable to a range of benzaldehyde
derivatives, either with an electron-donating or electron-
withdrawing substituent at the para, meta, and ortho positions,
to afford the corresponding alkylation products in high yields
and high enantioselectivities The reactions of a,b-unsaturated
aldehydes also proceed in an efﬁcient manner to give the corre-
sponding allylic alcohols with high enantioselectivity. Aliphatic
aldehydes are less reactive, affording the corresponding prod-
ucts in lower yields but with high selectivities.

The scope of the catalytic enantioselective arylation reaction

such as ester/amide carbonyls, cyano groups, or bromine
atoms, afford the corresponding functionalized diarylmetha-

Aryl bromides would be preferable precursors for func-
tionalized Grignard reagents in light of their stability, availabil-
ity, and low cost. Although Br/Mg exchange of aryl bromides
is a less efﬁcient process with iPrMgCl, the turbo Grignard

reported to undergo the exchange reaction.[28] The resulting

The Zr-catalyzed carboalumination of terminal alkynes has
been well established as a reliable method for the generation of
b,b-disubstituted vinylaluminum reagents of E geometry.[45]
Despite their accessibility, the vinylaluminum reagents had not
been used in the enantioselective addition to aldehydes, prob-
ably because of their high reactivity that degrades the selectivity
through non-catalyzed background reaction. Taking advantage
of the high activity of the DPP-H8-BINOL-derived titanium
catalyst system, a simple one-pot method was developed begin-
ning with terminal alkynes, including those bearing an oleﬁnic
moiety, a chlorine atom, and a silyloxy group, and aromatic or
heteroaromatic aldehydes (Scheme 25).[46] Thus, disubstituted
vinylaluminum reagent 26 is prepared by the Zr-catalyzed car-
boalumination of a terminal alkyne with Me3Al and treated
with an aldehyde in the presence of Ti(OiPr)4 and DPP-H8-

is generally accomplished within 30 min to provide the corre-
sponding b,b-disubstituted allylic alcohol in high yield and in
good to high enantioselectivity. The reaction is carried out at
relatively dilute conditions (0.01 M for aldehydes) to suppress
the background reaction.

6.2. Origin of High Catalytic Activity
The structures of titanium complexes derived from BINOL
derivatives and Ti(OiPr)4 have been extensively studied in the
solid state by X-ray crystallography and in solution by
NMR.[11b,51] With a 1:2 ligand/Ti ratio, bis-titanium complex
35 has been characterized for BINOL[51a] and H8-BINOL
(Scheme 34).[11b] For the H8-BINOL-derived complex (35;
R,R0 5 H), bond lengths Ti(1)–O(1) and Ti(2)–O(2) (2.11–
2.14 A˚) are longer than Ti(1)–O(2) (1.92–1.93 A˚) and Ti(2)–
O(1) (1.98–1.99 A˚), implying that the titanium complex can
be regarded as the intramolecular aggregate of the two ArO-
Ti(OiPr)3 moieties (350). Inspection of the molecular structure
shows that the substitution of a sterically demanding aryl
group is allowable only at the 3-position of the 1,10-biaryl-
2,20-diolate ligand (i.e., R 5 Ar, R0 5 H). Indeed, we were suc-
cessful in the isolation of the DPP-H8-BINOL derivative (35;
R 5 3,5-diphenylphenyl, R0 5 H) and conﬁrmed the structure
by X-ray analysis.[52] In comparison with the parent H8-
BINOL derivative, the bridging Ti(1)–O(1) and Ti(2)–O(2)
bond distances of the DPP-H8-BINOL derivative are longer
by 0.02 and 0.05 A˚, respectively, implying weakening of intra-
molecular aggregation by the steric constraint around the 3,5-
diphenylphenyl group.

derivatives.[52] The characteristic behavior of the DPP-H8-
BINOL-derived complex is rationalized by the decrease in the
degree of the intramolecular aggregation, facilitating the for-
mation of tetracoordinate bis-titanium intermediate 36, which
might also contribute to the intermolecular iPrO group
exchange through an associative mechanism.
A plausible catalytic cycle for the titanium-catalyzed aryla-
tion is outlined in Scheme 35.[54] First, the aryl group on
ArTi(OiPr)3 is transferred to 35 to generate complex 37.
Recently, the isolation and X-ray crystal analysis of the (S)-
BINOL derivative (37; Ar5 Ph, R5 H) has been reported by
Gau et al.[55] Complex 37 is then coordinated by an aldehyde to
form activated complex 38, which undergoes facile arylation to
give intermediate 39 enantioselectively. In complex 38, substitu-
ent R at the 3-position is located distal to the reaction center,
which is consistent with the fact that the substituents are not inﬂu-
ential on the inherent enantioselectivity of the 3-aryl H8-BINOL
derivatives. Complex 39 then undergoes aryl group transfer with
ArTi(OiPr)3, giving rise to the formation of product titanium alk-
oxide 40 with simultaneous regeneration of complex 37.

7. Conclusion
It was demonstrated that chiral titanium complexes derived
from BINOL derivatives bearing a sterically demanding aryl
group at the 3-position exhibit high catalytic activity in the
enantioselective alkylation, vinylation, arylation, and heteroar-
ylation of aldehydes. Various organometallic reagents, includ-
ing Grignard, organolithium, organoboron, organozinc, and
organoaluminum reagents, can be employed as the carbon
nucleophile. The enantioselective addition of functionalized
alkyl and aryl groups is possible using appropriately function-
alized organometallic reagents. The organometallic reagents
are used with Ti(OiPr)4 to generate the organotitanium deriva-
tives as the reacting species. Although the organotitanium spe-
cies are reactive towards the carbonyl group, the activity of the
chiral titanium catalyst is high enough to overwhelm the back-
ground racemic reaction. Taking advantage of the high catalyst
activity, the reactions are carried out at low catalyst loadings of
less than 5 mol %. In some instances, 0.5 mol % of the catalyst
is sufﬁcient to obtain high enantioselectivities. Despite low cat-
alyst loadings, the reactions proceed rapidly and are accom-
plished within several hours.
The present results suggest that, in the catalytic enantioselec-
tive addition reaction, the reacting organometallic species is not
necessarily non-reactive or less reactive towards a carbonyl group,
provided that the catalytic pathway is fast enough to override the
background racemic reaction.[56] To realize a catalyst system with
high turnover frequency, rate enhancement is indispensable both
for the carbonyl addition step and for the catalyst turnover step of
the catalytic cycle. The use of reactive organometallic reagents
might be advantageous in accelerating the addition step. Rapid
ligand exchange often observed in metal alkoxide and aryloxide
complexes can be exploited to accelerate the catalyst turnover
step. The survey of new catalyst systems based on metals other
than titanium is promising for the future development of catalytic
enantioselective carbonyl additions of practical utility.

Carboxylation Reactions with Carbon
Dioxide Using N-Heterocyclic Carbene-
Copper Catalysts

Abstract: The development of versatile catalyst systems and new transformations for the
utilization of carbon dioxide (CO2) is of great interest and significance. This Personal Account
reviews our studies on the exploration of the reactions of CO2 with various substrates by the use
of
N-heterocyclic
carbene
(NHC)-copper
catalysts.
The
carboxylation
of
organoboron
compounds gave access to a wide range of carboxylic acids with excellent functional group
tolerance. The C� H bond carboxylation with CO2 emerged as a straightforward protocol for the
preparation of a series of aromatic carboxylic esters and butenoates from simple substrates. The
hydrosilylation of CO2 with hydrosilanes provided an efficient method for the synthesis of silyl
formate on gram scale. The hydrogenative or alkylative carboxylation of alkynes, ynamides and
allenamides yielded useful α,β-unsaturated carboxylic acids and α,β-dehydro amino acid esters.
The boracarboxylation of alkynes or aldehydes afforded the novel lithium cyclic boralactone or
boracarbonate products, respectively. The NHC-copper catalysts generally featured excellent
functional group compatibility, broad substrate scope, high efficiency, and high regio- and
stereoselectivity. The unique electronic and steric properties of the NHC-copper units also
enabled the isolation and structural characterization of some key intermediates for better
understanding of the catalytic reaction mechanisms.
Keywords: alkynes, carbon dioxide, carboxylation, copper catalysts, N-heterocyclic carbene
1. Introduction
The efficient utilization of sustainable feedstocks for the
production of value-added chemicals is of great importance. In
recent years, carbon dioxide (CO2) has been attracting
considerable
attention
for
being
used
as
an
abundant,
inexpensive, and renewable one-carbon (C1) building block in
organic synthesis.[1] Various catalyst systems, especially tran-
sition metal catalysts, have been developed for the trans-
formation of CO2 into carboxylic acids and their derivatives,
which are privileged structural units in biologically active
molecules and synthetically useful fine chemicals.[2] Despite
these progresses, the use of cheap and well-defined catalysts for
achieving efficient and selective CO2 conversion still represents
a persistent challenge. On the other hand, the designing of
new routes for incorporating CO2 into valuable compounds
with novel structures remains a formidable opportunity for the
applicable transformation of CO2.
We have developed a series of carboxylation reactions of
CO2 with various organic substrates by using N-heterocyclic
carbene
(NHC)-copper
catalysts.
The
reaction
generally
proceeded through the facile insertion of CO2 into an NHC-
organocopper species generated in situ in a catalytic circle.
Various
types
of
carboxylic
acids
or
esters
have
been
synthesized from efficient and selective conversions of simple
and readily available starting materials. Remarkably, the
boracarboxylation of alkynes and aldehydes with CO2 and
diboron reagents could be selectively achieved to afford unique
lithium cyclic boralactone and boracarbonate products with
novel molecular structures, respectively. The NHC-copper
platform enabled isolation and structural characterization of
some key intermediates, thus providing important insights into
the mechanistic details. This account mainly summarizes our
studies on NHC-copper-catalyzed carboxylation reactions with
CO2. Related studies by other groups are also described briefly.
2. Catalytic Carboxylation of Organoboron
Compounds
2.1. Carboxylation of Aryl- and Alkenylboronic Esters
Due to its high thermodynamic stability and low reactivity,
the use of CO2 as a C1 building block for the formation of
C� C bonds usually requires highly nucleophilic organometallic
reagents, such as alkyllithium compounds and Grignard
reagents. However, sensitive functional groups are generally
not tolerated in the presence of these strong organometallic
nucleophiles.
Transition-metal-catalyzed
addition of
carbon nucleo-
philes, in particular, less nucleophilic organoboron com-
pounds, to CO2 has attracted much attention.[3] Iwasawa and
co-workers have reported the Rh(I)-catalyzed carboxylation of
aryl- and alkenylboronic esters with CO2, which is potentially
useful for the synthesis of valuable carboxylic acid derivatives
because of the accessibility of various functionalized organo-
boronic esters.[4] However, the Rh catalyst systems showed
only limited tolerance toward some reactive functional groups,
such as bromo, iodo, and vinyl groups. Besides, information

In 2008, we have reported an excellent NHC� Cu(I)
catalyst system for the carboxylation of aryl- and alkenylbor-

tional group compatibility, but also afforded structurally
characterizable active catalyst species.[5]
Systematic screening revealed that the isolated NHC� Cu
(I) chloride complex [(IPr)CuCl][6] (Figure 1) shows high
activity for the carboxylation reaction. The use of a less steric
demanding NHC ligand, such as IMes·HCl, led to a lower
yield of the carboxylation product. The reaction could not
proceed in the absence of CuCl or an NHC ligand or KOtBu
under the same conditions.
Various aryl- and alkenylboronic esters could be used as
suitable substrates under the optimized reaction conditions
(Table 1). The efficiency of these reactions was not affected by
either electron-donating or electron-withdrawing groups on
the substrates. Notably, a variety of reactive functional groups,
such as vinyl, epoxy, carbonyl, halide, and propargyl ether,
were tolerated. The reactions of boronic esters with sterically
demanding aryl groups, heteroaromatic derivatives, and even
alkenyl
substituents
took
place
selectively
to
give
the
corresponding carboxylation products in high yields.
Sequential stoichiometric reactions of NHC-copper com-
plexes were examined to gain some information on the
reaction mechanism (Scheme 1). Under a N2 atmosphere,
[(IPr)CuCl] reacted with 1 equivalent of KOtBu in THF at
room temperature, giving a known copper alkoxide complex

A possible catalytic cycle for the NHC-copper catalyzed
carboxylation of organoboronic esters with CO2 was proposed
(Scheme 2). The organocopper complex C would be generated
from the reaction of an organoboronic ester with the alkoxide
complex [(IPr)Cu(OtBu)], which was formed from the meta-

intermediate D, which reacted with KOtBu to release RCO2K
and regenerate [(IPr)Cu(OtBu)]. After hydrolysis with HCl,
the potassium salt was converted to the final product RCO2H.
A CuI/bisoxazoline catalyst system reported by Iwasawa
also shew good functional group tolerability for the carbox-

2.2. Carboxylation of Alkylboranes
Compared to the carboxylation of aryl- and alkenylboronic
esters, the reaction of alkylboranes with CO2 is challenging
because the generation of a transition metal alkyl intermediate
showing appropriate stability and high activity towards CO2
from an alkylborane is more difficult. Besides, although
alkylboranes have been widely used as substrates in transition
metal-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions,[9] the isolation and
characterization of the intermediate in the transmetallation of
an organoboron compound to a transition metal is rare.[10]
Thus,

A variety of reactive functional groups, such as propargyl,

compatible with the present reaction conditions. Moreover,
synthetically useful protecting groups, such as silyl ether, N-

terminal alkene bearing a tertiary substituent and even styrene
with 9-BBN and CO2 afforded the corresponding products in

catalytic cycle, several sequential stoichiometric reactions of
NHC-copper complexes were examined (Scheme 3). When

instantly. X-ray crystallographic studies revealed that E is
formed by the interaction between the oxygen atom in [IPrCu
(OMe)] and the boron atom in alkylborane. When a solution
of E in THF was exposed to a CO2 atmosphere at 70°C, the
carboxylate complex F was isolated in 90% yield. Alterna-
tively, F could also be obtained by the one-pot reaction of

was found that [IPrCu(OMe)], E and F all showed high
catalytic activity for the carboxylation reaction under the
standard conditions. The isolation of the novel copper-
methoxide/alkylborane adduct complex E has provided im-
portant information of the mechanistic details. Although the
interaction between a basic metal alkoxide or hydroxide with
an organoboron substrate has been thought critically important
in
related
transition
metal-catalyzed
cross-coupling
reactions,[13] the structure of E demonstrates unambiguously
that such bonding interaction does exist for the first time.
An analogous carboxylation of alkylboranes with CO2
catalyzed by a CuOAc/1,10-phenanthroline catalyst system

4. Hydrosilylation of CO2
Various transition metal catalysts have been reported for the
hydrogenation of CO2 with H2 for the synthesis of formic
acid.[28] Because this transformation is thermodynamically
unfavorable, it generally requires relatively high pressure of
CO2 and H2. Alternatively, the hydrosilylation of CO2 with a
hydrosilane is thermodynamically favorable, which could serve
as a promising route for the preparation of silyl formates from
CO2.[29] However, the catalytic activities of reported transition
metal catalysts for hydrosilylation of CO2 need to be
improved.
It was reported that the combination of Cu(OAc)2·H2O/
1,2-bis(diphenylphosphino)benzene
efficiently
catalyze
the
one-pot
synthesis
of
formic
acid
from
CO2
and
hydrosilanes.[30] Because silyl formates can be used as formylat-
ing agents in organic synthesis and as a building block for
silicon-based materials, the exploration of efficient catalyst
systems for the direct synthesis of silyl formates from the
hydrosilylation of CO2 is of great significance. We have
reported a copper-catalyzed hydrosilylation of CO2 for the
synthesis of silyl formate in multi-gram quantity under mild
conditions.[31] It was found that the hydrosilylation of CO2
(1 atm) with (EtO)3SiH (0.15 mmol) at 100°C was completed
within 1 h in the presence of 0.0025 mmol of [(IPr)Cu
(OtBu)]. The less sterically demanding catalyst [(IMes)Cu
(OtBu)] gave a lower yield under the same conditions. When
the hydrosilylation reaction was carried out at 60°C, high
conversion of (EtO)3SiH was also achieved in 1 h. Even at
room temperature, the reaction could be completed in a longer
reaction time (10 h).
To show the practical usefulness of the current reaction,
the hydrosilylation of CO2 with (EtO)3SiH on a 50 mmol
scale was carried out under neat conditions with 0.01 mol% of
[(IPr)Cu(OtBu)] (Scheme 7). Triethoxysilyl formate was gen-
erated in 75% yield in 6 h, showing a TON of 7489 and a
TOF of 1248 h� 1. The resulting triethoxysilyl formate product
was readily isolated in 71% yield by distillation.
As reported previously, the reaction of [(IPr)Cu(OtBu)]
with (EtO)3SiH at room temperature generated instantly a
copper hydride complex.[7] It’s in situ reaction with CO2 at
room temperature afforded the corresponding copper formate
complex [(IPr)CuO2CH] K in 81% yield (Scheme 8). The
instant formation of [(IPr)CuH] was confirmed by 1H NMR
analysis when adding 1.0 equivalent of (EtO)3SiH into a
solution of complex K in benzene. The isolated formate
complex K was also proved to be an efficient catalyst for the
hydrosilylation of CO2. As revealed by X-ray diffraction study,
the formate unit in complex K is connected to the Cu atom in
a η1-bonding mode. In contrast, the formate unit is bonded to
the Cu atom through both two oxygen atoms in the
triphosphine-ligated copper formate complexes.[32] The η1-
bonding mode in complex K may due to the unique steric
hindrance and electron donating property of the NHC ligand,
which may account for the high activity of this catalytic
system.
In a possible reaction mechanism (Scheme 9), the initial
reaction of NHC-copper alkoxide complex with (EtO)3SiH
generates an active copper hydride. The following insertion of
CO2 into the Cu� H bond affords the corresponding copper
formate complex L. The final reaction of (EtO)3SiH with the
copper formate L releases the desired silyl formate product and
regenerates the copper hydride catalyst.

Me2Zn, both Et2Zn and Bu2Zn are also suitable for this
reaction without the observation of β-hydride elimination,
which is often observed in the related catalyst systems.[44] In all
cases, the reactions took place in a syn manner, introducing the
alkyl group to the β-position of the ynamides and the carboxyl
group to the α-position selectively. Ynamides bearing 2-
oxazolidinone, pyrrolidine-2-one, and Evans’ chiral oxazolidin-
2-one moieties were found to be good substrates in this
catalytic alkylative carboxylation reaction, affording the desired
products in high yields when different kinds of dialkylzinc
reagents were used. It was also found that acyclic Boc-
protected ynamides are suitable substrates for ethylative and
butylative carboxylation with Et2Zn and Bu2Zn, giving the
desired products in good yields, while Me2Zn is not applicable
to these acyclic substrates.
A possible reaction mechanism for this copper-catalyzed
alkylative carboxylation of ynamides with CO2 and dialkylzinc
reagents is illustrated in Scheme 14. The initial transmetalla-
tion between [(IPr)CuCl] and R2Zn would form an alkylcop-
per species [(IPr)CuR)]. The carbonyl group of ynamide works
as a directing group in the following carbocupration step,
generating the alkenylcopper intermediate R regioselectively.
